posting-consistently-when-motivation-is-.title: Posting consistently on days I don't feel like it
posting-consistently-when-motivation-is-.excerpt: Some weeks the content calendar is the only reason a post goes out at all. Here's what actually keeps it going when the enthusiasm doesn't show up.
posting-consistently-when-motivation-is-.content:
The honest version: most posts don't come from inspiration. They come from a half-built list of topics I add to whenever an idea shows up, so that on a low-energy day there's still something waiting instead of a blank page.

The backlog is the whole system

Whenever I notice something genuinely confusing in a lecture, or a concept clicks for me in an unexpected way, it goes on the list immediately — even just as a one-line topic. That list is doing more work than any burst of motivation ever has.

What a low-effort post actually looks like

Sometimes it's just a clean version of my own study notes, lightly designed. Not every post needs to be a big production. Lowering the bar for what counts as "good enough to post" is most of what keeps the schedule alive.

Why consistency matters more than quality, some weeks

A mediocre post that goes out keeps the account alive and keeps me in the habit. A perfect post that never gets finished does neither. I'd rather ship something slightly rough on schedule than sit on a "someday" masterpiece.

A few rules I keep for myself

  • If an idea shows up, it goes on the list before I forget it, even if it is only a few words.
  • One small post is better than a perfect plan.
  • If a week goes badly, I do not try to "catch up" — I just pick up the next topic on the list.

What I'd tell someone starting out

Do not wait to feel inspired. Build a list, lower the bar for "good enough", and give yourself permission to be rough. Consistency is built from ordinary days, and the audience is usually far more forgiving than you are. The habit of showing up matters more than any single post, and it is the part you can actually control.

It also helps to separate the two jobs: choosing a topic and making the post are different tasks, and doing them on different days keeps a low-energy day from becoming an empty one.

What a bad week taught me

There was a week when exams, work shifts and a flat mood all landed together, and I posted nothing for six days. I expected the account to fall apart. It did not. People were still reading older posts, and the backlog was still waiting when I came back. That showed me something I had not believed before: a quiet week is not a disaster, it is just a gap. What matters is the restart, so I keep the restart small. One topic from the list, one clean image, one short caption, and I am back in the rhythm without any speech to myself about discipline.

why-i-post-anatomy-mnemonics.title: Why I post anatomy mnemonics instead of just studying quietly
why-i-post-anatomy-mnemonics.excerpt: Making a graphic out of something I'm learning forces me to actually understand it well enough to explain it. That's the real reason, not the follower count.
why-i-post-anatomy-mnemonics.content:
People assume the content comes after the studying — learn it first, then simplify it for a post. Honestly, half the time it's the other way around. I don't fully understand something until I've tried to explain it in one image with almost no words.

The Feynman thing, basically

There's a well-known idea that you don't really know a concept until you can teach it simply. Making a graphic is a harsher version of that test than just talking, because a graphic has no room for hand-waving. If I can't fit the cranial nerves mnemonic onto one clean image, it usually means I don't actually have it memorized properly yet — I'm still leaning on notes.

What surprised me about the audience

I expected mostly classmates. Instead a good chunk of engagement comes from people further along than me — working nurses, other allied health students — correcting small details or adding context I didn't have. The comments have quietly become one of my better study resources.

The actual workflow

Pick a concept I'm reviewing anyway. Try to compress it. Fail the first attempt, usually. Simplify again. Post it. The studying and the content-making aren't two separate activities anymore — they're the same pass through the material, done properly once instead of twice.

What this means for how I study

Because I treat every graphic as a test of my own understanding, I now study with a question in mind: could I fit this on one clean image? If not, I go back to the notes. That single question has done more for my revision than any timetable, because it forces me to find out what I really know and what I am only recognising.

A suggestion if you are a student

You do not need an audience to try this. Pick one topic from this week and try to explain it on a single page, with as few words as possible. If the page comes out cleanly, you understand it. If it does not, you have just found your next revision task, and you found it cheaply.

Why mnemonics specifically

A mnemonic is the simplest form of compression: a whole list squeezed into a sentence you can carry in your head. That makes it perfect for anatomy, where the lists are long and the exam questions are blunt. I also like that a good mnemonic is a little ridiculous, because the silly ones are the ones people remember. When a student comments that a sentence from a graphic came back to them during a test, that is the best feedback I can imagine, because it means the image did its job at the exact moment it was needed.

a-day-at-the-cyber-cafe.title: A day at the cyber café
a-day-at-the-cyber-cafe.excerpt: Printing, typing, KRA returns, and teaching someone's grandmother to use email — a normal shift at JULO Enterprises.
a-day-at-the-cyber-cafe.content:
JULO Enterprises' cyber café is where I spend most weekdays right now — a temporary stop while I look for theatre practice roles properly. It's a smaller job than "theatre technologist," but it's kept me sharp in a different way.

What actually happens in a shift

A typical day is printing and photocopying, typing up documents for people who'd rather not, and walking someone through their eCitizen or KRA returns filing step by step. Somewhere in there, someone's grandmother needs help checking her email for the first time, and that's usually the best part of the day.

Why it's not wasted time

Every machine that jams, every browser that won't cooperate, every "why won't this print" — it's small-scale troubleshooting, over and over. It's the same instinct I use editing a video for Instagram at home, just with a paper jam instead of a bad take.

The overlap

Patience under a queue of impatient customers isn't that different from patience in a sterile field. Different stakes, same discipline: stay calm, work the problem, don't skip a step because you're in a hurry.

The customers who stick with you

There's a woman who comes in every month to file her returns, and every month she apologizes for "not being good with computers" before I've even said anything. I've stopped correcting her mid-task and started just narrating what I'm doing as I go — turns out most people don't want to be handled, they want to understand, even a little. A few of them now type their own passwords instead of handing me their phone. That's the actual win, not the transaction fee.

What it's taught me about patience

Cyber café patience is a specific muscle. It's not the dramatic kind — nobody's yelling, mostly. It's the fortieth time explaining that a photo won't attach to an email because the file's too large, said in the same tone as the first time. I didn't have that muscle before this job. I do now, and I don't think it's a coincidence that it's the same muscle theatre work asks for.

The part that surprised me

I expected this job to feel like a pure delay — something to get through before "real" work starts. Instead it's quietly taught me how ordinary people actually interact with technology and bureaucracy, which is useful information for someone who's about to spend a career explaining medical things to worried people. Different subject matter, same skill.

If you are thinking of a similar job

Expect repetition, and expect to learn from it. Learn the common problems and their fixes, keep calm with people who are anxious about technology, and be honest when you do not know the answer. Explaining as you work builds trust, and it makes people more confident next time.

life-after-college-the-gap-nobody-talks-.title: Life after college: the gap nobody talks about
life-after-college-the-gap-nobody-talks-.excerpt: Nobody warns you about the strange, formless stretch between finishing your studies and actually starting the career you trained for.
life-after-college-the-gap-nobody-talks-.content:
I'm technically done with the hard academic part of my diploma, and I still haven't started working in theatre. That gap — trained but not yet practicing — is a specific kind of limbo nobody really prepares you for.

The waiting isn't empty, it just feels like it

Right now I'm at a cyber café, not a theatre. On paper that looks like a detour. In practice it's rent money, routine, and proof I can hold down responsibility while I wait for the right opening.

Comparison is the real enemy here

Classmates post placements, some already working, and it's easy to read that as being behind. I've had to keep reminding myself that a placement date isn't a scoreboard — it's just timing, and timing isn't the same as worth.

What I'm doing with the gap

Building things. This website, the content on Instagram and TikTok, the books. Not because they replace theatre work, but because "waiting" doesn't have to mean "idle." The gap is real. It doesn't have to be wasted.

What the gap actually costs

Nobody warns you that the gap has a real financial and emotional cost, not just a psychological one. Rent doesn't pause because your placement hasn't started. Family expectations don't pause either — there's always a cousin's wedding where someone asks, kindly but pointedly, "so what are you doing now?" I've had to get comfortable answering that honestly instead of dressing it up.

Talking to others in the same gap

A few classmates and I check in with each other every couple of weeks, mostly just to say "still nothing yet, still fine." It sounds small, but knowing the gap is shared rather than a personal failing changes how it feels day to day. I'd recommend that to anyone in the same spot — find the other people also waiting, even if none of you can fix the waiting itself.

What I'd tell someone entering this gap now

Pick one thing you can control and put real effort into it while the placement clock is out of your hands. For me that's been this website, the content, the books. It won't replace theatre work. It just means the gap has something to show for itself besides waiting.

A short list I come back to

  • The gap is temporary, even when it does not feel like it.
  • Keep skills fresh and documents ready.
  • Stay in touch with the people who know your work.
  • Ask for help early instead of late.

None of this makes the waiting easy. It just makes it less empty.

what-i-wish-i-knew-before-cyber-cafe-job.title: What I wish I knew before taking the cyber café job
what-i-wish-i-knew-before-cyber-cafe-job.excerpt: I took it as a stopgap. A year in, it's taught me more about patience and small-business reality than I expected from a 'temporary' job.
what-i-wish-i-knew-before-cyber-cafe-job.content:
I said yes to this job expecting it to be forgettable — something to fill the gap before theatre practice starts, nothing more. A year in, that assumption was wrong in a few specific ways.

It's a real business, with real math

Watching JULO Enterprises run day to day taught me things about margins, slow seasons, and customer trust that no classroom covers. Printing costs, toner, downtime — all of it adds up in ways that are invisible until you're the one watching the numbers.

The skill that transferred most

Reading what a customer actually needs, not just what they said. Someone asking to "print this form" sometimes means they need help filling it out correctly first. That kind of reading-between-the-lines turned out to be exactly the same skill I now use figuring out which part of an anatomy topic is actually confusing someone versus which part they just haven't asked about yet.

What I'd tell past me

Stop treating it as a placeholder. A job you're mentally discarding teaches you less than one you're actually paying attention to, even if it's not the job you want long-term.

Small lessons that surprised me

Customers remember how you made them feel more than how fast you were. Patience is a skill you can practise, and a queue is a good gym for it. A job that looks routine hides a lot of judgment: what to say, when to step in, and when to let someone try for themselves.

If you are about to take a "temporary" job

Treat it as training. Ask what the owner pays attention to, learn the numbers, notice what the regular customers need, and write down anything you would do differently. You may not stay forever, but the habits you build there will follow you into whatever comes next, including a clinical career.

The part about people

Most of the job is not the machines at all. It is the person standing at the counter who is worried about a deadline, a form that must be submitted today, or a document they do not quite understand. Learning to stay calm for them, explain without talking down and never make anyone feel foolish for asking has been the quiet training I did not expect. It has already changed how I speak to classmates I tutor, and I am sure it will change how I speak to patients and colleagues once I am in theatre. A counter is a surprisingly good classroom for bedside manner.

scrubbing-in-what-attachment-taught-me.title: Scrubbing in: what my theatre attachment taught me
scrubbing-in-what-attachment-taught-me.excerpt: Four c-section cases, a WHO checklist, and the kind of focus you can't fake — notes from Likuyani Sub-County Hospital.
scrubbing-in-what-attachment-taught-me.content:
Between February and April 2024 I did my field attachment at Likuyani Sub-County Hospital's theatre department. On paper it's a line on a CV. In practice it's where the diploma stopped being theory.

The checklist that never gets skipped

The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist sounds like paperwork until you watch a whole theatre team pause, together, before the first incision — every single time, no exceptions, no matter how routine the case looks. That's the moment it clicked for me: precision isn't about being tense, it's about never letting "routine" become an excuse to skip a step.

Four cases, and counting

I scrubbed in on a handful of caesarean section cases and observed several more, on top of sterilisation and instrument checks between procedures. None of it is glamorous. All of it is the difference between a theatre that runs and one that doesn't.

What stuck with me

Getting commended for discipline and time management meant more than I expected — not because I needed the praise, but because it confirmed something: the quiet, careful, unnoticed work is the actual job. I'm still waiting to start practicing properly, but that attachment is the reason I know this is the right field.

The case I still think about

One of the caesarean sections ran longer than expected — nothing went wrong exactly, but everything took more concentration than usual, and by the end my hands were tired in a way I hadn't felt before. What stuck with me wasn't the difficulty, it was watching the whole team adjust in real time without anyone raising their voice once. That's a specific kind of professionalism I hadn't seen up close before, and it reset what I thought "staying calm under pressure" actually looks like.

What the supervisors actually watch for

I assumed clinical skill was the main thing being assessed. It matters, but from what I could tell, just as much attention went to whether I showed up on time, whether I asked when unsure instead of guessing, and whether I could be trusted with a repetitive task without cutting corners once it stopped feeling new. Those are teachable, unlike raw talent — which made the whole attachment feel less like an audition and more like a real apprenticeship.

Going back, eventually

I haven't started full theatre practice yet — that's still ahead of me. But this attachment is the reference point I keep returning to whenever the cyber café job makes the actual goal feel far away. It happened. It was real. It's still coming.

What I would tell a student about to start

Arrive early, ask questions, and write down what you saw the same day. Do not be embarrassed by what you do not know yet; the people teaching you were beginners once too. The attitude that earns trust is simple: careful, honest and willing to repeat the same task properly as many times as it takes.

writing-five-books-at-once.title: Why I'm writing five books at once (badly, on purpose)
writing-five-books-at-once.excerpt: A memoir, a theatre-attachment account, a study companion, a diploma survival guide, and a slow philosophical one. All at once. Progress over polish.
writing-five-books-at-once.content:
I have five different manuscripts open right now, in five different states of unfinished. That's not a productivity hack — I just can't help chasing an idea the moment it shows up, even if I'm halfway through a different one.

What's actually on the desk

A Life Becoming is the memoir — faith, family, figuring myself out, written honestly rather than heroically. Notes from the Sterile Field is a first-hand account of training as a Perioperative Theatre Technologist — the attachment, the mistakes, the cases that stayed with me. The Theatre Companion is turning my own anatomy mnemonics and safety checklists into an actual reference book, built directly from the content I already make. The Smooth Sailing is a survival handbook for anyone in a demanding clinical diploma program. And Correction is the odd one out — a slow, personal book about unresolved questions, more philosophical than the rest.

Why they cluster around the same thing

Unlike an earlier, more scattered list I used to keep, all five of these actually talk to each other now. The memoir and Correction cover who I am becoming. Notes from the Sterile Field and The Theatre Companion cover what I'm becoming it as — a theatre technologist. The Smooth Sailing sits between the two, since surviving the diploma is part of both stories.

The plan

No release dates yet, and I'm not promising any. This page updates as any of them get closer to something shareable.

How I keep five projects from collapsing

I do not try to work on all five every day. I follow whichever one is pulling at me, and I keep a short note on each so I can re-enter it later without rereading everything. The notes are not impressive; they are only a line or two about where I stopped and what comes next. That small habit makes it possible to leave a manuscript for weeks and still return to it.

What I have learned so far

Unfinished writing is not wasted writing. Each draft has made the others clearer, and the ones about theatre technology have sharpened how I explain things on this site. If you also have more ideas than time, write them down anyway, and let the strongest one ask for your attention.

Why I keep the list public

Writing about the books here is a small way of keeping myself honest. It is easy to let a project disappear quietly when nobody knows it exists. Naming each one, even as unfinished, gives it a place to live and gives me a gentle reminder that it is waiting. I would rather have a visible, slow-moving list than a perfect plan that nobody, including me, ever looks at again.

why-i-write-books-nobody-asked-for.title: Why I write books nobody asked for
why-i-write-books-nobody-asked-for.excerpt: No one requested a memoir or a theatre-training account from me. I'm writing them anyway — because they're the two things I actually have to say.
why-i-write-books-nobody-asked-for.content:
There's no publisher waiting, no audience demanding these books. I write them because the alternative — not writing them — feels worse than the discomfort of writing badly toward something.

It's not about being read

Some of this is just for me: working out what I actually think about faith, family, and my own path, on paper instead of in my head where it's easier to avoid. That's A Life Becoming and Correction, really — the same question asked two different ways.

The theatre-technology ones are different

Notes from the Sterile Field and The Theatre Companion exist because I noticed how much of what I'm learning — the field attachment reality, the mnemonics, the checklists — either lives only in scattered notes or gets taught the hard, slow way. If I don't write it down properly, that's not guaranteed to happen for the next student either.

Unfinished is still worth something

None of the five are done. I've made peace with that. A drawer with five honest unfinished manuscripts still beats an empty one.

What I get out of it anyway

Writing slows my thinking down enough to notice it. A worry that feels huge in my head often turns out to be two clear sentences once it is on paper, and a vague opinion often turns out not to be mine at all. That is useful whether anybody ever reads the result.

For anyone with their own unasked-for project

Give it a small, regular slot in your week and protect it. Do not wait for permission, an audience or a finished plan. Start with the page in front of you, and let the structure arrive later. If it eventually helps someone else, that is a bonus on top of what it already did for you.

The patience it teaches

A blog post can be written and published in an evening. A book cannot, and that difference is the point. Working on something that takes months, with no instant reaction, trains a patience I do not get from anything else in my life. I learn to sit with a half-formed chapter, to throw away pages that sound clever but say nothing, and to come back the next morning and see what is actually there. Those habits spill into my studying, my content and even my work at the cyber café, where being patient with a slow printer or a confused customer is the same muscle. Even if no one reads a single page, that training is already paid for.

things-nobody-tells-you-about-content-cr.title: Things nobody tells you about making educational content
things-nobody-tells-you-about-content-cr.excerpt: It's slower, lonelier, and more technical than it looks from the outside — and also more useful to my own learning than I expected going in.
things-nobody-tells-you-about-content-cr.content:
From the outside it looks like: think of an idea, make a nice graphic, post it, done. From the inside there's a lot more friction than that, most of it invisible unless you're doing it yourself.

The design part takes longer than the knowledge part

I usually know the anatomy or theatre concept cold before I start designing. The layout — what to cut, what order to present it in, how to make it scannable in three seconds on someone's phone — takes longer than reviewing the actual medical content did.

It's quieter than people assume

There's no team, no editorial calendar meeting, no one to bounce an idea off before it goes out. Just me deciding whether a post is ready. That's freeing some days and just lonely on others.

The part that actually helped my studying

Explaining something publicly, even to a small audience, raises the stakes on getting it right in a way that private study notes never do. I fact-check harder for a post than I ever did for an assignment. That habit has quietly made me more careful generally.

What I do now because of it

I plan the layout before I open a design tool, I check every fact against my notes and textbook, and I keep a list of corrections people send me so I can fix them openly. I also stopped measuring a post only by its numbers. A graphic that one student says helped them is worth more to me than a spike of views that taught nobody anything.

If you want to try making content

Start with one concept you have just learned, and make one clear graphic. Show it to a classmate before you post it. If they understand it in a few seconds, you are on the right track. Repeat that loop, and the quality improves without any big plan.

Corrections are part of the job

Sooner or later someone will point out a mistake, and the first reaction is always a small drop in the stomach. I have learned to treat each correction as a free reviewer who read my work more carefully than I did. I check the point, fix the graphic if they are right, and thank them in the comments so others can see that corrections are welcome. For medical education this matters even more, because a confident graphic that is wrong can mislead someone studying late at night. Being willing to be corrected in public is the thing that makes people trust the content over time, far more than never making a mistake at all.

balancing-diploma-job-and-content.title: Balancing the diploma, the cyber café job, and content — honestly
balancing-diploma-job-and-content.excerpt: I don't have this figured out. Here's what the actual week looks like, including the parts that don't fit neatly.
balancing-diploma-job-and-content.content:
Update: I graduated in December 2025. I wrote this while I was still in the diploma; the same rotation now applies to the cyber café, the job search and content.

People sometimes ask how I "manage" all three — the diploma, the job, the content. The honest answer is imperfectly, and some weeks one of them quietly loses.

What a real week looks like

Cyber café shifts take priority because they're scheduled and someone's counting on me being there. Diploma coursework comes next because it has hard deadlines. Content gets whatever's left — which some weeks is a lot, and other weeks is one rushed post on a Sunday night.

The trade-off I've made peace with

Content is the one I let slip first when something has to give, and I used to feel guilty about that. I don't anymore — it's the one thing on the list that doesn't have someone else depending on it showing up on time. That makes it the safest place to absorb the pressure.

What actually keeps all three alive

Not balance, exactly — more like rotation. Something is always getting less attention than it deserves. The goal isn't to fix that, it's to make sure it's never the same thing two weeks running.

Rules that keep the rotation fair

  • Things with deadlines or with other people depending on me come first.
  • Content gets a fixed slot instead of "whenever I have time", even if the slot is short.
  • If one area gets squeezed, it gets a catch-up slot the next week.
  • Rest is not optional; it is part of the schedule.

A note on guilt

Guilt is usually a signal that a value is being neglected, not that I am failing. When I feel it, I ask which of my commitments needs attention this week and adjust, instead of punishing myself. That small change has made the whole arrangement easier to sustain.

What I stopped pretending

I stopped pretending that I can give one hundred per cent to everything at once. Some days the honest plan is to attend class, do my shift, eat properly and sleep, and call that a win. Content waits, and so does the polishing of notes. When I allowed myself to say that out loud, the pressure dropped and, strangely, the work got better, because I was no longer doing three things badly out of fear of dropping one. If you are juggling something similar, decide in advance what slips first, tell the people who depend on you, and let the plan be good enough rather than perfect.

A small habit that helps

Every Sunday I write down the one thing in each area that must happen next week. Three lines, no more. It takes two minutes and removes most of the dread, because nothing important is left floating in my head.

what-nobody-tells-you-about-diploma-prog.title: What nobody tells you about diploma programs in Kenya
what-nobody-tells-you-about-diploma-prog.excerpt: A diploma looks like a shortcut on paper. In practice, it comes with its own specific set of invisible costs.
what-nobody-tells-you-about-diploma-prog.content:
Diploma programs get talked about as the practical, faster route compared to a degree. Nobody mentions the parts that make it its own particular kind of hard.

The respect gap

There's a quiet hierarchy some people apply — degree over diploma, regardless of what the diploma actually trains you to do with your hands. I've had to stop measuring my worth against that scale.

The practical load is real

Field attachments, practical assessments, hands-on hours that a purely theoretical course doesn't ask for. My Perioperative Theatre Technology diploma packed a full hospital attachment into an already tight timeline.

What made it worth it

I came out knowing how to actually do the job, not just describe it in an exam. That's the trade — less prestige talk, more actual competence. I'll take that trade again.

The comparison trap

It's easy to end up measuring a diploma against a degree on the degree's terms — years spent, titles earned — and lose every time on that scale, because it's the wrong scale. A diploma in a hands-on field like this one is measured in competence, not prestige, and those are genuinely different metrics that don't convert cleanly into each other.

What the practical load actually looks like week to week

It's not just more contact hours — it's a different rhythm entirely. Lecture-then-exam has a predictable shape. Lecture-then-practical-assessment-then-hospital-attachment means the material has to actually work in your hands, under supervision, with a real (if controlled) consequence for getting it wrong. That pressure is uncomfortable in a useful way that a purely theoretical course doesn't apply.

What I'd tell someone choosing this path

Go in expecting to be underestimated by people who haven't looked closely at what the qualification actually demands, and let the work answer that instead of arguing about it. It's a slower kind of vindication, but it's the one that actually holds up once you're the person someone's trusting in a real theatre.

A practical tip

Keep a record of every skill you practise and every supervisor who signed you off. When the time comes to apply for work, that record turns "I did my attachment" into a clear list of what you can actually do.

The people who made the difference

The lecturers and clinical supervisors who took the time to correct my technique, repeat an explanation or let me try a task twice were what made the programme work. Not all of them were patient, and some were tough, but the ones who cared taught me to ask for help early and to accept feedback without taking it personally. If you are in a diploma programme now, find those people, thank them and stay in touch, because they are also the ones who will later know your work well enough to recommend you.

what-nobody-tells-you-about-diploma-prog.meta_description: A diploma looks like a shortcut on paper. In practice, it comes with its own specific set of invisible costs.

the-parts-of-college-life-nobody-warns-y.title: The parts of college life nobody warns you about
the-parts-of-college-life-nobody-warns-y.excerpt: Nobody tells you that the hardest part of college isn't the coursework — it's learning to run your own life for the first time.
the-parts-of-college-life-nobody-warns-y.content:
Everyone prepares you for the workload. Nobody prepares you for the part where you're suddenly the only person responsible for whether you eat, sleep, show up, or fall apart quietly in a rented room.

The syllabus isn't the syllabus

The real curriculum in college is logistics: budgeting fare and food off whatever came this week, figuring out who to trust in a new town, learning that "I'll do it tomorrow" compounds like interest, except against you.

The loneliness nobody mentions

You can be surrounded by classmates all day and still feel like nobody actually knows you. That's not a personal failure — it's just what happens when everyone around you is also new, also adjusting, also pretending they've got it figured out.

What actually helped

Routine, mostly. A fixed wake-up time. One or two people I could be honest with instead of thirty I performed for. And accepting early that some semesters are just about surviving with your integrity intact, not excelling.

The skill nobody grades you on

Knowing who to ask for help, and how to ask, turned out to matter more than most of what was actually on the syllabus. Some lecturers respond well to direct questions after class; others need an email first. Some classmates will actually explain a concept twice without judgment; others will make you feel behind for asking. Learning to read that quickly saved me more than any single study technique did.

The homesickness that doesn't look like homesickness

It rarely showed up as missing home directly. It showed up as irritability over small things, or a flat kind of tiredness that sleep didn't fix. It took a while to connect those symptoms to actually just needing a call home, not a nap.

What I'd do differently

Build the routine earlier instead of waiting for a "settled" feeling that takes a full semester to arrive on its own. The routine is what creates the settled feeling, not the other way around — I had that backwards for longer than I'd like to admit.

One thing I would pass on

Choose two or three habits that you can keep when everything else is chaotic, such as a wake-up time, a weekly call home and a short daily review. They will not solve every problem, but they hold the rest of your life together while you adjust.

A small reminder

If you are in the middle of a hard semester right now, you are not behind and you are not alone. Most of your classmates are working through the same things quietly. Be kind to yourself, keep the routine, and reach out to one person this week.

what-a-perioperative-theatre-technologis.title: What does a perioperative theatre technologist actually do?
what-a-perioperative-theatre-technologis.excerpt: A plain-language walk through a theatre technologist's work before, during and after an operation — and why most of it goes unnoticed.
what-a-perioperative-theatre-technologis.content:
If you ask ten people what happens in an operating theatre, nine will describe the surgeon. Almost nobody mentions the person who made sure the room, the equipment and the instruments were ready before the patient ever arrived. That person is often a perioperative theatre technologist, and the job is bigger than it looks from outside.

Before the case: making the room safe

Preparation starts well before the first incision. The theatre is cleaned and checked, the lights and suction are tested, the operating table is set up, and the instrument sets and consumables for the planned procedure are collected. Sterile packs are inspected: is the wrapping intact, is the indicator showing it went through sterilisation, is it within its expiry? Anything doubtful is set aside, not "probably fine". It is repetitive work, and repetition is exactly the point, because the checks only protect the patient if they happen every single time.

During the case: supporting the team

Once the patient is in, a technologist works within the surgical team. Depending on the hospital and the day, that can mean assisting at the sterile field, passing instruments, keeping track of swabs and sharps, positioning the patient, or fetching what the team suddenly needs. The common thread is anticipation. A good technologist watches the procedure and knows what is likely to be asked for next, so nobody has to stop and wait.

Counting matters more than people expect. Instruments, swabs and needles are counted before, during and after, and the numbers must reconcile. It is a small, dull-looking task that prevents a serious and entirely avoidable mistake.

After the case: closing the loop

When the patient leaves, the work continues. Used instruments are handled safely, decontaminated, cleaned, inspected, packed and sent for sterilisation. The room is cleaned and turned over for the next patient. Documentation is completed so there is a record of what was used and what was done. If anything went wrong, such as a faulty instrument or a broken seal on a pack, it is reported so it can be fixed.

The skills nobody puts on the poster

  • Calm under pressure: emergencies arrive without warning.
  • Discipline: not skipping a step because you are tired or the list is long.
  • Communication: short, clear, and without ego.
  • Physical stamina: long cases on your feet in heavy gowns.

A note on roles

Exactly who does what varies between hospitals and countries, and between public and private facilities. Titles overlap with theatre nurses and other staff, and local policy decides the boundaries. If you are a student, treat this post as a general picture and rely on your supervisors and your institution's guidance for the specifics of your own setting.

What stays constant is the purpose: make the environment safe, keep the team supplied, and protect the patient from avoidable harm. It is quiet work, and when it is done well, nobody notices it at all.

Quick revision points

  • The job spans before, during and after surgery: preparation, support, and turnover.
  • Counts of instruments, swabs and needles must always reconcile.
  • Sterility checks apply to every pack, every time.
  • Roles overlap and differ between facilities, so follow local policy.

who-is-who-in-the-operating-theatre.title: Who is who in the operating theatre: the surgical team explained
who-is-who-in-the-operating-theatre.excerpt: Surgeon, anaesthetist, scrub nurse, circulating nurse, technologist — what each role does and how the team works as one unit.
who-is-who-in-the-operating-theatre.content:
A theatre can look chaotic to a first-time observer: people in identical scrubs and masks, moving around a patient under bright lights. In reality it is highly organised, and every person has a defined job. Knowing the roles makes it much easier to understand what you are seeing on attachment.

The surgeon

The surgeon leads the operation and is responsible for the surgical decisions. They perform the procedure, often with one or more assistants. Before the case they confirm the plan, the consent and the site of surgery with the rest of the team.

The anaesthetist

The anaesthetist (or anaesthetic clinician) keeps the patient asleep, pain-free and physiologically stable. They manage the airway, breathing, circulation and medication throughout, and they watch the monitors continuously. Their position at the head of the table is deliberate: they need access to the airway and a clear view of the patient's face and the screens.

The scrub practitioner

The scrub person works inside the sterile field. They set up the instrument trolley, pass instruments and supplies to the surgeon, and keep careful track of everything that goes on and off the field. Because they are sterile, they do not leave the field to fetch things, which is where the next role comes in.

The circulating practitioner

The circulator is not sterile and moves around the room. They open sterile packs onto the field without contaminating it, bring equipment, label specimens, manage the documentation, and act as the link between the sterile team and the outside world. They are also usually responsible for coordinating the swab and instrument counts with the scrub person.

The theatre technologist

Technologists support equipment, instruments, sterility and turnover, and in many facilities they also scrub or circulate. Their strength is knowing the equipment and the sterile processing chain, so the rest of the team can trust that what arrives on the field is safe.

Why the pause matters

Before the first incision, the whole team stops for a "time out" using a safety checklist: confirming the patient's identity, the procedure, the site, allergies and equipment. This pause is not a formality. It puts every role in the same conversation, so a concern from the quietest person in the room can be heard before it becomes a problem.

Learning the room as a student

On attachment, learn the names and the jobs, then learn the rhythm: who speaks to whom, in what order, and how requests are phrased. Ask your supervisor when you are unsure, and never guess near the sterile field. Roles and titles differ between hospitals, so use this as a framework and follow local practice.

A good theatre team is less about heroics and more about reliability: everyone doing their own job properly, and trusting that the others are doing theirs.

Quick revision points

  • Scrub practitioners work inside the sterile field; circulators work outside it.
  • The anaesthetist manages airway, breathing, circulation and medication.
  • The time out puts the whole team on the same page before incision.

A question students ask

Can a student speak up during a case? Yes, politely and at the right moment. If you see a possible safety problem, tell your supervisor immediately. Everyone in the room is expected to raise concerns, and a quiet, clear sentence is better than silence.

cleaning-disinfection-sterilisation-diff.title: Cleaning, disinfection and sterilisation: what is the difference?
cleaning-disinfection-sterilisation-diff.excerpt: Three words people use interchangeably, and why mixing them up is dangerous. A clear explanation for students.
cleaning-disinfection-sterilisation-diff.content:
In everyday speech, "clean", "disinfected" and "sterile" all sound like the same thing. In a hospital they mean three different levels of safety, and confusing them is how infections spread. This is one of the most examined topics in any theatre or infection control course, so it is worth getting straight.

Cleaning: removing the dirt

Cleaning is the physical removal of visible soil, blood, tissue and organic material, usually with water, detergent and mechanical action such as brushing. It does not necessarily kill microorganisms, but it is the essential first step, because dirt shelters germs and blocks disinfectants and sterilising agents from reaching the surface. An item that has not been cleaned properly cannot be reliably disinfected or sterilised.

Disinfection: reducing germs to a safe level

Disinfection uses chemicals (or sometimes heat) to destroy most disease-causing microorganisms on an object. It does not reliably kill every form, especially bacterial spores. Disinfection is often described in levels: low, intermediate and high. High-level disinfection is used for items that touch mucous membranes or non-intact skin but do not enter sterile tissue. The right level depends on how the item will be used.

Sterilisation: removing all microbial life

Sterilisation destroys or removes all forms of microbial life, including spores. It is required for instruments that enter sterile tissue or the vascular system, such as surgical instruments. Common methods include steam under pressure (autoclaving), dry heat, ethylene oxide gas and low-temperature plasma, with the choice depending on whether the item can tolerate heat and moisture.

How we know it worked

Sterilisation is verified, not assumed. Packs carry chemical indicators that change colour when exposed to the process, and sterilisers are monitored with biological indicators containing resistant spores. If an indicator fails, the load is not used. This is why checking the indicator on a pack before opening it is never optional.

A simple way to remember

  • Clean = dirt removed.
  • Disinfected = most germs killed.
  • Sterile = all germs, including spores, gone.

Common mistakes

Skipping the cleaning step before sterilising. Using a disinfectant for something that needs to be sterile. Opening a pack with a damaged wrapper "because it looks fine". Storing sterile items in damp or dusty places, which can compromise them. Each of these is easy to do when you are busy, which is why good departments build routines that make the right action the default.

Always follow your facility's policy and the manufacturer's instructions for the item and the process. The principle underneath is simple: the more a device touches the patient's body, the higher the standard of safety it needs.

Quick revision points

  • Cleaning must come before disinfection or sterilisation.
  • Only sterilisation reliably removes spores.
  • Indicators are checked on every pack before use.
  • The riskier the use of an item, the higher the level of processing it needs.

A question students ask

Why not sterilise everything? It would be slow, costly and unnecessary. Floors and bed rails need cleaning and disinfection; instruments entering sterile tissue need sterilisation. Matching the method to the risk keeps patients safe without wasting resources.

who-surgical-safety-checklist-explained.title: The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist, explained step by step
who-surgical-safety-checklist-explained.excerpt: What the three pauses — sign in, time out, sign out — actually check, and why the whole team stops for them every time.
who-surgical-safety-checklist-explained.content:
The World Health Organization introduced its Surgical Safety Checklist to reduce preventable errors and complications in surgery. It is short, it takes only a few minutes, and it is built around a simple idea: even highly trained teams forget things, and a shared pause catches mistakes before they reach the patient.

The three phases

The checklist is divided into three moments in the patient's journey through theatre: before anaesthesia, before the incision, and before the patient leaves the room.

Sign in: before anaesthesia

At this stage the team confirms the basics with the patient where possible: identity, the planned procedure, the site and side of surgery (marked if applicable), and consent. They check that the anaesthesia machine and medication checks are complete and the pulse oximeter is on and working. They ask about known allergies, about any difficult airway or aspiration risk, and about the risk of significant blood loss and whether the right fluids and access are ready.

Time out: before the incision

Everyone stops and the team introduces themselves by name and role. They confirm aloud the patient, the site and the procedure. The surgeon, anaesthetist and nursing team each state any critical concerns. Antibiotic prophylaxis timing is confirmed where relevant, sterility of the instruments is confirmed (including indicator results), and essential imaging is displayed if needed. This is the moment where the whole room is literally on the same page.

Sign out: before the patient leaves

The team confirms the name of the procedure that was actually performed, that instrument, swab and needle counts are correct, and that any specimens are labelled properly. They also state any equipment problems that need fixing, and agree the key concerns for recovery and aftercare.

Why it works

The checklist works less because of any single item and more because of what it does to the room. It gives everyone permission to speak, regardless of seniority. A student, a junior nurse or a technologist can raise a concern at the time out, and it is heard. Many near-misses are noticed by the person who is not the most senior, and the checklist makes sure there is a moment for them to say so.

Where it goes wrong

Teams that treat it as a box-ticking ritual, reading it from memory while people are still moving about, lose most of the benefit. The pause only works when everyone actually stops, looks up, and listens.

As a student

Learn what each phase checks, and watch how your attachment theatre does it. Local versions are often adapted, so follow the version your hospital uses. Whatever the format, the habit it builds is the one to carry through your whole career: never let a routine case become a reason to skip a check.

Quick revision points

  • Three pauses: sign in (before anaesthesia), time out (before incision), sign out (before the patient leaves).
  • Counts, specimens and equipment problems are covered at sign out.
  • The checklist works when everyone stops and listens.

rules-of-the-sterile-field.title: Rules of the sterile field: what you can and cannot touch
rules-of-the-sterile-field.excerpt: The simple principles behind sterile technique — and why a field is only as safe as its weakest moment.
rules-of-the-sterile-field.content:
The sterile field is the area around the surgical site that has been prepared to be free of microorganisms: the draped patient, the instrument trolley, the gowned and gloved team. Everything inside it must stay sterile for the duration of the case. The rules look strict, and they are, because a single break can carry bacteria into a wound.

Sterile touches sterile

This is the foundation. A sterile item may only touch another sterile item. If a sterile instrument touches something non-sterile, or you are not sure whether it did, it is considered contaminated and must be replaced. "I think it was fine" is not an acceptable standard.

Know the boundaries

Only the area above waist level at the front of a sterile gown is considered sterile. Sleeves are sterile from just above the elbow to the cuff, but the underarm area is not. Tables are sterile only on the top surface; anything hanging below table level is not. Keep your hands in view and above the waist, away from your face, and do not fold them under your armpits.

Respect the edges

The outer one inch or so of a sterile drape edge is treated as a boundary zone. Items are opened so that the contents drop onto the field without the non-sterile hands touching them or the circulator reaching over the field. Sterile packs are opened away from the body, and flipped back so the sterile contents are not passed under non-sterile areas.

Move with care

  • Face the sterile field when you pass it, and keep a safe distance.
  • Pass back to back or front to front, according to your local procedure, and never reach across a sterile field.
  • If you must move around a sterile team, do it so you do not brush against them.
  • Keep talking to a minimum near an open field to reduce droplets.

Time and events

Sterility is event-related as much as time-related. A pack that is dropped, torn, wet or stored badly may not be sterile, even if it has not reached the expiry date. Moisture is especially important: a wet drape can act as a bridge for bacteria from non-sterile layers underneath to the field above.

If you break sterility

Say so immediately and clearly. This is not a confession, it is a safety action. The affected item is changed, the person re-gowns or re-gloves if needed, and the case continues safely. Teams that punish honesty teach people to hide mistakes, which is far more dangerous than the original slip.

The mindset

Good sterile technique is mostly attitude: assume nothing, check everything, and be comfortable stopping to fix a problem. Follow your hospital's policies, as details differ, but the principles stay the same everywhere.

Quick revision points

  • Sterile touches sterile only.
  • A damp drape or torn wrapper is considered contaminated.
  • If in doubt, throw it out and say so.
  • Keep hands above waist level and in sight.

A question students ask

What if nobody saw me touch something? It does not matter. Sterility depends on what happened, not on who noticed. Reporting it immediately is the professional response and protects the patient.

surgical-instruments-families-explained.title: Surgical instruments by family: scissors, forceps, clamps and retractors
surgical-instruments-families-explained.excerpt: A student-friendly way to sort the instrument tray into families by function, so the names start to make sense.
surgical-instruments-families-explained.content:
A full instrument set can look like a hundred unrelated pieces of steel. The trick to learning them is to stop memorising individual names and start sorting by function. Almost every instrument belongs to one of a handful of families, and once you know the family, you can guess what a new instrument does.

Cutting and dissecting

This family includes scalpels (handles with detachable blades) and scissors. Scissors differ by use: straight and curved scissors for tissue, and heavier ones for tougher material such as sutures or dressings. Dissecting instruments separate tissue layers without cutting, and are usually delicate. Treat the sharp ones with respect, and never pass a blade in a way that exposes the handler.

Grasping and holding

Forceps hold tissue or other items. Toothed forceps grip firmly but can damage delicate tissue; smooth (atraumatic) forceps are gentler. Tissue-holding forceps, dressing forceps and specialised grasping instruments all fall in this group. The shape of the tips tells you what they are designed to hold.

Clamping and occluding

Haemostats and clamps compress blood vessels or tissue to control bleeding or hold structures. They have ratcheted handles that lock closed so the surgeon's hand is free. Many have curved or straight jaws, with fine or heavy serrations depending on the tissue involved. Their names often come from the people who designed them, which is why a reference chart is helpful at first.

Retracting and exposing

Retractors hold tissue out of the way so the surgeon can see and work. Some are hand-held and need an assistant; others are self-retaining and hold themselves open. Different sizes and blade shapes suit different depths and wound sizes.

Suturing

Needle holders grip curved needles so they can be driven through tissue. They look like clamps but have shorter, stronger jaws designed to hold a needle securely without bending or damaging it.

Suction, probes and specialised tools

Suction tips remove fluid and blood; probes and dilators measure or gently open passages; specialised sets for orthopaedics, obstetrics and other fields add their own instruments. Learn the general families first, then the specialties you meet on placement.

Study tips

  • Sort real or pictured instruments into families, then name them.
  • Learn the tips and jaws, because they decide the function.
  • Practise assembling a basic set in the order it is used.
  • Handle and count instruments safely on attachment, with permission.

Names vary between regions and manufacturers, so be ready to learn local terms from your supervisors. The families, though, stay the same everywhere, and they are the key to making the tray make sense.

Quick revision points

  • Families: cutting, grasping, clamping, retracting, suturing, suction and specialist tools.
  • Tips and jaws reveal the function.
  • Count and handle sharps with care.

Practise it

Photograph the instruments you are allowed to handle during practicals, sort them into families, and test yourself by covering the labels. Within a week of regular review, names that once looked random start to follow patterns.

sutures-and-needles-basics.title: Sutures and needles: the basics every theatre student should know
sutures-and-needles-basics.excerpt: Absorbable or not, cutting or round-bodied — what the labels on a suture packet are telling you.
sutures-and-needles-basics.content:
A suture packet is covered in codes and numbers, and it is easy to ignore them until a surgeon asks for something specific. Learning to read a packet is a small skill that saves time and prevents mistakes, particularly when the room is busy.

What a suture is

A suture is a thread used to close wounds or tie off vessels, often supplied attached to a needle (swaged). The choice of material, thickness and needle depends on the tissue being repaired and how long it needs support.

Absorbable and non-absorbable

Absorbable sutures are broken down by the body over time, so they do not need removing. They are used in internal tissues that heal reasonably quickly. Non-absorbable sutures stay in place, either permanently inside the body or until they are removed from the skin. The choice depends on how long the tissue needs support and the site.

Natural, synthetic, braided and monofilament

Sutures can be made from natural or synthetic materials. A monofilament is a single strand that passes smoothly through tissue and is less likely to harbour bacteria; a braided suture has several strands twisted together, which handles well and ties securely but can trap more microorganisms. Knowing the difference helps explain why different surgeons request different types.

Reading the size

Suture thickness is written as a number of zeros, such as 2-0 or 4-0. The more zeros, the finer the thread. Fine sutures are used for delicate tissue and the face, heavier ones for fascia or places under tension. The packet will also show the length of the thread and the type of needle.

Needles

Surgical needles have a body shape, a curve, and a point. Cutting needles have a sharp edge that passes through tough tissue such as skin. Round-bodied needles spread the tissue fibres instead of cutting them, and are used for softer tissue such as bowel or fat. Curvature is described as a fraction of a circle, such as half or three-eighths. A wrong needle can tear tissue or make suturing needlessly hard.

Handling safely

  • Never recap or hand over a needle in a way that exposes the point; follow the "no-touch" or neutral zone method used in your theatre.
  • Count needles in and out, every time.
  • Dispose of needles in a sharps container immediately.
  • Open packets only when asked, and check the type before passing.

Why this matters

Needle-stick injuries are among the most common occupational hazards in theatre, and an incorrect suture can cause a patient more harm. Learn the labels, practise reading them aloud, and treat every needle as the dangerous object that it is. Follow your hospital's protocols and ask your supervisor to teach you the local set of sutures.

Quick revision points

  • Absorbable sutures dissolve; non-absorbable stay or are removed.
  • More zeros means finer thread.
  • Cutting needles suit tough tissue; round-bodied suit soft tissue.
  • Count needles in and out, every case.

stages-of-wound-healing-explained.title: The four stages of wound healing, explained simply
stages-of-wound-healing-explained.excerpt: Haemostasis, inflammation, proliferation and remodelling — what happens in the body after a cut, in the order it happens.
stages-of-wound-healing-explained.content:
Every wound, from a paper cut to a surgical incision, goes through the same basic sequence to repair itself. Understanding the order helps you make sense of dressings, wound care instructions and why some wounds need more time than others. It is also a reliable exam question.

Stage 1: haemostasis (stopping the bleeding)

Within moments of injury, blood vessels narrow to reduce blood loss. Platelets stick to the damaged vessel wall and to each other, forming a plug, and the clotting cascade produces a fibrin mesh that stabilises it. The clot also acts as a temporary seal against germs and as a scaffold for the cells that arrive next.

Stage 2: inflammation (cleaning up)

Over the next few days, the area becomes red, warm, swollen and tender. This is not a problem, it is the repair crew arriving. White blood cells move in to remove bacteria, dead tissue and debris, and they release chemical signals that call in more help. Inflammation is necessary, but if it is prolonged by infection, poor circulation or foreign material, healing stalls.

Stage 3: proliferation (rebuilding)

New tissue starts to form. Fibroblasts produce collagen, new small blood vessels grow into the area (angiogenesis), and the wound fills with granulation tissue, which looks pink and bumpy. At the same time, skin cells at the edges migrate across the surface to close it, and the wound edges begin to pull together. This phase often runs from a few days to a few weeks.

Stage 4: remodelling (strengthening)

The last phase can last months. Collagen is reorganised and strengthened, excess tissue is broken down, and the scar slowly matures, becoming flatter and paler. Even a fully healed scar never regains the full strength of the original skin, which is one reason why wounds need protection long after they look closed.

What helps healing

  • Good nutrition, especially adequate protein, vitamin C and zinc.
  • Good blood supply and oxygenation.
  • Clean, appropriately dressed wounds kept at suitable moisture.
  • Control of conditions such as diabetes.

What slows it down

Infection, smoking, poor nutrition, reduced circulation, pressure on the wound, certain medicines, and some long-term illnesses all delay healing. This is why theatre staff pay attention to sterility and to protecting the patient's skin during surgery: the way a wound begins affects how it heals.

Primary, secondary and tertiary intention

Wounds closed neatly with sutures heal by primary intention. Wounds left open to heal from the base up heal by secondary intention, which takes longer and leaves more scarring. Delayed closure after a period of observation is called tertiary intention. Knowing the terms will help you follow ward rounds.

A simple memory aid for the order is: stop, clean, build, strengthen. This post is general education; clinical decisions about any wound belong to a trained clinician.

Quick revision points

  • Order: haemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, remodelling.
  • Redness and swelling early on are part of normal inflammation.
  • Infection, poor nutrition and poor blood supply slow healing.

preventing-hospital-acquired-infections.title: How hospitals prevent hospital-acquired infections
preventing-hospital-acquired-infections.excerpt: Why infections spread inside hospitals, and the everyday habits — from handwashing to theatre discipline — that stop them.
preventing-hospital-acquired-infections.content:
A hospital is a place where sick people gather, and where germs from one patient can reach another. An infection that a patient gets because of their healthcare, and was not present on admission, is called a hospital-acquired or nosocomial infection. They add pain, cost and sometimes death, and a large share of them are preventable.

How germs move

Infection spreads when there is a source (a patient, a staff member, a contaminated surface), a route, and a susceptible person. The main routes are contact (hands, equipment, surfaces), droplets (coughs and sneezes over short distances), airborne particles, and contaminated blood or fluids. Interrupting any link in the chain stops the infection.

Hand hygiene comes first

Clean hands are the single most effective measure. The World Health Organization describes "five moments" for hand hygiene: before touching a patient, before a clean or aseptic procedure, after body fluid exposure risk, after touching a patient, and after touching the patient's surroundings. Alcohol-based hand rub works when hands are not visibly dirty; soap and water is needed when they are.

Personal protective equipment

Gloves, gowns, masks, eye protection and caps protect staff and patients, but only when used correctly. They are put on and removed in a set order to avoid contaminating yourself, and they do not replace hand hygiene. Gloves are not a licence to skip washing.

Clean environment, safe equipment

Regular cleaning of surfaces, correct handling of laundry and waste, and proper decontamination of reusable equipment all reduce risk. Single-use items should never be reused. Sharps are disposed of at the point of use in puncture-proof containers.

Theatre-specific measures

  • Sterile instruments and checked indicators for every case.
  • Surgical hand scrubbing and sterile gowns and gloves.
  • Appropriate skin preparation of the patient.
  • Limiting traffic and door opening during surgery.
  • Timely antibiotic prophylaxis where indicated by the team.

Antimicrobial resistance

Overuse and misuse of antibiotics lets resistant bacteria survive and spread, making infections harder to treat. Good infection prevention reduces the need for antibiotics in the first place, which is one reason it is treated as a priority in every hospital.

Everybody's job

Infection control is not only for infection control nurses. Cleaners, porters, students, technologists and surgeons all have a part. Speaking up when someone skips a step, politely and early, is part of the job. Follow your hospital's infection prevention policy; this post covers principles only.

Quick revision points

  • Break the chain: source, route, susceptible person.
  • Five moments for hand hygiene.
  • PPE supports hand hygiene; it never replaces it.
  • Single-use means single-use.

What you can do as a student

Practise perfect hand hygiene, learn the correct order for putting on and removing PPE, report spills and broken equipment, and politely remind colleagues when a step is missed. Small, consistent habits are what prevent infection, far more than any single piece of equipment.

Remember also that patients and visitors need guidance. A clear explanation of why visiting rules exist makes people far more willing to follow them, and helps keep the ward safer for everyone.

safe-patient-positioning-in-theatre.title: Safe patient positioning in theatre: protecting skin, nerves and joints
safe-patient-positioning-in-theatre.excerpt: An anaesthetised patient cannot protect themselves. Here is how the team prevents pressure injuries and nerve damage.
safe-patient-positioning-in-theatre.content:
Once a patient is anaesthetised, they cannot shift their weight, move a limb that is going numb, or tell anyone it hurts. That makes the way they are positioned on the operating table a serious responsibility. Most positioning injuries are preventable, and preventing them is one of the quiet duties of the whole theatre team.

Why positioning injuries happen

Prolonged pressure over bony areas reduces blood flow to skin and tissue, causing pressure injuries. Stretching or compressing a nerve can cause temporary or lasting weakness or numbness. Joints forced beyond their normal range can be damaged. Long operations, thin or frail patients, poor nutrition and some medical conditions all raise the risk.

Common positions

The main surgical positions include supine (on the back), prone (face down), lateral (on the side), lithotomy (legs supported and apart) and various tilted or seated versions. Each position has typical pressure points and typical nerve risks. For instance, the heels, sacrum and back of the head matter in supine; the face, chest, knees and genitals matter in prone; the shoulder and hip bones matter in lateral.

Principles that apply to all

  • Neutral alignment: keep the head, neck and spine in a natural line.
  • Pad the pressure points: use appropriate gel pads or supports, not folded linen that creases.
  • Avoid stretching: arms are not abducted beyond what is comfortable, and not left hanging.
  • Protect the eyes: especially in prone positions.
  • Avoid pressure from equipment: straps, tubes, instruments or the team leaning on the patient.

Teamwork when moving the patient

Moving an anaesthetised patient needs coordination. The anaesthetist leads when the airway and lines are involved, and everyone moves on a clear command. Lifting, rather than dragging, protects skin from shear and friction, and using enough people protects staff from back injuries too.

Check again

Positioning is checked after the patient is placed, before the drapes go on, and again if the table is tilted or adjusted. Once draped, many pressure points are no longer visible, so checking early is essential. Long procedures may need position checks at intervals, according to local protocol.

Document and handover

The position, supports used, and the state of the skin before and after surgery are recorded. If there is redness that does not fade or any new numbness or weakness reported afterwards, this should be communicated at handover so it can be assessed promptly.

As a student

Ask to be shown how your theatre positions patients, and learn the standard supports. Do not move or adjust a patient without a supervisor's instruction. Safe positioning is rarely praised, because when it works nothing happens, and that is exactly the outcome we want.

Quick revision points

  • Neutral alignment, padded pressure points, no stretching.
  • Check position before draping and after any table adjustment.
  • Report new redness, numbness or weakness at handover.

how-to-build-your-own-anatomy-mnemonics.title: How to build your own anatomy mnemonics (and why they work)
how-to-build-your-own-anatomy-mnemonics.excerpt: Mnemonics are not tricks, they are a way of hooking dry lists onto things your brain already remembers. Here is how to make good ones.
how-to-build-your-own-anatomy-mnemonics.content:
Anatomy asks you to memorise long lists: bones of the wrist, branches of a nerve, layers of the abdominal wall. Mnemonics turn those lists into something easier to hold. Students have used them for generations, and for good reason: they work with the way memory is built.

Why they work

Your brain remembers vivid, odd, emotional or rhythmic things much better than abstract lists. A mnemonic attaches an ordered, forgettable list to a phrase, a story or an image that sticks. It also gives you a ready-made order to follow, which is useful when the order itself is part of the answer.

The main types

  • Acronyms: each letter stands for an item, such as a word spelled from the initials.
  • Phrase mnemonics: a sentence where each word starts with the same letter as the list item. A well-known one for the cranial nerves starts "Oh Oh Oh To Touch And Feel..."
  • Rhymes and songs: rhythm helps recall.
  • Visual stories or memory palaces: placing items in a familiar place or scene.

How to build one

  1. Get the list right first. Check it against your textbook. A mnemonic for a wrong list is worse than none.
  2. Pick a format. Letters work well for ordered lists of similar items; images work better for things with meaning.
  3. Make it personal and strange. A phrase about your own life or a funny scene is easier to recall than a bland one.
  4. Keep it short. If the mnemonic is harder to learn than the list, drop it.
  5. Test it. Write the list from memory the next day and the next week.

Where mnemonics fall short

A mnemonic gives you the names, not the understanding. Knowing the order of the carpal bones does not tell you why a scaphoid fracture is troublesome. Use mnemonics for retrieval, and pair them with understanding: location, function and clinical relevance.

Check before you share

If you publish mnemonics online, double-check the content against a reliable source and credit where you found it. A catchy but wrong mnemonic can spread quickly, and learners rarely check it again.

Make it a habit

Pair mnemonics with spaced review. Revisit them after a day, a few days, then a week, and mix in practice questions. The mnemonic opens the door, but repeated retrieval is what keeps the memory in place. Start with one list you find hardest, build a mnemonic for it this week, and see whether it holds in seven days.

Quick revision points

  • Verify the list before building a mnemonic.
  • Personal and odd beats polite and bland.
  • Mnemonics give names; understanding gives meaning.

Try this today

Choose a list of five to eight items you struggle with. Write the first letters, then brainstorm words for each letter that connect to your life. Say the phrase aloud three times, write it from memory tomorrow, and then check it against your textbook. If it works, share it with a classmate and see whether it works for them too.

Keep a small notebook of the mnemonics that stick, and retire the ones that do not. Over a semester it becomes your own personalised revision guide.

active-recall-and-spaced-repetition-for-.title: Active recall and spaced repetition: study methods that actually work
active-recall-and-spaced-repetition-for-.excerpt: Re-reading feels productive but works poorly. Two evidence-backed methods — and how to use them with a limited budget and a busy schedule.
active-recall-and-spaced-repetition-for-.content:
Most students study by re-reading notes and highlighting. It feels productive, because the material looks familiar. But familiarity is not the same as being able to recall something under exam pressure. Research on learning keeps pointing to two techniques that do better: active recall and spaced repetition.

Active recall

Active recall means pulling information out of your memory instead of putting it in. Close the book and write down everything you remember about a topic. Answer a question without looking. Explain a concept aloud as if teaching a classmate. The effort of retrieving the answer, even when you get it wrong, strengthens the memory more than reading the answer again.

Spaced repetition

Spacing means reviewing material at increasing gaps: soon after you learn it, then a few days later, then after a week or two, and so on. Forgetting is natural, and each time you retrieve something just as it is fading, the memory becomes more durable. Cramming everything the night before gives a short-term boost, but it fades quickly.

A simple weekly system

  • Same day: after class, spend ten minutes writing questions from your notes.
  • Next day: answer them from memory. Mark the ones you missed.
  • Day 3-4: test the missed ones again.
  • End of week: do a mixed set across topics.
  • Before exams: repeat with past papers under time pressure.

Low-cost tools

You do not need an app. Index cards, a notebook with a question on the left and the answer folded away on the right, or a phone notes list will do. If you use a flashcard app, keep cards small and specific: one fact per card.

Mix topics

Studying one topic at length feels smooth, but mixing topics in a session forces your brain to choose which idea applies, which is closer to what an exam demands. After learning a topic, interleave it with earlier ones.

Protect the basics

Sleep, food and breaks are part of studying. Memories consolidate during sleep, and a tired mind forgets faster. Short focused sessions, such as 25 to 45 minutes with a short break, usually beat marathon sittings.

Start small

Pick one subject this week. After each class, write five questions from it and answer them two days later. Notice what you forget, and that gap is exactly where to study. It feels harder than re-reading, and that difficulty is the sign it is working.

Quick revision points

  • Test yourself instead of re-reading.
  • Review at widening gaps: day 1, day 3, day 7, day 14.
  • One fact per flashcard.
  • Sleep protects what you studied.

Common objections

"I don't have time." Self-testing is more efficient per minute than re-reading, so it often saves time overall. "It feels harder." That is the point: effortful retrieval builds stronger memory. Give it two weeks before judging.

how-to-use-past-papers-properly.title: How to use past papers properly (not just read them)
how-to-use-past-papers-properly.excerpt: Past papers are the best revision tool you have — if you use them to find your gaps, not to feel reassured.
how-to-use-past-papers-properly.content:
Past papers are one of the most powerful revision tools available, and one of the most misused. Many students read through them, nod at the questions, and feel prepared. Reading a question and recognising it is very different from producing a good answer in a timed exam. Here is how to get real value from them.

Know what you are looking for

A past paper tells you three things: the format of the exam, the style of the questions, and the topics that come up repeatedly. Before you answer anything, scan several years and note the structure, the marks per section and the command words, such as "describe", "explain", "list" or "compare". Each word asks for a different kind of answer.

Step 1: learn first, then test

Do not start with past papers on a topic you have not studied yet. Use them after you have covered the material, so the practice shows you what has actually stuck.

Step 2: attempt under real conditions

Set a timer, close your notes, and write full answers on paper. Practise writing at exam speed, because handwriting under time pressure is a skill of its own. If you cannot do a whole paper, do a section, but keep the timing realistic.

Step 3: mark honestly

Compare your answers with a marking guide or your lecturer's notes where available. Mark yourself strictly, using the same criteria an examiner would. A common mistake is giving yourself credit for an answer that was "sort of right". Examiners award marks for specific points, so check whether you included them.

Step 4: build a gap list

Write down every question you missed or struggled with, and group them by topic. This is your personalised revision plan. Study those gaps, then retest them a few days later using active recall.

Step 5: look at patterns

  • Which topics appear almost every year?
  • Which question types cost you the most marks?
  • Do you run out of time on one section?

Do not memorise answers

Questions change, and a memorised answer to last year's question may not fit this year's wording. Aim to understand the idea behind each question, so you can adapt.

Study in a group, carefully

Swapping papers with a classmate and marking each other's answers helps spot blind spots, as long as you stay honest and focused. Explaining why an answer earns marks is excellent revision for both people.

Find notes, past papers and study units in the Materials section of this site, and use them as a tool for practice rather than reassurance.

Quick revision points

  • Learn first, then test.
  • Attempt under timed, closed-book conditions.
  • Mark strictly and keep a gap list.
  • Look for patterns in topics and question types.

If marking guides are missing

Ask a lecturer, compare answers with classmates and check them against your textbook. Even without an official guide, writing your answers and then verifying each key point against a reliable source teaches you more than reading a paper silently.
