consolata-medical-college-theatre-techno.title: Sister Leonella Consolata Medical College: theatre technology details to confirm
consolata-medical-college-theatre-techno.excerpt: What one college's public page says about its perioperative theatre technology courses, and why you should confirm conflicting details before applying.
consolata-medical-college-theatre-techno.content:
This post is an example of how to read a college page critically, using the public page for the perioperative theatre technology course at Sister Leonella Consolata Medical College. It is not an endorsement.

What the page describes

The course page describes training to support a hospital operating theatre, including care for patients in recovery. It lists a diploma of about two and a half years and a certificate of about one year. The topics include preparing the operating room for surgery, sterilising equipment, caring for clients in theatre and testing and maintaining equipment. The diploma adds administrative and managerial duties.

The conflict you should notice

Different parts of the same site list different entry requirements and intake months. One part gives KCSE C- for the diploma and D for the certificate; another lists C and C- respectively. Intakes are also listed differently.

What to do when a page conflicts with itself

  • Contact the college and ask for the current requirements in writing.
  • Ask for the admission letter template and fee structure.
  • Confirm accreditation independently.
  • Keep screenshots with dates.

Lesson

Read every college page this way. A single inconsistent page is not a scandal, but it is a reason to ask direct questions before you pay.

Quick revision points

  • Read college pages critically.
  • Note conflicting entry requirements.
  • Get requirements in writing.
  • Confirm accreditation independently.
  • Keep dated screenshots.

kcse-entry-requirements-for-theatre-tech.title: KCSE entry requirements for theatre technology: what guides say and what to confirm
kcse-entry-requirements-for-theatre-tech.excerpt: Typical requirements quoted online for the diploma and certificate, why they differ, and how to confirm the one that applies to your college.
kcse-entry-requirements-for-theatre-tech.content:
Online guides often quote KCSE C- with biology for the diploma and lower grades for the certificate. Other pages quote slightly different grades. Both can be "true" for different institutions or different years.

What guides commonly say

  • Diploma: a mean grade around C- or C, with biology among the subjects taken.
  • Certificate: a mean grade around D or C-.
  • Alternative route: a certificate in the same field from a recognised institution, then progress to diploma.

Treat these as ranges, not rules.

Why they differ

Institutions set their own admission cut-offs within regulator standards, and requirements change by intake. Some pages are updated, others are not.

What to do

Ask the college for the requirement for your intake in writing. Ask whether bridging or a certificate-first route is accepted if your grade is lower.

If your grades are borderline

Consider a certificate and upgrade, or a related course, but never pay a person who "fixes" grades. Genuine admission needs genuine documents.

Quick revision points

  • Requirements vary by college and intake.
  • Biology is commonly requested.
  • A certificate can lead to a diploma.
  • Get requirements in writing.
  • Never pay for altered grades.

certificate-vs-diploma-in-theatre-techno.title: Certificate or diploma in theatre technology: which should you choose?
certificate-vs-diploma-in-theatre-techno.excerpt: The differences in length, scope and prospects between the certificate and the diploma in perioperative theatre technology, and how to decide.
certificate-vs-diploma-in-theatre-techno.content:
A common question is whether to start with the certificate. The answer depends on your grades, your budget and your plan.

What the programmes say

One college page describes the certificate as about one year, focused on theatre preparation, sterilisation, patient care and equipment testing. The diploma is described as about two and a half years and includes administrative and managerial duties.

Pros of the certificate

  • Faster and usually cheaper.
  • Gets you into the field sooner.
  • Can be a bridge to the diploma.

Pros of the diploma

  • Broader scope and deeper knowledge.
  • Often preferred by employers for fuller roles.
  • A better base for further study.

How to decide

Look at job adverts and ask employers which qualification they accept. If your grades allow, the diploma is usually the stronger long-term option; if money or grades limit you, the certificate can be a stepping stone.

Quick revision points

  • The diploma is longer and broader.
  • The certificate is a faster entry route.
  • Check what employers accept.
  • Plan the upgrade path.
  • Choose based on grades, budget and goals.

how-to-verify-a-medical-college-in-kenya.title: How to verify a medical college in Kenya before you pay a shilling
how-to-verify-a-medical-college-in-kenya.excerpt: A step-by-step method to check whether a college is real, accredited and approved for the course you want.
how-to-verify-a-medical-college-in-kenya.content:
Every year students pay fees to colleges that cannot give them what they promised. Verification takes an hour and can save years.

Step 1: Get the exact name and location

Names can be similar. Write the full legal name and campus.

Step 2: Check TVETA or CUE

Technical and vocational institutions are generally regulated by the TVET Authority, and universities by the Commission for University Education. TVETA publishes pages on accredited institutions and courses. CUE publishes information on universities and programmes.

Step 3: Check the programme, not just the college

A college may be registered but not approved for every course it advertises. Ask for the approval letter for your programme.

Step 4: Check the professional regulator

Many health cadres are regulated by councils and boards, for example the Nursing Council of Kenya or the Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentists Council. Ask whether graduates of the programme can register or be licensed, and confirm with the regulator where applicable.

Step 5: See the place

Visit, speak to students and ask where clinical placement happens.

Quick revision points

  • Verify the college and the programme.
  • Use TVETA, CUE and professional regulators.
  • Ask for approval letters.
  • Visit the campus.
  • Never pay before verifying.

tveta-accreditation-explained-for-studen.title: TVETA accreditation explained for students
tveta-accreditation-explained-for-studen.excerpt: What the TVET Authority does, what accreditation means for a college, and how to use it as a student.
tveta-accreditation-explained-for-studen.content:
The Technical and Vocational Education and Training Authority (TVETA) regulates technical and vocational institutions in Kenya. Many middle-level health training colleges fall in its sphere, depending on their type and status.

What accreditation means

Accreditation means the institution has been assessed against standards for facilities, staff and programmes. It is different from simply being registered as a business.

How to use it

  • Visit the TVETA site and look for the accredited institutions page.
  • Search for the exact name.
  • Check whether the course you want is listed or approved.
  • Ask the college for its certificate and check the dates.

What it does not do

TVETA accreditation is not the same as professional licensing. After training, you may still need to register with a relevant professional body, where applicable.

Related bodies

TVET CDACC works on curricula and assessment for competency-based training, KNEC handles national examinations and certification, and KNQA coordinates qualification frameworks.

Quick revision points

  • TVETA accredits technical and vocational institutions.
  • Search the accredited list by exact name.
  • Accreditation is not the same as professional licensing.
  • Check the course as well as the college.
  • Other bodies handle curricula and exams.

Sources and links

  • TVET Authority
  • Kenya National Qualifications Authority
  • KNEC

cue-and-university-accreditation-explain.title: CUE and university accreditation: what health students should check
cue-and-university-accreditation-explain.excerpt: The Commission for University Education regulates universities. Here is what that means for students of medicine, nursing and other health degrees.
cue-and-university-accreditation-explain.content:
If you plan a degree in a health field, you will deal with CUE and often with a professional regulator as well.

What CUE does

The Commission for University Education regulates and accredits universities and their academic programmes in Kenya.

What to check

  • The university is chartered or otherwise legally recognised.
  • The specific degree programme is approved.
  • The programme has a clinical training arrangement where required.
  • Graduates are eligible for registration with the relevant professional body.

Public and private

Both public and private universities train health professionals. Fees and entry routes differ. KUCCPS handles placement into government-sponsored places, while private or self-sponsored admission may be direct.

Practical tip

Ask the university for the approval status of the programme in writing, and compare it with the official information.

Quick revision points

  • CUE regulates universities and programmes.
  • Check the specific programme, not only the university.
  • Confirm professional registration eligibility.
  • Ask about clinical placement.
  • Get approval status in writing.

Sources and links

  • Commission for University Education
  • KUCCPS

kuccps-placement-explained-for-health-co.title: KUCCPS placement explained for health courses
kuccps-placement-explained-for-health-co.excerpt: How the Kenya Universities and Colleges Central Placement Service ranks and places students, and how that affects competitive health courses.
kuccps-placement-explained-for-health-co.content:
KUCCPS is the state corporation that places eligible candidates into universities and colleges. For health courses, competition can be intense.

The basic idea

Candidates choose programmes. KUCCPS ranks applicants by their cluster points for that programme and places them according to each institution's approved capacity. At the release of the 2026/27 placement results, KUCCPS leadership explained that universities admit up to their capacity in order of ranking, and that no two universities have the same cut-off.

What students should do

  • Learn the cluster subjects for your target course.
  • Compare the previous year's cut-offs with your points.
  • Choose a mix of ambitious and safer options.
  • Use the revision window if you are unhappy or unplaced.

Remember

Cut-offs change every year, so last year's figures are guides, not promises.

Where to look

Use the official KUCCPS site for the application process and notices.

Quick revision points

  • KUCCPS ranks and places students by capacity.
  • Cut-offs differ between universities and years.
  • Choose a mix of ambitious and safe options.
  • Use revision windows.
  • Rely on the official site.

medicine-slots-702-and-6500-applicants-w.title: 702 medicine slots, 6,500 applicants: what the numbers mean
medicine-slots-702-and-6500-applicants-w.excerpt: Reporting on the 2026/27 university placement said about 6,500 applicants competed for 702 medicine slots. What this means for health students.
medicine-slots-702-and-6500-applicants-w.content:
News report from the 2026/27 KUCCPS placement release, as reported by The Standard. Numbers are from that report and may be revised.

What was reported

The Standard reported that the MBChB programme received about 6,500 applications for a combined 702 places across public and private universities, leaving nearly 5,800 qualified applicants without placement through the government placement system. The report also said that, in the 2025 KCSE, 1,936 candidates scored an A plain and 1,535 of them applied for medicine, and a further 3,328 medicine applicants had an A-.

What it means

Medicine is extremely competitive, even for top students. A strong grade does not guarantee a place.

Planning with this in mind

  • Apply for related courses as alternatives: clinical medicine, nursing, medical laboratory, pharmacy, physiotherapy and others.
  • Consider diploma-to-degree pathways.
  • Do not pay anyone who promises a guaranteed medicine slot.
  • Look at accredited private options only after verifying them.

A note on this article

I am summarising a news report, not official statistics. For the official position, check KUCCPS announcements.

Quick revision points

  • Medicine places are far fewer than applicants.
  • Reported: about 6,500 applicants for 702 slots.
  • Good grades still need a plan B.
  • Related courses and pathways exist.
  • Beware of anyone selling guaranteed slots.

Sources and links

universities-offering-medicine-in-kenya-.title: Universities offering medicine (MBChB) in Kenya: a 2026 list and what to check
universities-offering-medicine-in-kenya-.excerpt: A list of universities reported to offer MBChB in Kenya in a January 2026 guide, with advice on verifying before applying.
universities-offering-medicine-in-kenya-.content:
This list comes from a Kenya Times guide dated 26 January 2026. It is a reported list, not an official accreditation register, so treat it as a starting point.

Universities named

The guide names these as offering Medicine and Surgery: University of Nairobi, Moi University, Kenyatta University, Egerton University, Kenya Methodist University, Maseno University, JKUAT, Mount Kenya University, Uzima University, MMUST, Kisii University and the Aga Khan University. It also lists dentistry at the University of Nairobi and Moi University.

Fees

The article gives estimated annual tuition figures that vary widely between institutions, from several hundred thousand shillings to well over a million. It does not state the effective year, so confirm fees with each university.

What to verify

  • That the programme is currently approved by CUE.
  • That graduates can register with the Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentists Council.
  • Clinical teaching hospital arrangements.
  • Current fee structure and intake.

Placement

Government placement goes through KUCCPS, which applies cluster points. Public and private universities set their own capacities.

Quick revision points

  • Use the list as a starting point, not as proof.
  • Verify with CUE and the professional council.
  • Confirm fees for the current intake.
  • Placement is via KUCCPS for sponsored places.
  • Check teaching hospital arrangements.

Sources and links

  • Kenya Times: accredited universities offering medicine (Jan 2026)
  • Commission for University Education
  • KMPDC

clinical-medicine-diploma-or-degree-how-.title: Clinical medicine: diploma or degree, how to decide
clinical-medicine-diploma-or-degree-how-.excerpt: A comparison of the clinical medicine diploma and degree routes in Kenya in terms of length, cost, scope and next steps.
clinical-medicine-diploma-or-degree-how-.content:
Clinical officers are a major part of Kenya's health workforce. Students often ask whether to start with a diploma or aim straight for a degree.

What is on offer

A 2026 guide lists clinical medicine programmes at several universities, with annual tuition estimates ranging from roughly KES 160,000 at one private university to over KES 500,000 at another. The same guide does not state the year the figures apply, so confirm directly. Diploma programmes are also offered by medical training colleges.

Things to compare

  • Total length and total cost, not just yearly fees.
  • Entry requirements and subject clusters.
  • Where clinical rotations are done.
  • Registration and licensing with the relevant professional council.
  • Credit transfer if you start with a diploma and plan to upgrade.

Think about money

A degree can be a good long-term step, but only if you can finish it. A diploma that you complete is better than a degree you cannot afford.

Ask the regulator

Contact the relevant council to confirm registration conditions for graduates of each programme.

Quick revision points

  • Compare total cost and length.
  • Confirm registration with the regulator.
  • Check credit transfer for upgrades.
  • Finish what you can afford.
  • Fee figures vary and change.

Sources and links

  • Kenya Times guide (Jan 2026)

nursing-career-pathways-in-kenya-college.title: Nursing career pathways in Kenya: college and university routes
nursing-career-pathways-in-kenya-college.excerpt: An overview of how nursing training is structured and why the Nursing Council of Kenya matters to every nursing student.
nursing-career-pathways-in-kenya-college.content:
Nursing is one of the most common entry points into health careers, and the Nursing Council of Kenya (NCK) is the statutory regulator for nursing and midwifery.

The role of the Council

The Nursing Council of Kenya runs registration and licensing and conducts licensing examinations. Its website has an online portal and a published exam calendar.

Typical routes

Training is offered at various levels by approved institutions, including public colleges and universities. Programme names and levels evolve, so always check the current NCK requirements.

Why it matters for theatre students

Perioperative nursing and theatre technology are different professions. Nurses train in a broader field and may specialise in perioperative nursing; theatre technologists train specifically for theatre support. Understanding the difference helps you explain your role and avoid confusion.

Next steps

If you are choosing between professions, speak to practitioners and shadow if you can.

Quick revision points

  • NCK regulates nursing and midwifery.
  • Check training approval before enrolling.
  • Licensing exams follow training.
  • Perioperative nursing differs from theatre technology.
  • Shadow practitioners before choosing.

how-much-does-health-college-really-cost.title: How much does health college really cost? A budget template
how-much-does-health-college-really-cost.excerpt: Tuition is only part of the cost. A template for budgeting a health diploma or degree, with the hidden costs people forget.
how-much-does-health-college-really-cost.content:
I will not quote fees, because they differ between colleges and change. What I can give you is a way to calculate your own total.

The categories

  • Tuition and other charges listed in the fee structure.
  • Accommodation and food.
  • Transport, especially to clinical attachment sites.
  • Uniforms, shoes, name tags and basic equipment.
  • Books and printing.
  • Exams, registration and licensing fees.
  • Emergency buffer.

A simple method

Ask the college for the full fee structure and for how fees are split across terms. Add your own monthly living costs times the number of months. Add one-off costs. This gives your total and your first-term cash need.

Ways to reduce cost

Compare colleges, look at public institutions, ask about instalments, apply for HELB or bursaries where eligible and share textbooks with classmates.

Warning

Do not pay large fees to an individual or an unofficial account. Pay only to the college's official channels and keep receipts.

Quick revision points

  • Tuition is only part of total cost.
  • Ask for the full fee structure in writing.
  • Budget for attachment travel and lodging.
  • Pay only through official channels.
  • Keep every receipt.

helb-loans-and-bursaries-for-college-stu.title: HELB loans and bursaries for college students: what to know
helb-loans-and-bursaries-for-college-stu.excerpt: A short guide to higher education loans and other funding options for health students, and how to avoid scams.
helb-loans-and-bursaries-for-college-stu.content:
Money is the reason many good students delay or drop training. Funding exists, but you must go through legitimate channels.

HELB

The Higher Education Loans Board (HELB) is the government body that provides loans to eligible students in higher education. Check its official site for who is eligible, the application steps and the current terms, because these change.

Bursaries

Counties, constituency funds, churches, foundations and some employers offer bursaries or sponsorships. Rules, amounts and deadlines vary. Visit the local office and ask early.

Scholarships

Search for scholarships offered by the institution itself, professional bodies or NGOs. Read the terms and check they are real.

Scams

Nobody should charge you for a guaranteed bursary or HELB approval. Use only official offices and websites.

Plan the repayment

If you take a loan, understand the repayment terms and how long it will take to repay on an expected salary.

Quick revision points

  • HELB is the official government loan body.
  • Bursaries come from many local sources.
  • Apply early and keep documents ready.
  • Never pay for guaranteed funding.
  • Understand repayment before borrowing.

red-flags-of-a-fake-or-risky-medical-col.title: Red flags in a medical college advert
red-flags-of-a-fake-or-risky-medical-col.excerpt: Ten warning signs that a college advert on social media or WhatsApp may be unreliable, and what to do instead.
red-flags-of-a-fake-or-risky-medical-col.content:
Social media has made it easy to advertise. It has also made it easy to hide.

Ten red flags

  • Guaranteed admission regardless of grades.
  • Pressure to pay today or lose the slot.
  • Payment to a personal phone number or account.
  • No physical address, or one that cannot be found.
  • No evidence of accreditation or programme approval.
  • Prices far below or above others without explanation.
  • Courses with names you cannot find anywhere else.
  • No clear attachment arrangement.
  • Refusal to put terms in writing.
  • Negative reports from former students.

What to do

Verify with the regulators, visit the campus, ask for written terms and talk to current students. Share suspicious adverts with friends so others are not caught.

Report

If you believe an institution is operating illegally, report it to the relevant authority.

Not every advert is bad

Many good colleges advertise. The test is whether they can answer verification questions clearly and in writing.

Quick revision points

  • Guaranteed admission is a red flag.
  • Pressure to pay quickly is a red flag.
  • Use official channels and written terms.
  • Verify with regulators.
  • Ask students who have been there.

Sources and links

  • TVET Authority

twenty-questions-to-ask-a-college-before.title: Twenty questions to ask a college before you pay fees
twenty-questions-to-ask-a-college-before.excerpt: A question list you can send by email or ask in person to test whether a college is organised and honest.
twenty-questions-to-ask-a-college-before.content:
Colleges with good answers usually answer quickly. Colleges that avoid questions are telling you something.

About the college

  • What is your accreditation and registration status, and can I have a copy?
  • Is this exact programme approved, and by whom?
  • Who is the principal and what is the physical address?
  • How many students are in a class?

About the programme

  • How long is it and what are the intake months?
  • What are the entry requirements in writing?
  • What practical facilities do you have (lab, skills room)?
  • Which hospitals do students attend for attachment, and who pays transport and lodging?

About cost

  • What is the full fee structure per term?
  • Are there extra costs such as exams, uniforms and attachment fees?
  • What is the refund policy?
  • Which account do I pay into, in the college's name?

About outcomes

  • Can graduates register or be licensed with the relevant body?
  • How many graduates were employed or placed last year?
  • Can I speak to a recent graduate?
  • How are complaints handled?

Quick revision points

  • Ask for approvals and fees in writing.
  • Ask about attachment arrangements.
  • Pay only to official accounts.
  • Ask about graduate registration.
  • Speak to recent graduates.

choosing-a-health-college-near-kitale-ka.title: Choosing a health college in western Kenya: a checklist for Kitale, Kakamega and Eldoret
choosing-a-health-college-near-kitale-ka.excerpt: A neutral checklist for choosing a college in or near Kitale, Kakamega, Eldoret and surrounding towns, without recommending any particular one.
choosing-a-health-college-near-kitale-ka.content:
Western Kenya has many training institutions in and around towns such as Kitale, Kakamega and Eldoret. I do not rank them, because I cannot verify each one from here. Use this checklist.

Start with verification

Check each college's accreditation and programme approval using the official bodies, then compare.

Local factors

  • How far is the college from public transport?
  • What does rent and food cost nearby?
  • Does it have an arrangement with a county or referral hospital for clinical placement?
  • Is the hospital busy enough to give you real experience?
  • Is the area safe for students, especially at night?

Ask students

Local students can tell you how the college really runs: how fees are handled, how lecturers treat students and how often attachment is organised.

If you want my older post

I have a separate post on certified medical colleges in Kitale. Read it together with this checklist, and always verify.

Quick revision points

  • Verify before you compare.
  • Check placement hospitals and distance.
  • Compare real living costs.
  • Talk to current students.
  • Do not choose by advert alone.

clinical-attachment-what-a-good-college-.title: Clinical attachment: what a good college should arrange for you
clinical-attachment-what-a-good-college-.excerpt: Attachment is where you become competent. Here is what to expect a college to organise, and what to do if it does not.
clinical-attachment-what-a-good-college-.content:
Good clinical attachment can make you employable. Poor attachment can leave you with a certificate and little confidence.

What a college should provide

  • A confirmed attachment site and dates.
  • A list of competencies you must achieve.
  • A logbook and clear assessment method.
  • A supervisor from the hospital and a link person at the college.
  • Guidance on conduct, uniforms and safety.

What to arrange yourself

Transport, accommodation, uniforms, personal protective equipment where not provided, and any vaccinations the hospital requires.

My own experience

My attachment at Likuyani Sub-County Hospital between February and April 2024 included theatre setup and turnover, CSSD sterilisation and the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist. The lesson was to ask questions, do the basics well and record what I learned every day.

If things go wrong

Write down what is happening, speak to your supervisor politely, and escalate to the college's link person if needed.

Quick revision points

  • Attachment needs a confirmed site and plan.
  • Keep a daily logbook.
  • Know your supervisor and link person.
  • Arrange transport and lodging early.
  • Escalate problems politely and early.

kcse-subjects-and-cluster-points-for-hea.title: KCSE subjects and cluster points for health courses, explained simply
kcse-subjects-and-cluster-points-for-hea.excerpt: What cluster subjects are, why biology and chemistry matter for health courses and how to read a cluster-points requirement.
kcse-subjects-and-cluster-points-for-hea.content:
Placement is not just about the mean grade. Many degree courses use cluster points based on specific subjects.

The idea

A cluster is a group of subjects relevant to a course. For competitive health courses reported in 2026, the cluster for medicine was said to involve mathematics, chemistry, biology and a language, and applicants are ranked by their cluster weight.

Why this matters

Two students with the same mean grade may have different cluster points. A strong biology and chemistry result is often more useful for health courses than a strong result in unrelated subjects.

How to use it

  • Check the course's required subjects on the official placement information.
  • Compare your cluster points with last year's cut-offs.
  • Choose a mixture of options.
  • Remember that diploma and certificate routes may have different requirements.

A caution

Formulas and cut-offs can change. Rely on official KUCCPS and institution notices.

Quick revision points

  • Cluster subjects matter, not just the mean grade.
  • Biology and chemistry are important for health courses.
  • Compare with past cut-offs, but expect change.
  • Choose a mix of options.
  • Rely on official notices.

Sources and links

  • KUCCPS

knqa-and-recognition-of-qualifications-w.title: KNQA and recognition of qualifications: what health graduates should know
knqa-and-recognition-of-qualifications-w.excerpt: What the Kenya National Qualifications Authority does and how it helps with alignment and recognition of qualifications.
knqa-and-recognition-of-qualifications-w.content:
The Kenya National Qualifications Authority (KNQA) was set up in 2015 to coordinate the quality assurance and comparability of qualifications.

What it does

According to its website, KNQA supports services such as recognition of prior learning, alignment and validation of qualifications and registration on the national qualifications database.

Why graduates should care

If you studied abroad, trained informally or want your qualification placed in the national framework, KNQA can be relevant. It also helps employers and institutions understand what level a qualification is.

What it is not

It does not replace professional regulators who license or register practitioners. You may need both.

Practical step

If you have questions about your certificate level or recognition, contact KNQA and ask for the current process.

Quick revision points

  • KNQA coordinates the national qualifications framework.
  • It supports alignment and recognition.
  • It does not replace professional regulators.
  • Check the current process on its site.
  • Keep original certificates safe.

how-to-set-up-a-theatre-before-the-list-.excerpt: A practical checklist for preparing an operating theatre before the first case: room, equipment, trays and communication.
how-to-set-up-a-theatre-before-the-list-.content:
The first case of the day goes well or badly depending on what happened in the twenty minutes before it. Here is a structure that works for students.

1. Know the list

Read the operating list: patient names, procedures, side, surgeon, anaesthetist and any special equipment. Ask what is different today.

2. Check the room

  • Surfaces clean, floor dry, doors closed.
  • Temperature and ventilation as per policy.
  • Lights positioned and working.
  • Operating table working and positioned.
  • Suction, diathermy and any gas supply tested.

3. Supplies and sets

Check the sterile sets for integrity, indicators and expiry. Open what you need only when the patient is ready, according to local practice. Have extras of common items near but unopened.

4. Talk to the team

Introduce yourself, confirm the first case and ask if anything is needed. A thirty-second chat avoids a ten-minute delay.

5. Leave a note

Write what you found faulty and report it. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Read the list before you touch anything.
  • Test equipment before the patient arrives.
  • Check sterile packs for integrity and expiry.
  • Open supplies only when appropriate.
  • Report faults immediately.

theatre-turnover-between-cases-a-safe-an.title: Theatre turnover between cases: a safe and fast checklist
theatre-turnover-between-cases-a-safe-an.excerpt: How to turn a theatre over between patients without cutting corners on cleaning, counts or sharps.
theatre-turnover-between-cases-a-safe-an.content:
Turnover is a balance between speed and safety. Speed that skips cleaning is not efficiency.

Order matters

  • Make sure the patient has left safely and the count and documentation are complete.
  • Dispose of sharps first, then waste and linen in the correct bags.
  • Remove used instruments for decontamination according to policy.
  • Clean and disinfect the table, lights, trolleys and high-touch surfaces.
  • Clean floors as required.
  • Reset the table, suction and equipment for the next case.

Protect yourself

Wear appropriate PPE and avoid handling sharps with bare hands. Report any needle-stick or splash immediately.

Work as a team

Assign tasks quickly and speak up. One person cleaning while another prepares the next set reduces delay.

Do not skip

A faster turnover is never a reason to skip a step in cleaning or counting. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Sharps first, then waste and linen.
  • Clean high-touch surfaces every time.
  • Wear PPE during cleaning.
  • Share tasks and communicate.
  • Never trade safety for speed.

surgical-hand-scrub-how-it-works-and-com.title: Surgical hand scrub: how it works and common mistakes
surgical-hand-scrub-how-it-works-and-com.excerpt: The logic of the surgical scrub, from nails to elbows, and the mistakes students make most often.
surgical-hand-scrub-how-it-works-and-com.content:
The surgical scrub reduces the number of microorganisms on the hands and forearms before gloving. It is different from routine hand washing.

Before you scrub

Remove jewellery, trim nails, check skin for cuts, put on the cap, mask and eye protection. Avoid artificial nails.

The principle

Start from the cleanest area and keep hands higher than elbows so water flows from fingertips to elbows. Follow the time and method set by your hospital and the product's instructions, whether it is a traditional scrub with antiseptic soap or an alcohol-based surgical hand rub.

Common mistakes

  • Touching the tap or sink after scrubbing.
  • Letting hands drop below the waist.
  • Rushing the nails and between fingers.
  • Dripping water onto the gown.
  • Re-contaminating while drying.

Practise

Practise the sequence in front of a supervisor and ask for feedback. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Hands stay higher than elbows.
  • Follow your hospital's timing and product.
  • Nails and between fingers need attention.
  • Do not touch unsterile items after scrubbing.
  • Practise with feedback.

Sources and links

  • WHO Safe Surgery resources

gowning-and-gloving-closed-and-open-tech.title: Gowning and gloving: closed and open technique explained
gowning-and-gloving-closed-and-open-tech.excerpt: What closed and open gloving mean, when each is used and how to avoid touching the outside of the glove with bare skin.
gowning-and-gloving-closed-and-open-tech.content:
Gowning and gloving look simple until you try with your hands inside long sleeves. A little understanding of the principle helps.

Closed technique

In closed gloving, your hands stay inside the gown sleeves until the glove is in place. This keeps bare skin from touching the outside of the glove and is the usual method for the scrubbed team.

Open technique

In open gloving, your hands are exposed and you take the glove by the inside of the cuff, then slide the second glove with gloved fingers under the cuff. It is used for quick tasks and where full gowning is not needed.

Key principles

  • Sterile touches sterile; unsterile touches unsterile.
  • Do not touch the outside of the glove with bare hands.
  • Check for holes; change gloves if torn or contaminated.
  • Keep hands above waist and below shoulders in the sterile zone.

Practise

Practise with a partner watching for contamination. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Closed technique keeps hands inside sleeves.
  • Open technique is for quick tasks.
  • Never touch the outside of the glove with bare skin.
  • Change gloves if torn or contaminated.
  • Practise with observation.

surgical-draping-basics-for-theatre-stud.title: Surgical draping basics for theatre students
surgical-draping-basics-for-theatre-stud.excerpt: Why we drape, how drapes create a sterile field and the principles behind placing them.
surgical-draping-basics-for-theatre-stud.content:
Draping turns a patient into a surgical field. A drape is only useful if it is placed once, correctly.

The purpose

Drapes create a sterile barrier between the surgical site and the rest of the patient and the room. They also protect equipment and define the working area.

Key principles

  • Drape after the skin prep has dried.
  • Place the drape from the near side to the far side, away from you, and avoid dragging it across unsterile areas.
  • Once placed, do not move a drape; a repositioned drape is contaminated.
  • Hold the drape by the folded edges and protect your gloved hands.

Types

There are towel drapes, fenestrated drapes, sheets and specialty drapes for different surgery. Reusable and disposable materials differ in how they are managed.

Ask and watch

Watch an experienced person drape, ask why each step is done and then practise. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Drape after prep is dry.
  • Place once; do not reposition.
  • Hold drapes by the folded edge.
  • Different surgery needs different drapes.
  • Learn by watching, then practising.

neutral-zone-and-safe-sharps-passing-in-.title: The neutral zone: passing sharps safely in theatre
neutral-zone-and-safe-sharps-passing-in-.excerpt: What the neutral zone is, why hand-to-hand passing of sharps causes injuries and how to apply the technique.
neutral-zone-and-safe-sharps-passing-in-.content:
Many sharps injuries happen during passing between people. A neutral zone is a simple way to prevent them.

The idea

A neutral zone is a designated area, such as a tray or a part of the field, where sharps are placed instead of being handed directly. The person passing puts the item down, and the person receiving picks it up.

Rules

  • Use a clear, agreed location.
  • Announce when you place a sharp.
  • Point the sharp away from people.
  • Load and unload blades with an instrument, not fingers.
  • Dispose of sharps in an approved container at the point of use.

Why it works

It removes the moment when two hands are near the same blade.

If an injury happens

Report immediately, follow your hospital's exposure protocol and seek assessment. Early reporting is part of safe practice. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Use a neutral zone for sharps.
  • Announce sharps when placing them.
  • Use instruments to load and unload blades.
  • Dispose of sharps immediately.
  • Report every injury straight away.

instrument-passing-and-receiving-techniq.title: Instrument passing and receiving: technique for students
instrument-passing-and-receiving-techniq.excerpt: How to pass instruments so the surgeon receives them in a ready-to-use position, with tips for learning the rhythm of a case.
instrument-passing-and-receiving-techniq.content:
Passing instruments is a skill you can practise at home with spoons, pens and a cloth.

Principles

  • Pass instruments so the surgeon can use them without adjusting.
  • Place the handle into the palm firmly with a clear sense of contact.
  • Keep sharp tips away from hands.
  • Return used instruments to the Mayo stand in an organised way.
  • Keep the field tidy and counted.

Anticipation

The best scrub staff watch the surgical field and predict the next step. They learn this by studying the procedure beforehand and observing the surgeon's preferences.

Practise

Practise naming and passing instruments with a classmate. Start slowly and add speed only when accuracy is solid.

Communication

Use short, clear words. If you do not know what the surgeon asked for, ask, rather than guessing. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Pass so the instrument is ready to use.
  • Keep sharp tips away from people.
  • Anticipate by studying the procedure.
  • Practise names and passing.
  • Ask if unsure.

theatre-lights-and-equipment-basics-for-.title: Theatre lights and equipment basics for new students
theatre-lights-and-equipment-basics-for-.excerpt: A basic orientation to surgical lights, tables, diathermy units, suction and other equipment you will meet in an operating theatre.
theatre-lights-and-equipment-basics-for-.content:
On your first day the room looks like machines and cables. Learn what each is for and how to check it.

Surgical lights

Lights provide bright, shadow-reduced illumination. Learn how to position and adjust them and how to handle them without breaking sterility. Report flickering or heat issues.

Operating table

Tables can be raised, lowered, tilted and fitted with attachments. Learn the controls and how to lock them. Never move a table with a patient unless you are trained and the team agrees.

Suction and gases

Suction removes fluid and smoke from the field; check that canisters are secure, tubing is connected and suction pressure is working. Know where the emergency gas shut-offs are, as per your hospital.

Diathermy

Diathermy (electrosurgery) cuts and coagulates tissue using electric current. Follow the safety rules in my diathermy safety post and your hospital's protocol.

Reporting

Faulty equipment should be labelled and reported, not quietly set aside. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Learn the controls before the first case.
  • Do not move a table with a patient unless trained.
  • Check suction function and connections.
  • Know emergency shut-offs.
  • Label and report faulty equipment.

tourniquet-safety-basics-in-orthopaedic-.title: Tourniquet safety basics in limb surgery
tourniquet-safety-basics-in-orthopaedic-.excerpt: What a pneumatic tourniquet does, what to check and why recording the inflation time matters.
tourniquet-safety-basics-in-orthopaedic-.content:
A tourniquet lets the surgeon work in a nearly bloodless field, but it is not harmless.

Before use

Check the cuff for leaks, the tubing for kinks and the machine for a working display. Place a protective layer under the cuff, avoid wrinkles and protect the skin from prep solution.

During use

The surgeon or protocol sets the pressure. Record the time of inflation and tell the team at regular intervals as per local practice.

After use

Deflate only when the surgeon or anaesthetist says so and note the time. Check the skin underneath.

Risks

Too much pressure or too long a duration can injure nerves, skin and tissue. This is why timing and pressure matter. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Check the cuff and machine before use.
  • Protect skin under the cuff.
  • Record inflation time.
  • Pressure is set per surgeon and protocol.
  • Report skin or nerve concerns.

handling-surgical-specimens-labelling-an.title: Handling surgical specimens: labelling and safety
handling-surgical-specimens-labelling-an.excerpt: Why specimen handling errors are serious and how to label, store and transport specimens correctly.
handling-surgical-specimens-labelling-an.content:
A mislabelled specimen can lead to the wrong diagnosis for the wrong patient. It is a classic never-event.

Principles

  • Confirm with the surgeon what the specimen is and from where.
  • Label the container with the patient details and specimen type at the point of collection, following local rules.
  • Use the right container and preservative if required.
  • Record the specimen in the theatre register.
  • Transport safely and record who received it.

Safety

Treat specimens as potentially infectious. Wear gloves, avoid spills and clean spills quickly according to protocol.

Read back

A read-back between scrub and circulating staff reduces mistakes: say what the specimen is, say what is on the label, and confirm.

If in doubt

Ask the surgeon before the specimen leaves the room. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Label at the point of collection.
  • Read back specimen details aloud.
  • Use the correct container.
  • Record in the register.
  • Treat all specimens as infectious.

laparoscopic-surgery-basics-for-theatre-.title: Laparoscopic surgery basics for theatre students
laparoscopic-surgery-basics-for-theatre-.excerpt: What laparoscopic (keyhole) surgery involves, the equipment stack and why it needs extra checking.
laparoscopic-surgery-basics-for-theatre-.content:
Laparoscopy uses small incisions, a camera and long instruments. For the theatre team, it adds equipment and a different rhythm.

The equipment stack

The usual setup includes a camera and monitor, a light source, an insufflator for gas, suction and irrigation, and diathermy. Learn the connections and test them before the patient is brought in.

Differences from open surgery

  • The view is on a screen, so positioning of monitors matters.
  • Instruments are long and delicate; handle and clean them carefully.
  • Gas flow and pressure are monitored.
  • The team must be ready to convert to an open operation if needed.

Cleaning and care

Delicate scopes and instruments need correct cleaning and sterilisation as per manufacturer and hospital procedure.

Learn by watching

Ask to observe, ask for the equipment layout and learn to troubleshoot basic problems such as a fogging lens. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Test the equipment stack before the case.
  • Monitor position matters.
  • Be ready to convert to open surgery.
  • Handle scopes carefully.
  • Follow manufacturer and hospital cleaning rules.

caesarean-section-theatre-set-up-what-to.title: Caesarean section: what the theatre team prepares
caesarean-section-theatre-set-up-what-to.excerpt: A general overview of how a theatre team prepares for a caesarean section, including emergencies and neonatal readiness.
caesarean-section-theatre-set-up-what-to.content:
Caesarean sections are among the most common operations in many hospitals, and many are emergencies.

Preparation

The theatre should be ready quickly: table, lights, suction, diathermy, instruments and swabs. Local protocols decide exact sets and drugs.

The baby

A resuscitation area for the newborn should be prepared with warmth, suction and equipment as per hospital protocols, and a person assigned to receive the baby.

Counts and safety

Swabs, instruments and sharps are counted before and after the procedure, and the WHO checklist is used at the key pauses.

Teamwork

Because many caesareans are urgent, clear roles and calm communication matter. Know who is calling whom and where equipment is stored. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Be ready quickly but do not skip checks.
  • Prepare a resuscitation area for the newborn.
  • Count swabs, sharps and instruments.
  • Use the WHO checklist pauses.
  • Know the roles in an emergency.

Sources and links

  • WHO Safe Surgery resources

orthopaedic-theatre-basics-power-tools-t.title: Orthopaedic theatre basics: power tools, trays and implants
orthopaedic-theatre-basics-power-tools-t.excerpt: An orientation to orthopaedic surgery from the theatre perspective: bone instruments, power equipment and implant handling.
orthopaedic-theatre-basics-power-tools-t.content:
Orthopaedic surgery is physical, noisy and equipment heavy. A new student should know what to expect.

Instruments and power tools

Bone surgery uses specialised instruments, drills, saws and sometimes saws with batteries or air power. These need correct assembly, cleaning and checking before use.

Implants

Implants such as plates, screws and joint components come in different sizes and sets. Check that the correct implant and size are available and recorded, and follow rules for opening only when needed.

Imaging

X-ray imaging may be used during the case. Follow radiation protection rules, including lead aprons and distance.

Ergonomics

Use safe lifting, team lifting and equipment aids. Orthopaedic cases can be physically demanding. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Check and assemble power tools correctly.
  • Record implant details accurately.
  • Open implants only when needed.
  • Follow radiation protection rules.
  • Use safe manual handling.

emergency-theatre-how-to-stay-calm-and-u.title: Emergency theatre: how to stay calm and useful
emergency-theatre-how-to-stay-calm-and-u.excerpt: What changes in an emergency case, how to prepare mentally and what to do as a student or new graduate.
emergency-theatre-how-to-stay-calm-and-u.content:
Emergency cases feel different: faster, louder, less predictable. But the fundamentals do not change.

What stays the same

Asepsis, counts, communication and patient safety remain essential, even when time is short. The checklist still matters.

Before an emergency

Know where emergency sets, extra sutures, suction and blood warming equipment are stored. Practise setting up quickly.

In the moment

  • Listen for the plan and your role.
  • Do the basics first: room, sets, suction, diathermy.
  • Ask short, specific questions.
  • Do not hide mistakes; say so immediately.
  • Keep sharps and counts under control.

After

Debrief when the case ends: what worked, what did not, what to restock. Taking care of yourself matters too. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Fundamentals do not change in emergencies.
  • Know where emergency equipment is stored.
  • Do the basics first.
  • Speak clearly and own mistakes.
  • Debrief and restock afterwards.

malignant-hyperthermia-awareness-for-the.title: Malignant hyperthermia: awareness for theatre staff
malignant-hyperthermia-awareness-for-the.excerpt: A rare but life-threatening anaesthetic reaction. What theatre staff should know to recognise and respond as a team.
malignant-hyperthermia-awareness-for-the.content:
Malignant hyperthermia (MH) is a rare inherited reaction to certain anaesthetic agents. It is an emergency requiring a rapid team response.

The basics

MH can be triggered by some volatile anaesthetic gases and a muscle relaxant used in anaesthesia. Signs can include a rapid rise in carbon dioxide on monitoring, fast heart rate, muscle rigidity and rising temperature. The anaesthetic team leads recognition and treatment.

What theatre staff do

  • Alert the team and help as directed.
  • Know where emergency drugs and cooling supplies are kept.
  • Be ready to assist with equipment, fluids and monitoring.
  • Follow the hospital's MH protocol.

Why awareness matters

In rare emergencies, minutes matter. If the whole team knows the plan, response is faster.

Note

This is awareness-level information. Learn your hospital's protocol and take part in drills. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • MH is rare but life-threatening.
  • The anaesthetic team leads treatment.
  • Know where emergency drugs are kept.
  • Practise the protocol in drills.
  • Speed and teamwork matter.

fire-safety-in-the-operating-theatre-the.title: Fire safety in the operating theatre: the fire triangle applied
fire-safety-in-the-operating-theatre-the.excerpt: Why fires can start in theatre and how oxygen, fuel and ignition sources come together, with practical prevention rules.
fire-safety-in-the-operating-theatre-the.content:
Operating theatres contain the three elements of fire in close proximity: oxygen, fuel and an ignition source.

The triangle

  • Oxidiser: oxygen or nitrous oxide-rich environments.
  • Fuel: drapes, gauze, alcohol-based prep, hair and some gases.
  • Ignition: diathermy, lasers, fibre-optic light sources and sparks.

Prevention

  • Allow alcohol-based skin preps to dry fully before draping and using diathermy.
  • Keep diathermy tips holstered when not in use.
  • Use moist swabs near oxygen-rich areas where appropriate.
  • Communicate between surgeon and anaesthetist when using ignition sources near oxygen.

Know your plan

Know the location of fire alarms, extinguishers and exits and how to turn off gases in an emergency. Practise drills.

In a fire

Follow your hospital's plan: rescue, alarm, contain, extinguish or evacuate. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Oxygen, fuel and ignition create fire risk.
  • Let alcohol preps dry.
  • Holster diathermy when not in use.
  • Communicate before using ignition near oxygen.
  • Know alarms, extinguishers and exits.

radiation-safety-in-theatre-time-distanc.title: Radiation safety in theatre: time, distance and shielding
radiation-safety-in-theatre-time-distanc.excerpt: How to protect yourself and patients when a C-arm or portable X-ray is used in theatre.
radiation-safety-in-theatre-time-distanc.content:
C-arm imaging is common in orthopaedic and some other surgery. Staff must protect themselves using simple principles.

Three basics

  • Time: reduce the time you are near the beam.
  • Distance: radiation drops quickly as you move away.
  • Shielding: wear lead aprons, thyroid collars and use shields where provided.

Practical steps

Wear a dosimeter if your hospital provides one and keep it where instructed. Store lead aprons hung, not folded, to avoid cracks. Announce 'X-ray' before exposures so everyone can step back.

Staff health

If you are or may be pregnant, tell your supervisor early so they can adjust your duties according to policy.

Radiation protection programme

Follow your hospital's radiation protection rules and training. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Use time, distance and shielding.
  • Wear lead aprons and collars.
  • Announce exposures aloud.
  • Store lead aprons properly.
  • Tell your supervisor if pregnant.

latex-allergy-and-allergy-awareness-in-t.title: Latex and other allergies: awareness in the operating theatre
latex-allergy-and-allergy-awareness-in-t.excerpt: Why patient allergies matter in theatre, how to ask the right questions and what to do if you are unsure.
latex-allergy-and-allergy-awareness-in-t.content:
Allergy information is confirmed repeatedly during the surgical safety checklist for a reason.

Common concerns

Patients may be allergic to latex, antibiotics, antiseptics, adhesives or other materials. Some allergies are severe and can cause anaphylaxis.

What the team does

  • Confirm allergy information from the patient, chart and wristband.
  • Make sure the whole team knows, including the person preparing supplies.
  • Use latex-free alternatives where required.
  • Be ready to call for help if a reaction occurs.

Your role as a student

If you notice an allergy in the chart that is not mentioned aloud, say so. If you are unsure, ask your supervisor.

Take your own allergies seriously

If you have glove or material allergies, tell your supervisor early. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Confirm allergies more than once.
  • Make sure everyone in the team knows.
  • Latex-free alternatives exist.
  • Know how to call for help.
  • Speak up if you notice a gap.

patient-identification-consent-and-site-.title: Patient identification, consent and site marking before surgery
patient-identification-consent-and-site-.excerpt: The three checks that prevent wrong-patient and wrong-site surgery, and how a theatre team confirms them.
patient-identification-consent-and-site-.content:
Wrong-patient and wrong-site surgery are rare but devastating. Systems exist to prevent them, and every team member is part of that system.

Identity

Confirm the patient's name, age or number against the wristband, theatre list and chart, asking the patient where possible.

Procedure and site

Confirm the planned procedure and the side or site. Many hospitals mark the site before the patient comes to theatre. If it is not marked, ask.

Consent

Confirm that consent has been obtained according to hospital policy. Theatre staff do not obtain consent but should notice if it is missing.

Time-out

The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist includes a pause before incision where the team confirms patient, site and procedure together. Anyone can stop the process if something does not match. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Check identity against wristband and chart.
  • Confirm procedure, site and side.
  • Notice if consent is missing and raise it.
  • Use the checklist time-out.
  • Anyone can speak up.

  • WHO Safe Surgery resources

sterile-packs-indicators-and-expiry-what.title: Sterile packs, indicators and expiry: what to check before opening
sterile-packs-indicators-and-expiry-what.excerpt: What to check on a sterile pack before use: integrity, indicators, labels and storage.
sterile-packs-indicators-and-expiry-what.content:
A sterile item is only sterile if the packaging has remained intact. Here is what to check every time.

Before opening

  • Is the wrapping intact, with no holes, tears or stains?
  • Is the pack dry?
  • Does the chemical indicator show the expected change?
  • Is it within the expiry or event-related limit used by your hospital?
  • Is the label correct?

If a pack fails

Do not use it. Set it aside, label it and tell your supervisor or CSSD.

Storage

Sterile supplies should be stored in a clean, dry, controlled area, handled minimally and not stored on the floor.

Indicators

A chemical indicator shows the pack has been exposed to a process, but it does not by itself prove sterility. Biological indicators and process monitoring give more confidence. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Check integrity, dryness, indicator and date.
  • Do not use a pack that fails any check.
  • Store sterile items properly.
  • Indicators show exposure, not proof alone.
  • Report failures to CSSD.

cssd-workflow-from-dirty-to-sterile-and-.title: CSSD workflow: from dirty to sterile and back
cssd-workflow-from-dirty-to-sterile-and-.excerpt: How instruments travel through a central sterile services department, and why the one-way flow matters.
cssd-workflow-from-dirty-to-sterile-and-.content:
The CSSD is the engine room of safe surgery. Understanding it makes you a better theatre team member.

One-way flow

The flow goes from dirty to clean to sterile and never back. Staff, trolleys and air should not cross from dirty to clean areas.

Steps

  • Collection and transport of used instruments in closed containers.
  • Cleaning, which removes soil, and decontamination.
  • Inspection for damage and function.
  • Packing with indicators and labels.
  • Sterilisation by a validated method.
  • Storage and issue to theatre.

What you can do

Send instruments back promptly, remove gross soil as per policy, keep sharps contained and report damaged instruments.

Respect

CSSD staff protect every patient. A friendly word to them goes a long way. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Flow goes dirty to clean to sterile.
  • Cleaning must come before sterilisation.
  • Inspect instruments for damage.
  • Send instruments back promptly and safely.
  • Respect CSSD teams.

closed-loop-communication-and-escalation.title: Closed-loop communication and escalation in theatre
closed-loop-communication-and-escalation.excerpt: How to speak so messages are understood in a noisy theatre, and how to escalate concerns respectfully.
closed-loop-communication-and-escalation.content:
Most errors in healthcare involve communication. Closed-loop communication is simple and powerful.

The loop

  • The sender names the person and states the request.
  • The receiver repeats it back.
  • The sender confirms it is correct.
  • The receiver tells the sender when it is done.

Example

Surgeon: 'Nurse, please give me a 3-0 suture.' Nurse: '3-0 suture, passing now.' Surgeon: 'Thank you.' It takes seconds and prevents mistakes.

Escalating concerns

Use a clear, calm structure: say what you see, say why it concerns you, say what you need. If the first person does not respond and safety is at stake, escalate to a senior.

Culture

Teams that welcome questions are safer. Thank colleagues who speak up. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Name the person and state the request.
  • Repeat back and confirm.
  • Say what you see, why it matters, what you need.
  • Escalate if safety is at risk.
  • Thank people who speak up.

Sources and links

  • WHO Safe Surgery resources

the-three-phases-of-perioperative-care-e.title: The three phases of perioperative care explained
the-three-phases-of-perioperative-care-e.excerpt: Preoperative, intraoperative and postoperative care: what happens in each phase and where theatre staff fit in.
the-three-phases-of-perioperative-care-e.content:
The word perioperative covers the whole surgical journey, not just the time in the operating room.

Preoperative

Includes assessment, tests, consent, fasting instructions, medication review and preparation. Many errors begin here, so checks are important.

Intraoperative

From the patient's arrival in theatre to leaving it: anaesthesia, positioning, skin prep, surgery, counts and the safety checklist.

Postoperative

Includes recovery room care, pain control, monitoring and ward care. See my post on the recovery room.

Why the term matters

Perioperative theatre technology is named for this wider view: you are part of a chain of care where handovers matter. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Perioperative means before, during and after surgery.
  • Preoperative checks prevent many errors.
  • Intraoperative work includes counts and the checklist.
  • Postoperative care starts in recovery.
  • Handovers connect the phases.

your-first-week-in-theatre-a-survival-ch.title: Your first week in theatre: a survival checklist
your-first-week-in-theatre-a-survival-ch.excerpt: What to bring, what to learn and what to ask in your first week of attachment or your first theatre job.
your-first-week-in-theatre-a-survival-ch.content:
The first week is overwhelming. Treat it as orientation, not as a test you must pass instantly.

Bring

Clean uniform and theatre shoes, a notebook, a pen, water and a snack. Learn the dress rules: caps, masks, shoe covers and jewellery.

Learn the room

Find where sets, linen, sharps bins, suction, emergency equipment and the scrub sink are. Learn the names of the team.

Ask well

Ask one good question per case, at a safe moment. Write the answer down.

Be reliable

Arrive early, wear your PPE correctly, keep your hands to yourself in the sterile field and own your mistakes.

Look after yourself

Eat, hydrate and sleep. Theatre days are long. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Treat week one as orientation.
  • Learn where everything is.
  • Ask one good question per case.
  • Arrive early and be reliable.
  • Look after your body.

back-and-body-care-for-theatre-staff-erg.title: Back and body care for theatre staff: ergonomics that last
back-and-body-care-for-theatre-staff-erg.excerpt: Standing for hours and lifting heavy trays can injure your back and feet. Simple habits to protect your body.
back-and-body-care-for-theatre-staff-erg.content:
Theatre work is physical. A career of thirty years begins with how you treat your body in the first three.

Feet and legs

Wear supportive, closed, non-slip shoes that suit theatre rules. Move your weight and avoid locking your knees.

Back

Keep your back neutral when lifting. Use your legs and ask for help with heavy trays and patients. Use slide sheets and transfer equipment where available.

Breaks and hydration

Take breaks when the list allows, stretch, drink water and eat properly. Dehydration and hunger can reduce concentration.

Mind

Long lists are mentally tiring. Short pauses, good sleep and talking to a trusted person help. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Good shoes matter.
  • Lift with your legs and ask for help.
  • Use transfer aids.
  • Stretch, drink and eat.
  • Mental rest counts too.

who-regulates-health-professions-in-keny.title: Who regulates health professions in Kenya? A simple map
who-regulates-health-professions-in-keny.excerpt: A plain map of the main boards and councils that regulate health training, registration and licensing in Kenya, and which question each answers.
who-regulates-health-professions-in-keny.content:
Newcomers to health careers hear many acronyms. Think of them as answering different questions.

The main bodies

  • Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentists Council (KMPDC): regulates medical practitioners and dentists under its Act.
  • Nursing Council of Kenya (NCK): regulates nursing and midwifery, including registration, licensing and licensing examinations.
  • Clinical Officers Council: regulates clinical officers.
  • Other boards cover areas such as pharmacy, laboratory, nutrition, physiotherapy and public health, each under its own law.
  • TVET Authority (TVETA) and the Commission for University Education (CUE) accredit institutions.
  • Kenya National Qualifications Authority (KNQA) coordinates the national qualifications framework.

Which question to ask whom

Is the college accredited? TVETA or CUE. Is the programme recognised for registration? The professional regulator. What level is my qualification? KNQA.

Where theatre technologists fit

Registration routes for some mid-level cadres have been discussed and changed over time. See my separate post on where theatre technologists register. Regulations and office-holders change, so confirm on the official website before acting on anything here.

Tip

Keep a folder with your certificates, transcripts, ID and any registration documents.

Quick revision points

  • Different bodies answer different questions.
  • Institutions are accredited by TVETA or CUE.
  • Professional councils register and license practitioners.
  • KNQA handles the qualifications framework.
  • Always confirm on official websites.

KMPDC is the statutory body that regulates medical and dental practice in Kenya under the Medical Practitioners and Dentists Act.

What it does

Typically a council like this registers practitioners, licenses them, sets standards for training and practice, and handles discipline. Its website describes its functions and lists contact details.

Why students mention it

Medical and dental students need to register with it after training. Other health students hear about it because it is the best-known health regulator and because it features in news about training standards and facility inspections.

Using the website

Use the official site to find the register, notices and application procedures rather than trusting a social media screenshot.

A caution

Regulations and office-holders change, so confirm on the official website before acting on anything here.

  • KMPDC regulates doctors and dentists.
  • It registers, licenses and sets standards.
  • Use its official notices.
  • Verify before paying anyone for registration help.

nursing-council-of-kenya-licensing-exams.content:
The Nursing Council of Kenya (NCK) is the statutory regulator for nursing and midwifery professionals.

What its website shows

The NCK site lists a registration and licensing service, a register search on its online service portal and an exam calendar for 2026-27, including exam centre placements. Past notices have announced when the portal was open for particular licensing exam sittings.

How to use it

  • Check your training institution is approved for your programme.
  • Watch the exam calendar and deadlines.
  • Create your account only on the official portal.
  • Keep your registration and licence details current.

Beware of fake notices

Because many students are anxious, scammers post fake portals and notices. Always type the official address yourself or use a link from the official site.

Relevance to theatre students

Nursing and theatre technology are separate professions, but you will work with nurses daily. Understanding their pathway builds respect and teamwork. Regulations and office-holders change, so confirm on the official website before acting on anything here.

Quick revision points

  • NCK regulates nursing and midwifery.
  • It runs licensing exams and a portal.
  • Use only the official portal and calendar.
  • Watch for fake notices.
  • Different professions have different regulators.

Clinical officers are a large part of Kenya's health workforce, especially in sub-county and rural facilities.

What the council does

In general, a professional council regulates education and practice for its cadre: it sets training standards, registers practitioners, handles discipline and issues practising licences. For exact functions, use the council's official publications.

Why theatre students care

Clinical officers work alongside theatre teams in many facilities, assessing patients, assisting in procedures within their scope and managing wards. Knowing their role helps you collaborate.

Choosing the course

If you are considering clinical medicine, read the posts on diploma and degree routes and verify the programme with the council.

Note

Regulations and office-holders change, so confirm on the official website before acting on anything here.

Quick revision points

  • Clinical officers are central to primary care.
  • A council regulates the cadre.
  • Registration is needed to practise.
  • Collaboration is part of theatre work.
  • Verify programmes with the council.

health-regulators-merger-and-new-authori.title: Plans to consolidate health regulators: what was reported and what to check
health-regulators-merger-and-new-authori.excerpt: Media reports in 2026 discussed consolidating health professional regulators under a new oversight authority. What it could mean, and why you should check the status.
health-regulators-merger-and-new-authori.content:
Several Kenyan outlets reported proposals to merge or restructure the bodies that regulate health professions, with a body referred to as the Kenya Health Professions Oversight Authority mentioned in coverage. I could not confirm the current legal status, so treat this as a reported plan, not a settled rule.

What is being discussed

The idea in the coverage is to reduce fragmentation by consolidating regulators or placing them under a single oversight body, with the aim of improving standards, discipline and registration processes. Details such as timelines, which councils are affected and transition rules were reported in different ways.

Why it matters to students

If regulators merge, registration routes and portals may change. Cadres without clear registration, which have been a recurring concern in the sector, may be clarified.

What not to do

Do not pay anyone who claims to have inside information on new registration. Do not assume old rules disappear overnight.

What to do

  • Follow your professional council's official notices.
  • Follow the Ministry of Health announcements.
  • Keep your documents in order.
  • Read the final law and transition notices when published.

Caution

I am summarising reports, not the law. Regulations and office-holders change, so confirm on the official website before acting on anything here.

Quick revision points

  • Mergers were reported; confirm the final status.
  • Registration processes may change.
  • Do not pay for insider promises.
  • Follow official council notices.
  • Keep your documents ready.

where-do-perioperative-theatre-technolog.content:
This is one of the most frequently asked questions from graduates, and I do not want to give you a false answer.

Why it is unclear

Mid-level cadres sometimes fall in gaps between regulators, and arrangements change by law and policy. Reports of plans to consolidate regulators add to the uncertainty. I do not have an official confirmation that I can quote for the current position.

How to find your answer

  • Ask your college registrar how graduates register or are recognised, and request it in writing.
  • Ask the Ministry of Health or the relevant council which body currently recognises your programme.
  • Ask hospital human resources what they require for employment.
  • Ask senior theatre technologists how they were employed and licensed.
  • Save written answers and dates.

In the meantime

Keep your certificate, transcripts and attachment records safe, and keep learning. Employers still look for skill and professionalism.

Please share

If you have an official, current answer, send it to me through the contact page so I can update this post. Regulations and office-holders change, so confirm on the official website before acting on anything here.

  • Ask the college, regulators and employers.
  • Get answers in writing.
  • Keep documents safe.

what-is-a-practising-licence-and-why-it-.title: What is a practising licence and why it matters
what-is-a-practising-licence-and-why-it-.excerpt: The difference between a degree or diploma, registration and a licence to practise, explained simply.
what-is-a-practising-licence-and-why-it-.content:
Many graduates think a certificate is enough. In regulated professions it usually is not.

The three steps

  • Certificate: proves you finished a programme.
  • Registration: your name is entered on the professional register.
  • Licence: permission to practise for a period, often renewed regularly.

Why it matters

Practising without the required licence can be illegal and can affect your employer and your patients. Employers often ask for current licences.

How to protect yourself

Keep copies of all documents, set reminders for renewals and avoid agents who promise shortcuts.

Check your cadre

Rules differ by profession and by the law that applies. Ask your regulator or college what applies to you. Regulations and office-holders change, so confirm on the official website before acting on anything here.

Quick revision points

  • Certificate, registration and licence are different.
  • A licence usually needs renewal.
  • Keep copies and set reminders.
  • Avoid shortcuts and agents.
  • Rules differ by cadre.

how-to-read-a-regulator-notice-without-b.title: How to read a regulator notice without being scammed
how-to-read-a-regulator-notice-without-b.excerpt: A checklist for deciding whether a notice about exams, licences or intakes is genuine before you act or pay.
how-to-read-a-regulator-notice-without-b.content:
Fake notices spread fast on WhatsApp and Facebook. A few habits protect you.

Checks

  • Find the same notice on the official website.
  • Do not click links in forwarded messages; type the address or use the official site.
  • Official payments go to official accounts. Be suspicious of personal numbers.
  • Check the date and reference numbers.
  • Look for spelling and design errors, but remember scammers copy well.

When unsure

Call or email the office using contact details from the official website, not from the notice.

Report

Warn classmates and report fake pages to the platform and to the relevant authority.

Remember

Urgency is a manipulation tool. A genuine deadline will still be there after you confirm it. Regulations and office-holders change, so confirm on the official website before acting on anything here.

Quick revision points

  • Find notices on official sites.
  • Do not click forwarded links blindly.
  • Pay only to official accounts.
  • Confirm using official contact details.
  • Urgency is a warning sign.
