Never leave specimens on the floor, in a pocket or unlabelled. Wash your hands. Never photograph a specimen. If a specimen is lost, report immediately.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Labelling later from memory.
  • Putting two patients' specimens in one bag.
  • Not recording in the register.
  • Using the wrong fixative.

Check yourself

What details go on the label?

Patient name and number, specimen, site and side, date and time.

Why read the label aloud?

To check it with a second person.

What if you cannot find a specimen?

Report immediately and search.

Quick revision points

  • Label at the table.
  • Fixative or fresh: ask the surgeon.
  • Read back and double check.
  • Register and sign.
  • Treat as infectious.

inside-the-operating-theatre-surgical-ha.title: Inside the Operating Theatre — Surgical Hand Scrub, 6 Steps
inside-the-operating-theatre-surgical-ha.caption: The six hand movements of a surgical scrub, then rinse and entry to theatre.
inside-the-operating-theatre-surgical-ha.body:
In short: A systematic scrub reaches every surface of the hand. This card shows six movements and what to do after scrubbing.

What the card shows

A red banner reads "Always scrub 2 to 5 minutes, nails and jewellery removed, no touch tap". Preparation: remove jewellery and watch, short nails with no polish, cap and mask on correctly, turn the tap on with the elbow and check the soap. The six steps are palm to palm, back of hands, interlace fingers, back of fingers to palms, thumbs in rotation, and fingertips in rotation, then rinse with hands up and elbows down, repeating for two to five minutes. After Scrub: hands up at chest level, do not shake or touch anything, keep hands higher than elbows, enter the theatre backwards and check there is no dripping in the gowning area.

Why this order

It follows a path through every surface of the hand, so no area is skipped. Doing it the same way every time turns it into muscle memory.

Common errors and habits

Touching the tap afterwards, letting the hands fall below the waist, flicking water, touching the face and water running back to the elbows. Practise before you go to theatre, watch a video, read the chart, use a three-minute timer, keep nails trimmed weekly and learn from the scrub nurse. Scrub times depend on the antiseptic and hospital policy, so follow yours. This card builds on the simpler Hand Scrub Technique card.

Why six movements

Palm to palm cleans the palms. Right palm over the back of the left hand cleans the backs. Interlaced fingers clean between the fingers. Back of fingers to opposing palms cleans the finger backs. Rotating the thumb in the opposite palm cleans the thumbs. Rotating fingertips in the opposite palm cleans the tips and nails. These movements are based on the WHO hand-rubbing technique and cover all common missed areas.

Repeat the sequence on each hand and continue up the forearm as your policy requires.

After the scrub

Rinse from fingers to elbows with hands up. Do not shake the hands. Enter the theatre backwards, holding hands up in front of the body at chest level, or as the unit requires. Dry with a sterile towel and proceed to gown and glove. Follow local timing and products.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Skipping thumbs and fingertips.
  • Touching the tap after scrubbing.
  • Rinsing in the wrong direction.
  • Rushing the sequence.

Check yourself

Which area is often missed?

Thumbs and fingertips.

How should you hold your hands after scrubbing?

Up and in front, above the elbows.

Why practise the sequence?

To make it automatic and complete.

Quick revision points

  • Six movements: palms, backs, between fingers, finger backs, thumbs, fingertips.
  • Rinse fingers to elbows.
  • Hands up.
  • Do not touch anything.
  • Follow local scrub times.

inside-the-operating-theatre-word-of-the.title: Inside the Operating Theatre — Word of the Day: Day 2
inside-the-operating-theatre-word-of-the.caption: Day 2 of the word series: HAEMOSTASIS, how bleeding stops and how surgeons help it.
inside-the-operating-theatre-word-of-the.body:
In short: Haemostasis is the process of stopping bleeding. This card explains the natural process and surgical methods.

What the card shows

Day 2 of the word series features HEMOSTASIS, pronounced "hee-mo-stay-sis", tagged as physiology, in orange cards. What It Means: the process that stops bleeding, through vasoconstriction, a platelet plug, clotting and fibrin sealing the vessel. Why It Matters in Theatre: it prevents excessive blood loss, keeps the surgical field clear and visible and reduces the need for transfusion. You Will See and Hear: the surgeon saying "achieve hemostasis", using diathermy, ligatures and pressure, and checking bleeders before closure. Ezra's Tip says good hemostasis saves lives, so watch how the surgeon checks every bleeder before closing. The Quick Quiz asks you to name two methods, with pressure, diathermy and ligation as answers.

The three steps of natural hemostasis

First the vessel narrows, then platelets stick to form a plug, and finally the clotting cascade builds a fibrin mesh that seals it. Surgery adds mechanical help on top of this natural process.

Why surgeons check before closing

Bleeding that is missed can collect inside the body, cause pain, infection and shock and force a return to theatre. As a student, notice how often the team pauses to check the field and how the swabs are used to look for oozing. Try explaining hemostasis to a friend in two sentences.

The natural process

When a vessel is damaged, it narrows (vasoconstriction), platelets stick to form a plug, and clotting factors build a fibrin mesh to strengthen it. Later the clot is dissolved as the vessel heals. This is called primary and secondary haemostasis.

Things that interfere include anticoagulant drugs, low platelets, clotting disorders, hypothermia and low calcium.

Surgical haemostasis

Surgeons add pressure, clamps and ties (ligatures), diathermy, sutures, topical agents such as gelatin sponges or haemostatic powders, and bone wax. Before closing, they check the field for oozing and count swabs. The theatre team ensures that suction, diathermy, ties and haemostatic agents are ready and monitors blood loss.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Closing before checking for bleeding.
  • Ignoring hypothermia.
  • Not preparing haemostatic agents.
  • Underestimating blood loss on swabs.

Check yourself

Name two surgical haemostasis methods.

Pressure and diathermy (or ligation).

What does vasoconstriction do?

Narrows the vessel to reduce bleeding.

Why does hypothermia worsen bleeding?

Clotting slows.

Quick revision points

  • Haemostasis = stopping bleeding.
  • Vessel narrows, platelet plug, fibrin clot.
  • Surgery adds pressure, diathermy, ties.
  • Keep the patient warm.
  • Check for bleeding before closure.

inside-the-operating-theatre-safe-instru.title: Inside the Operating Theatre — Safe Instrument Handling
inside-the-operating-theatre-safe-instru.caption: Safe passing and handling of instruments and sharps, and what students may and may not do.
inside-the-operating-theatre-safe-instru.body:
In short: Most instrument injuries are avoidable. This card sets out safe passing, sharps rules and boundaries for students.

What the card shows

The banner reads "Always pass sharp away from you, use tray, no hand-to-hand sharps". Sharps Safety: never pass a scalpel blade hand to hand, use a kidney tray, pass the handle first, do not recap, dispose of sharps immediately in a box closed at three-quarters full, wear eye protection and if a sharp falls, let it fall and pick it up with forceps. Instrument Passing: know the names (forceps, scissors, needle holder), pass the handle to the surgeon with the tip away from you, hold firmly, ask if unsure, never throw instruments and learn ten basic instruments in the first week. Student Boundaries: do not hold retractors unless taught, do not load or remove blades, do not handle diathermy, do not adjust suction without asking and keep your hands visible.

Why the tray method

Hand-to-hand sharp passing is the classic cause of sharps injuries. A neutral zone, like a tray, means nobody is ever holding the blade at the same time as another person.

Common errors and habits

Catching a falling sharp, pointing sharps at someone, loading a blade without training, touching the diathermy pedal, forgetting eye protection and passing the wrong instrument. Learn the tray technique, watch the scrub nurse, practise with blunt instruments and say "I am not trained for this" when needed. Double glove when handling sharps and thank the scrub nurse for teaching you.

Safe passing

Use a neutral zone such as a kidney dish or tray for sharps. Announce when you place a sharp. Pass instruments handle first with tips away from people. Use instruments, not fingers, to load and unload blades. Do not catch falling sharps. Discard sharps immediately in a rigid container. Wear eye protection and consider double gloving.

Know the names of basic instruments so you can respond quickly and pass the right one.

Student boundaries

Do not handle blades or diathermy, hold retractors, adjust suction or equipment unless taught and supervised. Keep your hands visible and ask first. Practise passing with blunt instruments in the skills lab. When asked to do something you have not been trained for, say so.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Hand-to-hand passing of sharps.
  • Recapping needles.
  • Catching a falling sharp.
  • Handling blades without training.

Check yourself

Where are sharps placed when passing?

In a neutral zone such as a tray.

What do you do if a sharp falls?

Let it fall and retrieve it with forceps.

Why wear eye protection?

To protect against splashes.

Quick revision points

  • Neutral zone for sharps.
  • Handle first, tip away.
  • Never recap.
  • Dispose immediately.
  • Students work within training.

inside-the-operating-theatre-needle-stic.title: Inside the Operating Theatre — Needle Stick Injury Protocol
inside-the-operating-theatre-needle-stic.caption: First aid, reporting and prevention after a needle-stick or sharps injury.
inside-the-operating-theatre-needle-stic.body:
In short: Acting fast after a sharps injury protects your health. This card shows the first steps and how to prevent injuries.

What the card shows

A red banner warns "Always report: do not hide, wash, do not squeeze, PEP within 72 hours". Immediate First Aid: wash with soap and water, do not squeeze, do not use bleach, let it bleed gently, cover with a plaster, do not touch with bare hands and remove gloves and wash hands. Report Now: tell your supervisor and the theatre in-charge, go to casualty, fill in the incident form, document date, time, device and source patient, get a PEP risk assessment and test the source if known. Prevention: never recap needles, dispose of sharps immediately in a box filled only three-quarters, never pass sharps hand to hand, use a tray or forceps, double glove and do not rush.

Why speed matters

Post-exposure prophylaxis works best when started early, and the card says within 72 hours. Reporting also protects you legally, so never hide an injury.

Common errors

Hiding the injury, scrubbing with bleach, squeezing the wound, working on without reporting, recapping a needle or putting sharps in the wrong bin. Best practices are knowing where casualty and the PEP service are, knowing the incident book, being vaccinated against hepatitis B, never carrying sharps in pockets and speaking up about unsafe disposal. Local protocols differ, so follow your hospital's policy.

What to do at once

Stop what you are doing safely, remove gloves, and wash the wound with soap and running water. Let it bleed gently; do not squeeze, scrub or use bleach. Cover the wound. For splashes to eyes, rinse with clean water or saline. Then report to your supervisor and go to the designated service for assessment and, if indicated, post-exposure prophylaxis, ideally as soon as possible after exposure.

Record the details: when, how, the device, the source patient and your vaccination status.

Prevention is the best protection

Vaccinate against hepatitis B, never recap, use neutral zones, dispose of sharps immediately, keep boxes below the fill line and do not carry sharps in pockets. Work calmly. Report unsafe disposal. Hospitals have local post-exposure protocols and counselling; follow them and keep follow-up appointments.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Hiding the injury.
  • Squeezing or scrubbing the wound.
  • Delaying reporting.
  • Skipping follow-up tests.

Check yourself

What do you do first after a needle-stick?

Wash with soap and water and let it bleed gently.

Why report quickly?

PEP and assessment work best early.

What vaccine protects health workers?

Hepatitis B.

Quick revision points

  • Wash, do not squeeze or scrub.
  • Report immediately.
  • Get PEP assessment.
  • Be vaccinated against hepatitis B.
  • Prevent: no recapping, neutral zone, dispose at once.

inside-the-operating-theatre-meet-your-d.title: Inside the Operating Theatre — Meet Your Defibrillator
inside-the-operating-theatre-meet-your-d.caption: What a defibrillator does and how to check it every day.
inside-the-operating-theatre-meet-your-d.body:
In short: Defibrillators restore a normal heart rhythm in certain cardiac arrests. This card shows the daily checks and safety points.

What the card shows

The banner reads "Always check: power, battery, pads, energy delivery", and three columns follow. 1 Daily Checks: power-on self-test, battery 100 per cent charged, pad expiry and seal intact, cables undamaged. 2 Energy Test: set a 200 J test charge, check that it delivers and sounds the alarm, sign the logbook and report if it fails. 3 Safety: nothing flammable nearby, clear the bed during a shock, check adult or paediatric pads and keep the trolley plugged in. Below are common errors (dead battery, expired pads, no daily test, broken cable) and best practices (same-time daily check, photo of expiry, a sticker with the next due date, a two-person check).

What a defibrillator does

It delivers a controlled electric shock to reset certain dangerous heart rhythms, such as ventricular fibrillation. Early shock is the most important factor in survival, so a machine that does not work is worse than no machine because people trust it.

Why the daily test

A machine that was fine last week may have a flat battery today. The test confirms power, charge and delivery in one go. Test energy settings can differ by machine, so follow your own manufacturer's test procedure. As a student, observe the check, learn where the machine is and never handle it unless trained.

What it does

A defibrillator delivers an electric shock that can stop a chaotic heart rhythm such as ventricular fibrillation and allow the heart's natural pacemaker to take over. It works only for certain rhythms; for others, CPR and drugs are the treatment. Automated external defibrillators analyse the rhythm and guide the user.

Early shock and high-quality CPR together give the best chance of survival.

Daily checks and safety

Check that the device powers on, the battery is charged, the pads are in date and sealed, the cables are intact and the self-test passes. Where a test discharge is part of policy, follow the manufacturer's instructions and sign the log. During use, keep everyone clear, remove oxygen sources from the chest area as protocol requires, avoid wet surfaces and follow the machine's prompts. Only trained staff operate it; students observe.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Skipping daily checks.
  • Using expired pads.
  • Touching the patient during a shock.
  • Leaving the machine unplugged or uncharged.

Check yourself

What rhythm can a defibrillator treat?

Ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia.

What must you do before shock?

Make sure everyone is clear.

What should be checked daily?

Power, battery, pads and cables.

Quick revision points

  • Defibrillators treat certain rhythms only.
  • Check daily and log.
  • Pads in date and sealed.
  • Keep clear during a shock.
  • Only trained staff use it.

inside-the-operating-theatre-perioperati.title: Inside the Operating Theatre — Perioperative Documentation for Students
inside-the-operating-theatre-perioperati.caption: What to document in theatre and how to write records and student logs.
inside-the-operating-theatre-perioperati.body:
In short: Documentation is part of patient safety. This card shows what to record, how to write it and how students should log their learning.

What the card shows

The banner says "Always document: time, date, signature, no blank space, no correction fluid". What To Write: patient name and IP number, diagnosis, procedure, surgeon and anaesthetist, time in and out, count correct, specimen details, implants, drains and catheters, complications and handover notes. How To Write: black pen, legible, no unclear abbreviations, 24-hour time, date as DD/MM/YYYY, cross out blank spaces, sign with name and designation, two-person check for counts and use approved forms only. Student Logs: be objective, say what you observed, your role, what you learned, skills practised, challenges and questions for the next day, and get your supervisor to sign daily.

Why documentation counts

A record that is missing, unsigned or unclear is treated as if the care never happened. It also protects the patient, the staff and the hospital in any later review.

Common errors and habits

Blank spaces, missing signatures or times, forgetting the count, using correction fluid, illegible handwriting, documenting before the procedure is done and writing a patient's name on scrap paper. Better habits are carrying a black pen, writing straight after the case and asking the circulating nurse what needs recording. Learn the forms: theatre register, recovery notes, count sheet and specimen book. Never post notes or patient names online.

The theatre record

Typical entries include patient identification, diagnosis, planned and performed procedure, team members, anaesthesia type, times, counts, specimens, implants, drains, complications and handover. Forms include the theatre register, anaesthesia chart, count sheet, implant log and recovery notes. Each must be legible, signed, dated and timed.

The written record is evidence that checks were done and care was given.

How to write well

Use black ink, clear handwriting and approved abbreviations. Use 24-hour time. Never leave blank spaces without crossing them out. Correct errors with a single line and initials. Write at the time or soon after. Students' logs should be honest, objective and free of patient identifiers.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Leaving blank lines.
  • Using correction fluid.
  • Documenting before the task is done.
  • Using unapproved abbreviations.

Check yourself

How should an error be corrected?

With a single line and initials.

Why use 24-hour time?

To avoid confusion between day and night.

What must a student's log not contain?

Patient identifiers.

Quick revision points

  • Write legibly, sign, date and time.
  • Document counts, specimens and implants.
  • No blank spaces.
  • Single line to correct.
  • Keep confidentiality.

inside-the-operating-theatre-maintaining.title: Inside the Operating Theatre — Maintaining the Sterile Field
inside-the-operating-theatre-maintaining.caption: How to keep the sterile field sterile throughout an operation.
inside-the-operating-theatre-maintaining.body:
In short: Sterility is easy to lose and hard to regain. This card shows the rules, the boundaries and the common breaks.

What the card shows

A red banner says "Always remember: sterile to sterile only, face the sterile field, hands at chest-to-waist level". Sterile Rules: sterile touches sterile only, non-sterile touches non-sterile only, hands stay between chest and waist, never turn your back to the field, keep one metre from non-sterile areas, do not touch your face, mask or cap and if in doubt, you are contaminated. Boundaries: the front from chest to waist is sterile, sleeves from two inches above the elbow to the cuff, below the waist is not, the back is not, do not tuck hands under armpits, stay in the sterile zone and do not walk out of theatre. What Breaks Sterility: hands below the waist, turning to the sterile trolley, touching a non-sterile person, reaching over a non-sterile area, touching the mask or face, sweat dripping and a torn gown or glove.

The golden habit

If you think you may be contaminated, say it out loud: "I am contaminated, change gown and glove." Nobody is blamed for speaking up.

Errors and habits

Hands in pockets, crossing arms under the armpits, touching bed rails and leaning on the trolley are the usual mistakes. Keep your hands clasped at chest height, check the path before moving, give others a wide berth and say "excuse me, sterile" when you need to pass.

The boundaries

On a sterile gown, the front from chest to waist level and the sleeves from about two inches above the elbow to the cuff are considered sterile; the back, shoulders, neck and below-the-waist are not. A sterile table is sterile only on top; edges and anything below the table are not. A one-inch border of drapes and the outside of pack wrappers should be treated as non-sterile.

Because sterility cannot be seen, trust and honesty matter.

Behaviours that protect it

Keep your hands in the sterile zone and visible; face the field; pass back-to-back or face-to-face with another sterile person as taught; do not reach over non-sterile surfaces; keep a metre from non-sterile areas; do not sit or lean on tables; and keep talking to a minimum. If sterility is in doubt, say so and correct it at once.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Turning your back to the field.
  • Reaching over a non-sterile area.
  • Allowing the table edge to count as sterile.
  • Hiding a possible break.

Check yourself

Which part of the gown is sterile?

Front from chest to waist and the sleeves.

What do you do if unsure?

Treat it as contaminated and fix it.

Is the edge of a sterile table sterile?

No.

Quick revision points

  • Sterile to sterile only.
  • Face the field.
  • Keep hands between chest and waist.
  • Treat doubt as contamination.
  • Speak up immediately.

layers-of-the-scalp-scalp-mnemonic.title: Layers of the Scalp — SCALP Mnemonic
layers-of-the-scalp-scalp-mnemonic.caption: The five layers of the scalp, the SCALP mnemonic and why the layers matter in injury and surgery.
layers-of-the-scalp-scalp-mnemonic.body:
In short: The scalp has five layers that are easy to remember with one word. Each layer explains something about scalp wounds, bleeding and infection.

What the card shows

A purple card lists the five layers of the scalp under the heading "Remember: SCALP": skin, connective tissue (dense), aponeurosis (the galea), loose areolar tissue and pericranium. A short box explains why the layers matter.

Why the layers matter

The dense connective tissue layer holds the walls of scalp vessels open, so scalp wounds can bleed freely. The loose areolar layer allows the galea to move over the skull, and it is also the layer through which infection can spread. Learning the order gives you a map of what a scalp wound passes through.

The five layers one by one

S - Skin: thick and hair-bearing, with many oil glands (a common site for sebaceous cysts). C - Connective tissue: dense, fatty tissue rich in blood vessels; its fibrous septa hold vessels open, so scalp cuts bleed heavily. A - Aponeurosis (galea aponeurotica): a tough sheet linking the frontalis and occipitalis muscles. L - Loose areolar tissue: a loose layer that lets the first three layers slide over the skull; infection and blood can spread here. P - Pericranium: the periosteum covering the skull bones.

The first three layers move together and are sometimes called the 'scalp proper'.

Why it matters clinically

Scalp lacerations bleed profusely but usually stop with firm pressure and suturing. A wound that cuts the galea needs careful repair to avoid gaping. Infection in the loose layer can travel through emissary veins into the skull, which is why it is called the 'danger area'. In theatre, neurosurgeons incise through these layers for craniotomy, and the scalp is closed in layers. Local anaesthetic with adrenaline is often injected to reduce bleeding.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Forgetting that the loose layer is the 'danger area'.
  • Underestimating scalp bleeding.
  • Mixing up galea and pericranium.
  • Not closing the galea in layered repair.

Check yourself

What does SCALP stand for?

Skin, Connective tissue, Aponeurosis, Loose areolar tissue, Pericranium.

Why do scalp wounds bleed heavily?

Vessels in the dense layer are held open by connective tissue.

Which layer is the danger area?

The loose areolar tissue layer.

Quick revision points

  • SCALP: Skin, Connective tissue, Aponeurosis, Loose areolar tissue, Pericranium.
  • Dense layer holds vessels open: heavy bleeding.
  • Loose layer: spread of infection.
  • The first three layers move together.
  • Close in layers after surgery.

word-of-the-day-haemostasis.title: Word of the Day: Haemostasis
word-of-the-day-haemostasis.caption: Haemostasis: the stopping of bleeding, naturally and in surgery.
word-of-the-day-haemostasis.body:
In short: Haemostasis is the process that stops bleeding. It is one of the first terms every theatre student must master.

What the card shows

A word-of-the-day card gives the pronunciation, the meaning and two memory hooks: haemo means blood and stasis means standing still.

In theatre

Surgeons and the team achieve haemostasis with pressure, clamps, ties, diathermy or topical agents. A bleeding vessel that is not controlled can quickly change the course of an operation, which is why swabs, suction and good lighting matter.

The word and its parts

Haemo- means blood and -stasis means standing still or stopping. In physiology, haemostasis has three steps: the vessel narrows, platelets form a plug and the clotting cascade builds fibrin to seal the break. In surgery, the term also describes the surgeon's efforts to stop bleeding by pressure, clamps, ligatures, diathermy, sutures and topical agents.

Compare it with 'haemorrhage' (bleeding) and 'haematoma' (collection of blood).

In theatre

The surgeon may say 'achieve haemostasis' before closing or 'check for bleeders'. The team keeps suction, swabs, diathermy and haemostatic products ready, counts swabs and watches blood loss. Patients with low platelets, clotting disorders, certain medicines or hypothermia are at higher risk of bleeding. Always report unusual bleeding or oozing early.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Closing without checking for bleeding.
  • Ignoring slow oozing.
  • Forgetting that cold slows clotting.
  • Not counting blood-soaked swabs.

Check yourself

What does 'stasis' mean?

Standing still or stopping.

Name two ways surgeons achieve haemostasis.

Diathermy and ligation or pressure.

What word means a collection of blood?

Haematoma.

Quick revision points

  • Haemostasis: stopping bleeding.
  • Haemo = blood; stasis = stopping.
  • Methods: pressure, clamps, ties, diathermy, topical agents.
  • Check before closure.
  • Keep the patient warm.

word-of-the-day-asepsis.title: Word of the Day: Asepsis
word-of-the-day-asepsis.caption: Asepsis: preventing contamination, and how it differs from antisepsis.
word-of-the-day-asepsis.body:
In short: Asepsis means keeping harmful microorganisms away. It is the principle behind everything in theatre from scrubbing to draping.

What the card shows

A green word-of-the-day card defines asepsis and notes how it differs from antisepsis. The memory hook reads: A means without, sepsis means infection.

Asepsis versus antisepsis

Asepsis is about preventing contamination in the first place, through hand scrub, sterile gowns and gloves and a protected sterile field. Antisepsis is the use of a chemical on living tissue, such as skin preparation, to reduce the number of germs. Both are needed in theatre.

The word and the idea

A- means without and sepsis refers to infection or putrefaction, so asepsis means 'without infection-causing germs'. It is achieved by sterilisation of instruments, sterile barriers, hand antisepsis and good behaviour in the field.

Antisepsis is the use of chemical agents on living tissue, such as alcohol, chlorhexidine or iodine, to reduce germs on the skin. Disinfection uses chemicals on objects. Sterilisation destroys all microbial life.

Putting it into practice

Aseptic technique includes scrubbing, gowning, gloving, draping, handling instruments without contamination and keeping traffic low. Mistakes include touching sterile items with unsterile hands, using wet or damaged packs and dropping items. If asepsis is broken, correct it immediately. Learn how to explain the difference between asepsis, antisepsis, disinfection and sterilisation in your own words.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Using antisepsis and asepsis interchangeably.
  • Believing disinfected means sterile.
  • Using wet packs.
  • Letting the field be crowded.

Check yourself

What does asepsis prevent?

Contamination and infection.

What is antisepsis?

Reducing germs on living tissue with a chemical.

Is disinfection the same as sterilisation?

No; sterilisation destroys all microbial life.

Quick revision points

  • Asepsis: prevent contamination.
  • Antisepsis: reduce germs on living tissue.
  • Disinfection kills many germs on objects.
  • Sterilisation kills all microbes.
  • Break in asepsis: correct immediately.

team-shout-out-cssd-and-cleaning-staff.title: Team Shout-Out: CSSD and Cleaning Staff
team-shout-out-cssd-and-cleaning-staff.caption: A thank-you to the people who clean, pack, sterilise and turn over theatres.
team-shout-out-cssd-and-cleaning-staff.body:
In short: Behind every safe operation is a team nobody sees. This card says thank you to CSSD and cleaning staff.

What the card shows

A blue shout-out card thanks the CSSD and cleaning teams, with three short reasons they deserve it: clean trays, fast turnover and quiet hard work.

Why it matters

Safe surgery starts long before the first incision. Instruments that were properly cleaned, packed and sterilised, and a room that was properly cleaned between cases, protect every patient. The people who do this work are rarely seen, so a thank-you is well deserved.

What they do

The central sterile services department (CSSD) receives used instruments, cleans them, inspects, packs, sterilises, stores and issues them. Cleaners turn over rooms between cases, clean high-touch surfaces, manage waste and keep the theatre ready. Porters move patients and equipment. These steps happen quietly but each one protects a patient.

Mistakes in cleaning or sterilising can cause infection, so their attention to detail matters.

How to support them

Return instruments promptly and safely, remove gross soil as per policy, keep sharps contained, report damaged instruments, segregate waste and speak politely. A simple thank-you and a clear handover message go a long way. If you are a student, spend time in CSSD to learn how it works.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Treating CSSD as a 'backroom'.
  • Returning instruments with sharps hidden in linen.
  • Dumping waste in the wrong bin.
  • Never saying thank you.

Check yourself

What does CSSD stand for?

Central sterile services department.

Why is cleaning before sterilising important?

Dirt shelters microbes.

How can staff help CSSD?

By returning instruments safely and promptly.

Quick revision points

  • CSSD and cleaners protect every patient.
  • Return instruments safely.
  • Segregate waste correctly.
  • Report damaged instruments.
  • Say thank you.

basic-general-surgery-set-example.title: Basic General Surgery Set (Example)
basic-general-surgery-set-example.caption: An example of what a basic general surgery instrument set may contain, grouped by function.
basic-general-surgery-set-example.body:
In short: A basic set can look like a pile of metal until you group it by job. This card lists an example and shows how to learn it.

What the card shows

A teal card lists an example tray for a basic general set: scalpel handle and blade, dissecting forceps, Mayo and Metzenbaum scissors, artery forceps, Allis tissue forceps, a needle holder, towel clips and sponge-holding forceps. A tip box reminds you that sets differ between hospitals.

Learn it by function

Group the items by what they do: cutting (scalpel, scissors), grasping (forceps), clamping (artery forceps), holding drapes (towel clips), holding swabs (sponge-holding forceps) and suturing (needle holder). It is easier to remember a tray as six jobs than as nine names. See the full article on how to learn instrument names fast.

Six jobs, nine instruments

Cutting: scalpel handle with blade, Mayo scissors (tough tissue), Metzenbaum scissors (delicate tissue). Grasping: dissecting forceps (toothed or plain). Clamping: artery forceps to control bleeding. Holding tissue: Allis forceps. Holding drapes: towel clips. Holding swabs: sponge-holding forceps. Suturing: needle holder. Retractors, suction tips and bowls are usually added by procedure.

The exact contents and names vary between hospitals, countries and surgeons.

How to learn a tray

Lay out a set and name each instrument by sight and touch. Sort them by job. Learn how to hold and pass each safely. After a case, check the count and return the set in the order used by the CSSD. Compare your hospital's tray list with this example and note differences. Ask the scrub practitioner why each item is included.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Assuming all hospitals use the same set.
  • Using instruments for the wrong job.
  • Not counting instruments.
  • Memorising names without handling them.

Check yourself

Which instrument holds the needle?

The needle holder.

What do artery forceps do?

Clamp vessels to control bleeding.

What are towel clips used for?

Holding drapes in place.

Quick revision points

  • Group instruments by function.
  • Know the use of each.
  • Sets differ by hospital.
  • Count before and after.
  • Practise handling and passing.

theatre-abbreviations-quick-list.title: Theatre Abbreviations — Quick List
theatre-abbreviations-quick-list.caption: Seven abbreviations used daily in theatre and what each stands for.
theatre-abbreviations-quick-list.body:
In short: Abbreviations save time and cause confusion if you do not know them. This card lists seven common ones.

What the card shows

A cream card lists seven common abbreviations: OT for operating theatre, CSSD for sterile services, PACU for the recovery unit, GA for general anaesthesia, LA for local anaesthesia, SSI for surgical site infection and PPE for personal protective equipment.

Learn more

There are many more, and some differ between hospitals. Read the longer list in common theatre and hospital abbreviations explained, and ask when you are not sure.

Seven essentials

OT: operating theatre. CSSD: central sterile services department, where instruments are cleaned and sterilised. PACU: post-anaesthesia care unit, the recovery area. GA: general anaesthesia. LA: local anaesthesia. SSI: surgical site infection. PPE: personal protective equipment.

Other frequent ones include NPO (nothing by mouth), IV, ECG, BP, SpO2, ASA (anaesthesia risk class), WHO checklist and DVT.

Using abbreviations safely

In documentation, use only approved abbreviations, because some are ambiguous (for example, 'MS' can mean morphine sulfate or magnesium sulfate). When unsure, write the full term. Keep a notebook of abbreviations you meet and check their meaning with your supervisor. Local lists differ, so learn your hospital's approved list.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Using unapproved abbreviations in records.
  • Assuming everyone uses the same meanings.
  • Writing abbreviations that can be misread.
  • Not asking when unsure.

Check yourself

What does PACU stand for?

Post-anaesthesia care unit.

What does SSI mean?

Surgical site infection.

Where is CSSD?

The central sterile services department.

Quick revision points

  • OT, CSSD, PACU, GA, LA, SSI, PPE.
  • Use approved abbreviations only.
  • If unsure, write it out.
  • Keep a personal glossary.
  • Learn your hospital's list.

monopolar-vs-bipolar-diathermy.title: Monopolar vs bipolar diathermy
monopolar-vs-bipolar-diathermy.caption: Monopolar: current leaves the active electrode, passes through the patient and returns by the return pad.
monopolar-vs-bipolar-diathermy.body:
In short: Monopolar: current leaves the active electrode, passes through the patient and returns by the return pad.

How The Current Flows

Monopolar: current leaves the active electrode, passes through the patient and returns by the return pad.

Bipolar: current passes only between the two tips of the forceps, so no return pad is needed.

Why it matters in theatre

Electrosurgical and energy devices cut and seal tissue with heat. Used correctly they limit bleeding; used carelessly they cause burns and fires, so the team must know the settings and the risks.

Remember

Bipolar is often chosen near nerves and for small structures.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about monopolar vs bipolar diathermy?

Bipolar is often chosen near nerves and for small structures.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

return-pad-where-and-how.title: Return pad: where and how
return-pad-where-and-how.caption: A quick list on return pad: where and how: Large, well-perfused muscular area close to the surgical site; Clean, dry, hairless skin.
return-pad-where-and-how.body:
In short: A quick list on return pad: where and how: Large, well-perfused muscular area close to the surgical site; Clean, dry, hairless skin.

Return pad: where and how

  • Large, well-perfused muscular area close to the surgical site
  • Clean, dry, hairless skin
  • Avoid bony prominences, scar tissue and implants
  • Full pad contact. Never reuse a single-use pad

Why it matters in theatre

Electrosurgical and energy devices cut and seal tissue with heat. Used correctly they limit bleeding; used carelessly they cause burns and fires, so the team must know the settings and the risks.

Remember

A pad with poor contact concentrates current and can burn the skin.

Check yourself

List the points covered under "Return pad: where and how".

Large, well-perfused muscular area close to the surgical site; Clean, dry, hairless skin; Avoid bony prominences, scar tissue and implants; Full pad contact. Never reuse a single-use pad.

cut-coag-and-blend-modes.title: Cut, coag and blend modes
cut-coag-and-blend-modes.caption: Cut: continuous waveform that cuts cleanly with little coagulation.
cut-coag-and-blend-modes.body:
In short: Cut: continuous waveform that cuts cleanly with little coagulation.

Waveforms

Cut: continuous waveform that cuts cleanly with little coagulation.

Coag: interrupted bursts of higher voltage that seal vessels but cause more tissue damage.

Blend: a mix of both.

Why it matters in theatre

Electrosurgical and energy devices cut and seal tissue with heat. Used correctly they limit bleeding; used carelessly they cause burns and fires, so the team must know the settings and the risks.

Remember

Use the lowest power that does the job.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about cut, coag and blend modes?

why-diathermy-burns-happen.title: Why diathermy burns happen
why-diathermy-burns-happen.caption: A quick list on why diathermy burns happen: Poor return-pad contact or a wet pad site; Pooled prep fluid under the patient.
why-diathermy-burns-happen.body:
In short: A quick list on why diathermy burns happen: Poor return-pad contact or a wet pad site; Pooled prep fluid under the patient.

Why diathermy burns happen

  • Poor return-pad contact or a wet pad site
  • Pooled prep fluid under the patient
  • Active electrode left on the drapes or on the patient
  • Capacitive coupling or insulation faults in laparoscopy

Why it matters in theatre

Electrosurgical and energy devices cut and seal tissue with heat. Used correctly they limit bleeding; used carelessly they cause burns and fires, so the team must know the settings and the risks.

Remember

Holster the active electrode whenever it is not in use.

Check yourself

alcohol-skin-prep-and-fire.title: Alcohol skin prep and fire
alcohol-skin-prep-and-fire.caption: Alcohol-based skin prep is flammable.
alcohol-skin-prep-and-fire.body:
In short: Alcohol-based skin prep is flammable.

Dry Before You Drape

Alcohol-based skin prep is flammable. It must dry fully before draping or using diathermy.

Check for pooling in the umbilicus, under the patient and in the hair.

Why it matters in theatre

Electrosurgical and energy devices cut and seal tissue with heat. Used correctly they limit bleeding; used carelessly they cause burns and fires, so the team must know the settings and the risks.

Remember

Follow the product's stated dry time. Do not guess.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about alcohol skin prep and fire?

Follow the product's stated dry time. Do not guess.

the-theatre-fire-triangle.title: The theatre fire triangle
the-theatre-fire-triangle.caption: A quick list on the theatre fire triangle: OXYGEN: enriched oxygen and nitrous oxide help fire spread; IGNITION: diathermy, laser, fibre-optic light cable.
the-theatre-fire-triangle.body:
In short: A quick list on the theatre fire triangle: OXYGEN: enriched oxygen and nitrous oxide help fire spread; IGNITION: diathermy, laser, fibre-optic light cable.

The theatre fire triangle

  • OXYGEN: enriched oxygen and nitrous oxide help fire spread
  • IGNITION: diathermy, laser, fibre-optic light cable
  • FUEL: drapes, alcohol, gauze, airway tubes
  • Airway fires are the highest risk in head and neck surgery

Why it matters in theatre

Electrosurgical and energy devices cut and seal tissue with heat. Used correctly they limit bleeding; used carelessly they cause burns and fires, so the team must know the settings and the risks.

Remember

Know the fire plan and who turns off the gas.

OXYGEN: enriched oxygen and nitrous oxide help fire spread; IGNITION: diathermy, laser, fibre-optic light cable; FUEL: drapes, alcohol, gauze, airway tubes; Airway fires are the highest risk in head and neck surgery.

surgical-smoke-is-not-harmless.title: Surgical smoke is not harmless
surgical-smoke-is-not-harmless.caption: Smoke from diathermy and lasers contains particles, chemicals and sometimes biological material.
surgical-smoke-is-not-harmless.body:
In short: Smoke from diathermy and lasers contains particles, chemicals and sometimes biological material.

Plume

Smoke from diathermy and lasers contains particles, chemicals and sometimes biological material.

A plain surgical mask does not filter the finest particles.

Use a smoke evacuator or suction held close to the source.

Why it matters in theatre

Electrosurgical and energy devices cut and seal tissue with heat. Used correctly they limit bleeding; used carelessly they cause burns and fires, so the team must know the settings and the risks.

Remember

Evacuate the plume at the source, not just wear a mask.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about surgical smoke is not harmless?

Evacuate the plume at the source, not just wear a mask.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

pacemakers-and-diathermy.title: Pacemakers and diathermy
pacemakers-and-diathermy.caption: Diathermy can interfere with a pacemaker or ICD.
pacemakers-and-diathermy.body:
In short: Diathermy can interfere with a pacemaker or ICD.

Risk

Diathermy can interfere with a pacemaker or ICD. It may inhibit pacing or trigger a shock.

Bipolar or short bursts, a return pad placed away from the device, and a defibrillator close by are the usual precautions.

Why it matters in theatre

Electrosurgical and energy devices cut and seal tissue with heat. Used correctly they limit bleeding; used carelessly they cause burns and fires, so the team must know the settings and the risks.

Remember

The device plan comes from the anaesthetist and cardiology team.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about pacemakers and diathermy?

The device plan comes from the anaesthetist and cardiology team.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

ultrasonic-and-vessel-sealing-devices.title: Ultrasonic and vessel-sealing devices
ultrasonic-and-vessel-sealing-devices.caption: Ultrasonic scalpels use blade vibration (around 55 kHz) to cut and seal, with less lateral heat spread than monopolar.
ultrasonic-and-vessel-sealing-devices.body:
In short: Ultrasonic scalpels use blade vibration (around 55 kHz) to cut and seal, with less lateral heat spread than monopolar.

Not All Energy Is The Same

Ultrasonic scalpels use blade vibration (around 55 kHz) to cut and seal, with less lateral heat spread than monopolar.

Bipolar vessel sealers combine pressure and energy with feedback to seal larger vessels.

Why it matters in theatre

Electrosurgical and energy devices cut and seal tissue with heat. Used correctly they limit bleeding; used carelessly they cause burns and fires, so the team must know the settings and the risks.

Remember

Jaws stay hot after use. Do not touch tissue with them.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about ultrasonic and vessel-sealing devices?

Jaws stay hot after use. Do not touch tissue with them.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

argon-plasma-coagulation.title: Argon plasma coagulation
argon-plasma-coagulation.caption: Argon gas flows over a monopolar current and carries it to the tissue without touching it.
argon-plasma-coagulation.body:
In short: Argon gas flows over a monopolar current and carries it to the tissue without touching it.

Non-Contact Coagulation

Argon gas flows over a monopolar current and carries it to the tissue without touching it. It is good for broad oozing surfaces.

Risk: argon gas can enter vessels and cause gas embolism, and it raises pressure in a closed cavity.

Why it matters in theatre

Electrosurgical and energy devices cut and seal tissue with heat. Used correctly they limit bleeding; used carelessly they cause burns and fires, so the team must know the settings and the risks.

Remember

Always keep a gas outflow route open.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about argon plasma coagulation?

Always keep a gas outflow route open.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

steam-sterilisation-time-and-temperature.title: Steam sterilisation: time and temperature
steam-sterilisation-time-and-temperature.caption: Two widely used steam cycles are about 121 °C (roughly 15 to 30 minutes) and about 134 °C (roughly 3 to 4 minutes for unwrapped, longer for wrapped loads).
steam-sterilisation-time-and-temperature.body:
In short: Two widely used steam cycles are about 121 °C (roughly 15 to 30 minutes) and about 134 °C (roughly 3 to 4 minutes for unwrapped, longer for wrapped loads).

Common Cycles

Two widely used steam cycles are about 121 °C (roughly 15 to 30 minutes) and about 134 °C (roughly 3 to 4 minutes for unwrapped, longer for wrapped loads).

Exact times depend on the steriliser, the load and the wrapping.

Why it matters in theatre

Sterilisation is what makes instruments safe to use inside the body. Knowing how each method works and how it is checked helps you spot a failed load before it reaches a patient.

Remember

The manufacturer's instructions decide, not memory.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about steam sterilisation: time and temperature?

The manufacturer's instructions decide, not memory.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

the-bowie-dick-test.title: The Bowie-Dick test
the-bowie-dick-test.caption: Run in an empty pre-vacuum steam steriliser before the first load of the day.
the-bowie-dick-test.body:
In short: Run in an empty pre-vacuum steam steriliser before the first load of the day.

Daily Air-Removal Test

Run in an empty pre-vacuum steam steriliser before the first load of the day.

It shows whether air was removed and steam reached the whole pack. A failed test means do not use the machine until it is checked.

Why it matters in theatre

Sterilisation is what makes instruments safe to use inside the body. Knowing how each method works and how it is checked helps you spot a failed load before it reaches a patient.

Remember

Not used for gravity-displacement sterilisers.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about the bowie-dick test?

Not used for gravity-displacement sterilisers.

chemical-vs-biological-indicators.title: Chemical vs biological indicators
chemical-vs-biological-indicators.caption: Chemical indicators change colour when exposed to certain conditions.
chemical-vs-biological-indicators.body:
In short: Chemical indicators change colour when exposed to certain conditions.

What Each Proves

Chemical indicators change colour when exposed to certain conditions. They show the pack was processed, not that it is sterile.

Biological indicators use resistant spores (Geobacillus stearothermophilus for steam). If the spores are killed, the cycle worked.

Why it matters in theatre

Sterilisation is what makes instruments safe to use inside the body. Knowing how each method works and how it is checked helps you spot a failed load before it reaches a patient.

Remember

Biological indicators are the gold standard check.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about chemical vs biological indicators?

Biological indicators are the gold standard check.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

wet-packs-are-not-sterile.title: Wet packs are not sterile
wet-packs-are-not-sterile.caption: A quick list on wet packs are not sterile: Moisture lets microbes travel through wrapping; Causes: overloaded trays, wrong packing, poor drying.
wet-packs-are-not-sterile.body:
In short: A quick list on wet packs are not sterile: Moisture lets microbes travel through wrapping; Causes: overloaded trays, wrong packing, poor drying.

Wet packs are not sterile

  • Moisture lets microbes travel through wrapping
  • Causes: overloaded trays, wrong packing, poor drying
  • Do not use. Repack and reprocess
  • Report the load to the sterile services lead

Why it matters in theatre

Sterilisation is what makes instruments safe to use inside the body. Knowing how each method works and how it is checked helps you spot a failed load before it reaches a patient.

Remember

A wet pack counts as contaminated. Never use it.

Check yourself

List the points covered under "Wet packs are not sterile".

Moisture lets microbes travel through wrapping; Causes: overloaded trays, wrong packing, poor drying; Do not use. Repack and reprocess; Report the load to the sterile services lead.

flash-immediate-use-sterilisation.title: Flash (immediate-use) sterilisation
flash-immediate-use-sterilisation.caption: Unwrapped steam sterilisation for an instrument needed at once.
flash-immediate-use-sterilisation.body:
In short: Unwrapped steam sterilisation for an instrument needed at once.

Last Resort

Unwrapped steam sterilisation for an instrument needed at once. It is meant for urgent situations, not convenience or a shortage of sets.

Risk: contamination during transfer, and less monitoring than a full cycle.

Why it matters in theatre

Sterilisation is what makes instruments safe to use inside the body. Knowing how each method works and how it is checked helps you spot a failed load before it reaches a patient.

Remember

Fix the instrument supply problem. Do not rely on flashing.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about flash (immediate-use) sterilisation?

Fix the instrument supply problem. Do not rely on flashing.

sterilisation-does-not-clean.title: Sterilisation does not clean
sterilisation-does-not-clean.caption: A quick list on sterilisation does not clean: Blood and tissue protect microbes from steam; Pre-clean at the point of use. Do not let blood dry.
sterilisation-does-not-clean.body:
In short: A quick list on sterilisation does not clean: Blood and tissue protect microbes from steam; Pre-clean at the point of use. Do not let blood dry.

Sterilisation does not clean

  • Blood and tissue protect microbes from steam
  • Pre-clean at the point of use. Do not let blood dry
  • Wash by hand or in a washer-disinfector, then inspect
  • Only clean, dry, working instruments are packed

Sterilisation is what makes instruments safe to use inside the body. Knowing how each method works and how it is checked helps you spot a failed load before it reaches a patient.

Remember

Dirty instruments can fail even a perfect cycle.

ultrasonic-cleaning-basics.title: Ultrasonic cleaning basics
ultrasonic-cleaning-basics.caption: The cleaner uses high-frequency sound to create tiny bubbles that lift debris from crevices.
ultrasonic-cleaning-basics.body:
In short: The cleaner uses high-frequency sound to create tiny bubbles that lift debris from crevices.

Cavitation

The cleaner uses high-frequency sound to create tiny bubbles that lift debris from crevices.

Open hinged instruments, avoid mixing dissimilar metals and change the solution often. Check the manufacturer's guidance for delicate or lensed items.

low-temperature-sterilisation.title: Low-temperature sterilisation
low-temperature-sterilisation.caption: Items that cannot take steam may use ethylene oxide or hydrogen peroxide gas plasma.
low-temperature-sterilisation.body:
In short: Items that cannot take steam may use ethylene oxide or hydrogen peroxide gas plasma.

For Heat-Sensitive Items

Items that cannot take steam may use ethylene oxide or hydrogen peroxide gas plasma.

Ethylene oxide is toxic and needs aeration afterwards. Plasma systems have limits on long narrow lumens and on liquids and paper-based materials.

Why it matters in theatre

Sterilisation is what makes instruments safe to use inside the body. Knowing how each method works and how it is checked helps you spot a failed load before it reaches a patient.

how-long-does-a-sterile-pack-stay-steril.title: How long does a sterile pack stay sterile?
how-long-does-a-sterile-pack-stay-steril.caption: Many guidelines treat sterility as event-related: the pack stays sterile until its integrity is compromised (torn, wet, dropped, opened).
how-long-does-a-sterile-pack-stay-steril.body:
In short: Many guidelines treat sterility as event-related: the pack stays sterile until its integrity is compromised (torn, wet, dropped, opened).

Event-Related Shelf Life

Many guidelines treat sterility as event-related: the pack stays sterile until its integrity is compromised (torn, wet, dropped, opened).

Storage must be clean, dry and off the floor. Policies may still set a maximum time.

Why it matters in theatre

Sterilisation is what makes instruments safe to use inside the body. Knowing how each method works and how it is checked helps you spot a failed load before it reaches a patient.

Remember

Check the seal, indicator and date every time.

Check yourself

prions-and-special-instruments.title: Prions and special instruments
prions-and-special-instruments.caption: Prions resist ordinary sterilisation.
prions-and-special-instruments.body:
In short: Prions resist ordinary sterilisation.

Cjd Risk

Prions resist ordinary sterilisation. For high-risk tissue, national guidance may require quarantine, single-use instruments, destruction or a special decontamination process.

Standard autoclave cycles are not enough on their own.

Why it matters in theatre

Sterilisation is what makes instruments safe to use inside the body. Knowing how each method works and how it is checked helps you spot a failed load before it reaches a patient.

Remember

Ask infection control before reprocessing any suspected case.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about prions and special instruments?

Ask infection control before reprocessing any suspected case.

reading-the-capnograph.title: Reading the capnograph
reading-the-capnograph.caption: Capnography shows each breath.
reading-the-capnograph.body:
In short: Capnography shows each breath.

End-Tidal Co2

Capnography shows each breath. A normal end-tidal CO2 is roughly 35 to 45 mmHg.

A flat or absent trace can mean a misplaced tube, a disconnection, an obstructed circuit or no circulation.

Why it matters in theatre

Anaesthesia removes pain and awareness but also takes over protective reflexes and breathing. Understanding the basics lets theatre staff support the anaesthetic team and notice problems early.

Remember

No trace means no ventilation until proven otherwise.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about reading the capnograph?

No trace means no ventilation until proven otherwise.

limits-of-pulse-oximetry.title: Limits of pulse oximetry
limits-of-pulse-oximetry.caption: A quick list on limits of pulse oximetry: SpO2 is normally 95 to 100 percent; It lags behind real changes in oxygenation.
limits-of-pulse-oximetry.body:
In short: A quick list on limits of pulse oximetry: SpO2 is normally 95 to 100 percent; It lags behind real changes in oxygenation.

Limits of pulse oximetry

  • SpO2 is normally 95 to 100 percent
  • It lags behind real changes in oxygenation
  • Poor perfusion, motion, cold fingers and some nail products reduce accuracy
  • Carbon monoxide poisoning can give a falsely normal reading

Why it matters in theatre

Anaesthesia removes pain and awareness but also takes over protective reflexes and breathing. Understanding the basics lets theatre staff support the anaesthetic team and notice problems early.

Remember

SpO2 does not measure how well the patient is breathing.

anaesthetic-gases-and-scavenging.caption: Common volatile agents include sevoflurane, isoflurane and desflurane.
anaesthetic-gases-and-scavenging.body:
In short: Common volatile agents include sevoflurane, isoflurane and desflurane.

Waste Gas

Common volatile agents include sevoflurane, isoflurane and desflurane. Nitrous oxide is used with them in many settings.

A scavenging system carries waste gas out of the theatre to reduce staff exposure.

Anaesthesia removes pain and awareness but also takes over protective reflexes and breathing. Understanding the basics lets theatre staff support the anaesthetic team and notice problems early.

when-the-oxygen-supply-fails.caption: A quick list on when the oxygen supply fails: Switch to the backup cylinder on the machine; Check the cylinder has enough contents before every list.
when-the-oxygen-supply-fails.body:
In short: A quick list on when the oxygen supply fails: Switch to the backup cylinder on the machine; Check the cylinder has enough contents before every list.

When the oxygen supply fails

  • Switch to the backup cylinder on the machine
  • Check the cylinder has enough contents before every list
  • Use a self-inflating bag with room air if oxygen is lost
  • Tell the whole team at once

Anaesthesia removes pain and awareness but also takes over protective reflexes and breathing. Understanding the basics lets theatre staff support the anaesthetic team and notice problems early.

Know where the backup cylinders and the bag are.

medical-gas-colours-differ-by-country.caption: Colour codes for gas cylinders follow national or regional standards.
medical-gas-colours-differ-by-country.body:
In short: Colour codes for gas cylinders follow national or regional standards.

Read The Label

Colour codes for gas cylinders follow national or regional standards. Under international ISO colours, oxygen is white and nitrous oxide is blue, but older cylinders and other countries differ.

Only the label and the pin-index or connector are reliable.

Why it matters in theatre

Anaesthesia removes pain and awareness but also takes over protective reflexes and breathing. Understanding the basics lets theatre staff support the anaesthetic team and notice problems early.

Never choose a cylinder by colour alone.

hypothermia-under-anaesthesia.title: Hypothermia under anaesthesia
hypothermia-under-anaesthesia.caption: Anaesthesia widens blood vessels and moves heat from the core to the skin.
hypothermia-under-anaesthesia.body:
In short: Anaesthesia widens blood vessels and moves heat from the core to the skin.

Why Patients Get Cold

Anaesthesia widens blood vessels and moves heat from the core to the skin. Cold fluids, cold air and exposure add to the loss.

Hypothermia raises the risk of bleeding, wound infection and shivering.

Why it matters in theatre

Anaesthesia removes pain and awareness but also takes over protective reflexes and breathing. Understanding the basics lets theatre staff support the anaesthetic team and notice problems early.

Remember

Use forced-air warming and warmed fluids.

  • Fast heart rate and stiff jaw muscles (masseter spasm)

Stop the triggers, call for help and get the dantrolene.

blood-pressure-cuff-size-matters.caption: A cuff that is too small gives a falsely high reading.
blood-pressure-cuff-size-matters.body:
In short: A cuff that is too small gives a falsely high reading.

A Wrong Cuff Gives Wrong Numbers

A cuff that is too small gives a falsely high reading. One that is too large reads falsely low.

The bladder width should be roughly 40 percent of the arm circumference.

Why it matters in theatre

Anaesthesia removes pain and awareness but also takes over protective reflexes and breathing. Understanding the basics lets theatre staff support the anaesthetic team and notice problems early.

Remember

Check the cuff size before the first reading.

the-arterial-line-basics.title: The arterial line basics
the-arterial-line-basics.caption: A cannula in an artery connects to a pressure transducer.
the-arterial-line-basics.body:
In short: A cannula in an artery connects to a pressure transducer.

Beat-To-Beat Pressure

A cannula in an artery connects to a pressure transducer. It shows blood pressure every beat and allows blood sampling.

The transducer is levelled at the heart and zeroed to atmospheric pressure.

Why it matters in theatre

Anaesthesia removes pain and awareness but also takes over protective reflexes and breathing. Understanding the basics lets theatre staff support the anaesthetic team and notice problems early.

Remember

Re-level and re-zero after any change in position.

What is the main thing to remember about the arterial line basics?

laryngospasm-vs-bronchospasm.title: Laryngospasm vs bronchospasm
laryngospasm-vs-bronchospasm.caption: Laryngospasm: the vocal cords close.
laryngospasm-vs-bronchospasm.body:
In short: Laryngospasm: the vocal cords close.

Two Different Problems

Laryngospasm: the vocal cords close. You may see stridor, then a silent chest and difficulty bagging.

Bronchospasm: the small airways narrow. You hear wheeze and see high airway pressures.

Both are emergencies.

Why it matters in theatre

Anaesthesia removes pain and awareness but also takes over protective reflexes and breathing. Understanding the basics lets theatre staff support the anaesthetic team and notice problems early.

Remember

Call the anaesthetist at once for either.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about laryngospasm vs bronchospasm?

Call the anaesthetist at once for either.

arm-abduction-and-the-brachial-plexus.title: Arm abduction and the brachial plexus
arm-abduction-and-the-brachial-plexus.caption: Arms on boards abducted beyond 90 degrees or pulled back can stretch the brachial plexus.
arm-abduction-and-the-brachial-plexus.body:
In short: Arms on boards abducted beyond 90 degrees or pulled back can stretch the brachial plexus.

90 Degrees

Arms on boards abducted beyond 90 degrees or pulled back can stretch the brachial plexus.

Keep the arm at or under 90 degrees with the palm up and the head in a neutral position.

Why it matters in theatre

The way a patient is placed can protect or injure nerves, skin and circulation, particularly when they cannot feel or move. Good positioning is a team responsibility.

Remember

Check arms again after any table tilt.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about arm abduction and the brachial plexus?

Check arms again after any table tilt.

ulnar-nerve-at-the-elbow.title: Ulnar nerve at the elbow
ulnar-nerve-at-the-elbow.caption: The ulnar nerve runs close to the skin behind the elbow.
ulnar-nerve-at-the-elbow.body:
In short: The ulnar nerve runs close to the skin behind the elbow.

Pad The Elbow

The ulnar nerve runs close to the skin behind the elbow. Pressure from the table or a hard edge can injure it.

Pad the elbow and avoid leaving the forearm in a position that squeezes the nerve.

Why it matters in theatre

The way a patient is placed can protect or injure nerves, skin and circulation, particularly when they cannot feel or move. Good positioning is a team responsibility.

Remember

Padding is only part of the protection. Position matters too.

common-peroneal-nerve-and-foot-drop.title: Common peroneal nerve and foot drop
common-peroneal-nerve-and-foot-drop.caption: The common peroneal nerve wraps around the fibular head below the knee.
common-peroneal-nerve-and-foot-drop.body:
In short: The common peroneal nerve wraps around the fibular head below the knee.

Lateral Leg

The common peroneal nerve wraps around the fibular head below the knee. Pressure from stirrups or straps can injure it and cause foot drop.

Pad the outside of the lower leg and avoid tight leg holders.

Why it matters in theatre

The way a patient is placed can protect or injure nerves, skin and circulation, particularly when they cannot feel or move. Good positioning is a team responsibility.

Remember

Check leg supports at every position change.

Check yourself

lithotomy-position-risks.caption: A quick list on lithotomy position risks: Nerve injury in the legs from stirrup pressure; Compartment syndrome in long cases.
lithotomy-position-risks.body:
In short: A quick list on lithotomy position risks: Nerve injury in the legs from stirrup pressure; Compartment syndrome in long cases.

Lithotomy position risks

  • Nerve injury in the legs from stirrup pressure
  • Compartment syndrome in long cases
  • Blood pressure changes when legs are raised or lowered
  • Raise and lower both legs together and slowly

The way a patient is placed can protect or injure nerves, skin and circulation, particularly when they cannot feel or move. Good positioning is a team responsibility.

Limit time in lithotomy where the surgery allows.

trendelenburg-tilt.caption: Head-down tilt raises venous return but also pressure in the head and eyes.
trendelenburg-tilt.body:
In short: Head-down tilt raises venous return but also pressure in the head and eyes.

Head Down

Head-down tilt raises venous return but also pressure in the head and eyes. Face and airway swelling can build up in long cases.

Patients can slide: use a non-slip mat and secure supports without pressing on the shoulders.

Why it matters in theatre

The way a patient is placed can protect or injure nerves, skin and circulation, particularly when they cannot feel or move. Good positioning is a team responsibility.

Remember

Shoulder braces can injure the brachial plexus.

head-up-positions-and-air-embolism.title: Head-up positions and air embolism
head-up-positions-and-air-embolism.caption: In sitting or beach-chair positions the surgical site can be above the heart.
head-up-positions-and-air-embolism.body:
In short: In sitting or beach-chair positions the surgical site can be above the heart.

When The Head Is Above The Heart

In sitting or beach-chair positions the surgical site can be above the heart. Air can be drawn into open veins, and blood pressure to the brain can fall.

Blood pressure should be measured at brain level, not on the arm.

Why it matters in theatre

The way a patient is placed can protect or injure nerves, skin and circulation, particularly when they cannot feel or move. Good positioning is a team responsibility.

Remember

Tell the anaesthetist about any sudden drop in ETCO2.

prone-position-checks.caption: A quick list on prone position checks: Eyes free of any pressure (corneal injury and vision loss risk); Neck in a neutral line.

pressure-injury-in-theatre.title: Pressure injury in theatre
pressure-injury-in-theatre.caption: Pressure injuries form over bony areas such as the sacrum, heels and back of the head.
pressure-injury-in-theatre.body:
In short: Pressure injuries form over bony areas such as the sacrum, heels and back of the head.

Pressure, Shear And Time

Pressure injuries form over bony areas such as the sacrum, heels and back of the head. Long cases, poor circulation and moisture raise the risk.

Pad bony areas and avoid dragging the patient across the surface.

Why it matters in theatre

The way a patient is placed can protect or injure nerves, skin and circulation, particularly when they cannot feel or move. Good positioning is a team responsibility.

Remember

Lift, do not drag, during transfers.

lateral-position-and-the-axillary-roll.caption: A roll is placed just below the armpit, supporting the chest wall so that the weight of the chest does not press on the lower arm and nerves.
lateral-position-and-the-axillary-roll.body:
In short: A roll is placed just below the armpit, supporting the chest wall so that the weight of the chest does not press on the lower arm and nerves.

Side-Lying

A roll is placed just below the armpit, supporting the chest wall so that the weight of the chest does not press on the lower arm and nerves.

Pad between the knees and support the upper arm.

The way a patient is placed can protect or injure nerves, skin and circulation, particularly when they cannot feel or move. Good positioning is a team responsibility.

Remember

The roll goes under the chest, not in the armpit.

Moving the unconscious patient

  • Use slide sheets. Lock all wheels

retained-surgical-items.title: Retained surgical items
retained-surgical-items.caption: Swabs are the most commonly retained items.
retained-surgical-items.body:
In short: Swabs are the most commonly retained items.

Counts

Swabs are the most commonly retained items. Counts happen before the procedure, before closing a cavity and at skin closure.

If a count is wrong, stop and recount. If still wrong, imaging may be needed before the patient leaves.

Why it matters in theatre

Theatre combines sharp tools, electricity, gases, radiation and many people. Routine safety habits prevent harm to patients and staff.

Remember

Never ignore a count discrepancy.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about retained surgical items?

Never ignore a count discrepancy.

count-rules-that-work.title: Count rules that work
count-rules-that-work.caption: A quick list on count rules that work: Count aloud, together, in the same order every time; No swabs or sharps leave the room.
count-rules-that-work.body:
In short: A quick list on count rules that work: Count aloud, together, in the same order every time; No swabs or sharps leave the room.

Count rules that work

  • Count aloud, together, in the same order every time
  • No swabs or sharps leave the room
  • Tell the surgeon at once about any discrepancy
  • Record every count in the notes

Count when relieved by another team member too.

The checklist has 19 items in three phases: Sign In (before anaesthesia), Time Out (before incision) and Sign Out (before the patient leaves the room).

It is a tool for team communication, not a tick box.

Sharps safety

latex-allergy.caption: Latex allergy can range from skin reactions to life-threatening anaphylaxis.
latex-allergy.body:

Risk

Latex allergy can range from skin reactions to life-threatening anaphylaxis. Risk is higher in people with repeated surgery, spina bifida or certain food allergies.

Plan latex-free equipment and list the patient first where possible.

Why it matters in theatre

Theatre combines sharp tools, electricity, gases, radiation and many people. Routine safety habits prevent harm to patients and staff.

Remember

Flag latex allergy on the board and at the Time Out.

radiation-protection-in-theatre.caption: Reduce time in the beam, stand as far away as possible and use shielding.
radiation-protection-in-theatre.body:
In short: Reduce time in the beam, stand as far away as possible and use shielding.

Time, Distance, Shielding

Reduce time in the beam, stand as far away as possible and use shielding. Radiation dose falls with the square of the distance.

Wear a lead apron, thyroid collar and a dosimeter badge when working near X-rays.

Why it matters in theatre

Theatre combines sharp tools, electricity, gases, radiation and many people. Routine safety habits prevent harm to patients and staff.

Remember

Step back, even by one metre.

Check yourself

Step back, even by one metre.

Choosing A Prep

Both chlorhexidine-alcohol and povidone-iodine reduce skin bacteria, and many guidelines favour chlorhexidine-alcohol for most surgery.

Chlorhexidine should not be used on the eyes, ears or exposed brain tissue. Check for allergy before use.

Why it matters in theatre

Theatre combines sharp tools, electricity, gases, radiation and many people. Routine safety habits prevent harm to patients and staff.

Remember

Let the prep dry fully before draping.

pneumoperitoneum-pressure.caption: Adult laparoscopy usually keeps intra-abdominal pressure around 12 to 15 mmHg.

Co2 Insufflation

Adult laparoscopy usually keeps intra-abdominal pressure around 12 to 15 mmHg.

Higher pressure reduces venous return and lung expansion. The aim is the lowest pressure that gives a safe view.

Keyhole surgery uses cameras and gas inside the body. It reduces recovery time but brings its own equipment problems and complications that staff must anticipate.

Report any rise in pressure or gas flow alarms.

why-carbon-dioxide-is-used.title: Why carbon dioxide is used
why-carbon-dioxide-is-used.caption: Carbon dioxide does not support combustion and is absorbed and cleared quickly if it enters a vessel.
why-carbon-dioxide-is-used.body:
In short: Carbon dioxide does not support combustion and is absorbed and cleared quickly if it enters a vessel.

The Gas Choice

Carbon dioxide does not support combustion and is absorbed and cleared quickly if it enters a vessel.

The trade-off: it raises blood CO2, can cause acidosis and often causes shoulder-tip pain afterwards.

Why it matters in theatre

Keyhole surgery uses cameras and gas inside the body. It reduces recovery time but brings its own equipment problems and complications that staff must anticipate.

Remember

The anaesthetist watches ETCO2 closely.

closed-vs-open-entry.caption: Closed entry uses a Veress needle with safety checks before insufflation.
closed-vs-open-entry.body:

Getting In Safely

Closed entry uses a Veress needle with safety checks before insufflation. Open (Hasson) entry cuts down to the peritoneum and places the port under vision.

Neither technique removes the risk of injury to bowel or vessels.

Keyhole surgery uses cameras and gas inside the body. It reduces recovery time but brings its own equipment problems and complications that staff must anticipate.

Remember

Report any sudden blood loss or low pressure on entry.

Rigid scopes are cleaned, then sterilised as the manufacturer allows. Channels must be brushed and flushed.

Keyhole surgery uses cameras and gas inside the body. It reduces recovery time but brings its own equipment problems and complications that staff must anticipate.

Keyhole surgery uses cameras and gas inside the body. It reduces recovery time but brings its own equipment problems and complications that staff must anticipate.

Spinal anaesthesia lets the awake patient show early signs.

Keyhole surgery uses cameras and gas inside the body. It reduces recovery time but brings its own equipment problems and complications that staff must anticipate.

Ports

Common laparoscopic ports are 5 mm, 10 to 11 mm and 12 mm. Larger ports are used for staplers, specimen bags and some instruments.

The size decides whether the fascia needs closing at the end.

Keyhole surgery uses cameras and gas inside the body. It reduces recovery time but brings its own equipment problems and complications that staff must anticipate.

how-long-absorbable-sutures-last.title: How long absorbable sutures last
how-long-absorbable-sutures-last.caption: Polyglactin 910 (Vicryl) is absorbed in roughly two to three months.
how-long-absorbable-sutures-last.body:
In short: Polyglactin 910 (Vicryl) is absorbed in roughly two to three months.

Before You Pick

Polyglactin 910 (Vicryl) is absorbed in roughly two to three months. Polydioxanone (PDS) holds strength longer, often around six months.

Plain gut is absorbed in days to weeks. Times vary with the tissue and the patient.

Why it matters in theatre

Sutures, needles and closure methods decide how well a wound holds and heals. Choosing and handling them correctly is part of every operation.

Choose by how long the tissue needs support.

suture-sizes-more-zeros-thinner-thread.body:

Usp Size

Sizes such as 3-0 and 6-0 get thinner as the number before the zero rises. A 0 is thicker than a 3-0, and a 6-0 is much finer.

Fine sutures are used for skin of the face and vessels. Thicker ones for fascia.

loading-the-needle-holder.body:

Grasp the needle roughly one-third to one-half of the way from the swage (thread end) towards the tip, at right angles to the jaws.

Gripping near the tip makes the needle blunt and difficult to drive. Near the swage it may bend or break.

Sutures, needles and closure methods decide how well a wound holds and heals. Choosing and handling them correctly is part of every operation.

Hold the needle only on its body, never the tip.

The specimen goes fresh, without formalin, and is labelled and sent at once.

Recognise Early

In short: A line between the top of the iliac crests (Tuffier's line) crosses roughly the L4 spine or L4-L5 space in adults.

Where To Go In

A line between the top of the iliac crests (Tuffier's line) crosses roughly the L4 spine or L4-L5 space in adults.

The adult spinal cord ends around L1 to L2. In young children it ends lower, around L3.

Why it matters in theatre

Anatomy is the map surgeons and theatre staff work from. Knowing landmarks and structures at risk explains why operations are done the way they are.

Remember

Needles go below the cord, never above.

Needles go below the cord, never above.
