propofol.title: Propofol
propofol.caption: Propofol is a common intravenous induction drug.
propofol.body:
In short: Propofol is a common intravenous induction drug.

Induction Agent

Propofol is a common intravenous induction drug. It acts fast and wears off quickly, but it can drop blood pressure and often stings on injection.

The emulsion can support bacterial growth, so it is drawn up under strict aseptic conditions and discarded within the time on the label.

Why it matters in theatre

Many drugs are used in theatre, several of them high-risk. Knowing what each does and when it is dangerous helps prevent drug errors.

Remember

Never save an opened propofol syringe for another patient.

ketamine.title: Ketamine
ketamine.caption: Ketamine gives pain relief and anaesthesia while usually keeping airway reflexes and blood pressure better than many other drugs.
ketamine.body:
In short: Ketamine gives pain relief and anaesthesia while usually keeping airway reflexes and blood pressure better than many other drugs.

Dissociative Anaesthetic

Ketamine gives pain relief and anaesthesia while usually keeping airway reflexes and blood pressure better than many other drugs.

It can raise heart rate and blood pressure and cause vivid dreams or agitation when waking.

Why it matters in theatre

Many drugs are used in theatre, several of them high-risk. Knowing what each does and when it is dangerous helps prevent drug errors.

It is often chosen in shocked or trauma patients.

neuromuscular-blockers-and-reversal.title: Neuromuscular blockers and reversal
neuromuscular-blockers-and-reversal.caption: Suxamethonium is a depolarising relaxant with a very short action.
neuromuscular-blockers-and-reversal.body:
In short: Suxamethonium is a depolarising relaxant with a very short action.

Muscle Relaxants

Suxamethonium is a depolarising relaxant with a very short action. Rocuronium, vecuronium and atracurium are non-depolarising.

Reversal uses neostigmine with an anticholinergic such as glycopyrrolate. Sugammadex reverses rocuronium and vecuronium.

Why it matters in theatre

Many drugs are used in theatre, several of them high-risk. Knowing what each does and when it is dangerous helps prevent drug errors.

Never reverse a patient who shows no sign of recovery.

opioids-in-theatre.caption: Fentanyl and morphine are common opioids.
opioids-in-theatre.body:
In short: Fentanyl and morphine are common opioids.

Pain Relief With A Price

Fentanyl and morphine are common opioids. Side effects include slowed breathing, nausea and vomiting, itching and constipation.

Naloxone reverses opioids but may wear off sooner than the opioid, so monitoring continues.

Why it matters in theatre

Many drugs are used in theatre, several of them high-risk. Knowing what each does and when it is dangerous helps prevent drug errors.

Watch breathing rate and sedation after any opioid.

local-anaesthetic-safe-doses.caption: Typical maximum doses are about 3 mg/kg for plain lignocaine, about 7 mg/kg with adrenaline, and about 2 mg/kg for bupivacaine.
local-anaesthetic-safe-doses.body:
In short: Typical maximum doses are about 3 mg/kg for plain lignocaine, about 7 mg/kg with adrenaline, and about 2 mg/kg for bupivacaine.

Approximate Limits

Typical maximum doses are about 3 mg/kg for plain lignocaine, about 7 mg/kg with adrenaline, and about 2 mg/kg for bupivacaine. A 1 percent solution holds 10 mg per mL.

Local protocols may differ. Calculate before drawing up.

Why it matters in theatre

Many drugs are used in theatre, several of them high-risk. Knowing what each does and when it is dangerous helps prevent drug errors.

Add up every dose given by every team member.

adrenaline-with-local-anaesthetic.title: Adrenaline with local anaesthetic
adrenaline-with-local-anaesthetic.caption: Adrenaline narrows blood vessels, which prolongs the block, reduces bleeding and slows absorption of the drug.
adrenaline-with-local-anaesthetic.body:
In short: Adrenaline narrows blood vessels, which prolongs the block, reduces bleeding and slows absorption of the drug.

Why It Is Added

Adrenaline narrows blood vessels, which prolongs the block, reduces bleeding and slows absorption of the drug.

It has traditionally been avoided in areas with end-arteries such as fingers, toes, the penis and the nose tip.

Why it matters in theatre

Many drugs are used in theatre, several of them high-risk. Knowing what each does and when it is dangerous helps prevent drug errors.

penicillin-allergy-labels.caption: Many people labelled as penicillin allergic are not truly allergic.
penicillin-allergy-labels.body:
In short: Many people labelled as penicillin allergic are not truly allergic.

Not Always True

Many people labelled as penicillin allergic are not truly allergic. Cross-reaction with cephalosporins is low, roughly 1 to 2 percent.

A clear history of the reaction (rash, swelling, breathing trouble, timing) guides the choice.

Many drugs are used in theatre, several of them high-risk. Knowing what each does and when it is dangerous helps prevent drug errors.

Antifibrinolytic

Tranexamic acid reduces breakdown of clots and lowers blood loss in surgery, trauma and postpartum bleeding.

Large trials such as CRASH-2 supported giving it early after injury, ideally within 3 hours.

Many drugs are used in theatre, several of them high-risk. Knowing what each does and when it is dangerous helps prevent drug errors.

Give it early. The benefit falls the longer you wait.

oxytocin-and-ergometrine.caption: Oxytocin makes the uterus contract after delivery.
oxytocin-and-ergometrine.body:
In short: Oxytocin makes the uterus contract after delivery.

Uterotonics

Oxytocin makes the uterus contract after delivery. Given as a fast IV bolus it can drop blood pressure, so it is usually given slowly or as an infusion.

Ergometrine also contracts the uterus but is avoided in high blood pressure and pre-eclampsia.

Why it matters in theatre

Many drugs are used in theatre, several of them high-risk. Knowing what each does and when it is dangerous helps prevent drug errors.

Remember

Check blood pressure before ergometrine.

spinal-vs-epidural.title: Spinal vs epidural
spinal-vs-epidural.caption: Spinal: a small dose goes into the cerebrospinal fluid below the cord.
spinal-vs-epidural.body:
In short: Spinal: a small dose goes into the cerebrospinal fluid below the cord.

Two Different Spaces

Spinal: a small dose goes into the cerebrospinal fluid below the cord. It works fast and gives a dense block.

Epidural: a larger dose goes into the epidural space, works slower, and a catheter can be left for top-ups.

Why it matters in theatre

Regional techniques numb part of the body instead of making the patient unconscious. They have clear benefits and specific risks that staff should recognise.

Remember

A spinal is a single shot. An epidural can continue.

Check yourself

common-effects-of-a-spinal.caption: A quick list on common effects of a spinal: Fall in blood pressure and slow heart rate; Nausea, often from low blood pressure.
common-effects-of-a-spinal.body:
In short: A quick list on common effects of a spinal: Fall in blood pressure and slow heart rate; Nausea, often from low blood pressure.

Common effects of a spinal

  • Fall in blood pressure and slow heart rate
  • Nausea, often from low blood pressure
  • High block that reaches the chest or neck (rare but serious)
  • Urinary retention and headache afterwards

Why it matters in theatre

Regional techniques numb part of the body instead of making the patient unconscious. They have clear benefits and specific risks that staff should recognise.

post-dural-puncture-headache.title: Post-dural puncture headache
post-dural-puncture-headache.caption: The headache is usually worse sitting or standing and better lying flat.
post-dural-puncture-headache.body:
In short: The headache is usually worse sitting or standing and better lying flat.

What It Looks Like

The headache is usually worse sitting or standing and better lying flat. It often starts one to three days after a spinal or epidural.

Treatment ranges from fluids and simple pain relief to an epidural blood patch.

Why it matters in theatre

Regional techniques numb part of the body instead of making the patient unconscious. They have clear benefits and specific risks that staff should recognise.

Remember

when-not-to-do-an-epidural.body:

  • The patient refuses
  • Infection at the puncture site or severe infection in the blood

  • Severe low blood volume or raised pressure inside the skull

Regional techniques numb part of the body instead of making the patient unconscious. They have clear benefits and specific risks that staff should recognise.

safe-nerve-block-technique.caption: Ultrasound guidance helps show the nerve and the spread of the drug.
safe-nerve-block-technique.body:

Stop Signs

Ultrasound guidance helps show the nerve and the spread of the drug.

Stop injecting if the patient reports sharp pain or the injection feels hard to push. Aspirate regularly to check for blood, and inject in small amounts.

Why it matters in theatre

Regional techniques numb part of the body instead of making the patient unconscious. They have clear benefits and specific risks that staff should recognise.

caudal-block-in-children.title: Caudal block in children
caudal-block-in-children.caption: A caudal block puts local anaesthetic into the epidural space through the opening at the bottom of the sacrum.
caudal-block-in-children.body:
In short: A caudal block puts local anaesthetic into the epidural space through the opening at the bottom of the sacrum.

The Sacral Hiatus

A caudal block puts local anaesthetic into the epidural space through the opening at the bottom of the sacrum. It is common in children for surgery below the umbilicus.

It gives pain relief after hernia repair, circumcision and similar operations.

Why it matters in theatre

Regional techniques numb part of the body instead of making the patient unconscious. They have clear benefits and specific risks that staff should recognise.

Keep the child still and watch for signs of toxicity.

tap-block-and-field-blocks.body:
In short: Local infiltration and field blocks such as the transversus abdominis plane (TAP) block numb the abdominal wall.

Reducing Opioids

Local infiltration and field blocks such as the transversus abdominis plane (TAP) block numb the abdominal wall. They can reduce pain and the need for opioids after abdominal surgery.

They are usually done under ultrasound.

Regional techniques numb part of the body instead of making the patient unconscious. They have clear benefits and specific risks that staff should recognise.

intravenous-regional-anaesthesia-bier-bl.body:
In short: The limb is emptied of blood, a tourniquet is inflated and local anaesthetic is injected into a vein.

Tourniquet And Local

The limb is emptied of blood, a tourniquet is inflated and local anaesthetic is injected into a vein. The tourniquet keeps the drug in the limb.

The cuff must stay inflated for long enough (usually at least 20 minutes) so the drug does not enter the circulation too fast.

Why it matters in theatre

Regional techniques numb part of the body instead of making the patient unconscious. They have clear benefits and specific risks that staff should recognise.

Early cuff release can cause drug toxicity.

Aortocaval Compression

In late pregnancy the uterus can press on the vena cava and reduce blood return to the heart. Lying flat can cause low blood pressure and fainting.

Tilt the table about 15 degrees to the left or push the uterus to the left by hand.

Obstetric and gynaecological surgery involves two patients or high-risk bleeding. Understanding the common situations helps the whole team respond quickly.

The Four Ts

PPH is often defined as more than 500 mL after vaginal birth or 1000 mL after caesarean.

Causes: Tone (uterus not contracting), Trauma, Tissue (retained placenta) and Thrombin (clotting problems).

Calcium gluconate is the antidote and should be at hand.

cervical-cerclage.caption: A cerclage is a stitch placed around the cervix to prevent it opening too early in some pregnancies.
cervical-cerclage.body:
In short: A cerclage is a stitch placed around the cervix to prevent it opening too early in some pregnancies.

Cervical Stitch

A cerclage is a stitch placed around the cervix to prevent it opening too early in some pregnancies.

It is usually removed near term, around 36 to 37 weeks, or earlier if labour or infection starts.

Why it matters in theatre

Obstetric and gynaecological surgery involves two patients or high-risk bleeding. Understanding the common situations helps the whole team respond quickly.

Remember

Record the type and plan for removal.

children-are-not-small-adults-the-airway.title: Children are not small adults: the airway
children-are-not-small-adults-the-airway.caption: Children have a larger head and tongue, a narrower nose, a higher larynx and a shorter trachea.
children-are-not-small-adults-the-airway.body:
In short: Children have a larger head and tongue, a narrower nose, a higher larynx and a shorter trachea.

Different Anatomy

Children have a larger head and tongue, a narrower nose, a higher larynx and a shorter trachea. The narrowest point is often described as the cricoid ring.

Oxygen levels also fall faster because oxygen use is higher and reserves are smaller.

Why it matters in theatre

Children differ from adults in airway, size, heat loss and drug dosing. Treating them as small adults is a common cause of error.

Remember

Pre-oxygenate and prepare the equipment earlier.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about children are not small adults: the airway?

Pre-oxygenate and prepare the equipment earlier.

estimating-a-child-s-weight.body:
In short: One common formula for children aged 1 to 10 is weight in kg = (age in years + 4) × 2.

When You Cannot Weigh

One common formula for children aged 1 to 10 is weight in kg = (age in years + 4) × 2.

A fluid bolus is often 10 to 20 mL per kg. Always check local protocols and confirm the real weight as soon as possible.

Why it matters in theatre

Children differ from adults in airway, size, heat loss and drug dosing. Treating them as small adults is a common cause of error.

Remember

Drug doses depend on weight.

paediatric-tube-size.caption: A rule of thumb for children over one year: uncuffed tube size = age ÷ 4 + 4.
paediatric-tube-size.body:

Endotracheal Tube

A rule of thumb for children over one year: uncuffed tube size = age ÷ 4 + 4. For cuffed tubes use about half a size smaller.

Have one size above and below ready.

Why it matters in theatre

Children differ from adults in airway, size, heat loss and drug dosing. Treating them as small adults is a common cause of error.

keeping-babies-warm.title: Keeping babies warm
keeping-babies-warm.caption: Babies lose heat fast because they have a large surface area and little fat.
keeping-babies-warm.body:
In short: Babies lose heat fast because they have a large surface area and little fat.

Heat Loss

Babies lose heat fast because they have a large surface area and little fat. Cold stress raises oxygen use and can cause low sugar and breathing problems.

Warm the room, use radiant heaters and warm blankets, and keep the head covered.

Why it matters in theatre

Children differ from adults in airway, size, heat loss and drug dosing. Treating them as small adults is a common cause of error.

Remember

Prepare the heating before the baby arrives.

paediatric-fasting-guidance.caption: A quick list on paediatric fasting guidance: Solid food and formula milk: often about 6 hours; Breast milk: often about 4 hours.
paediatric-fasting-guidance.body:
In short: A quick list on paediatric fasting guidance: Solid food and formula milk: often about 6 hours; Breast milk: often about 4 hours.

Paediatric fasting guidance

  • Solid food and formula milk: often about 6 hours
  • Breast milk: often about 4 hours
  • Clear fluids: 1 to 2 hours, depending on local policy
  • Follow your hospital protocol

Children differ from adults in airway, size, heat loss and drug dosing. Treating them as small adults is a common cause of error.

Long fasting causes dehydration and low sugar in babies.

emergence-delirium.title: Emergence delirium
emergence-delirium.caption: Some children wake up agitated, crying and difficult to console, most often preschool age after sevoflurane.
emergence-delirium.body:

Agitation On Waking

Some children wake up agitated, crying and difficult to console, most often preschool age after sevoflurane.

Check for pain, a full bladder and hypoxia first. Parental presence and a calm room often help.

Why it matters in theatre

Children differ from adults in airway, size, heat loss and drug dosing. Treating them as small adults is a common cause of error.

Rule out pain and low oxygen before labelling it delirium.

heart-rates-in-children.title: Heart rates in children
heart-rates-in-children.caption: Normal resting heart rate falls with age.
heart-rates-in-children.body:
In short: Normal resting heart rate falls with age.

Age Matters

Normal resting heart rate falls with age. Roughly: newborn 120 to 160, infant 100 to 160, toddler 90 to 150, school age 70 to 110 beats per minute.

A slow heart rate in an unwell child is an urgent warning sign.

Why it matters in theatre

Children differ from adults in airway, size, heat loss and drug dosing. Treating them as small adults is a common cause of error.

Know the normal range for the child's age.

Hypoglycaemia

Babies and young children have small glucose stores and can become hypoglycaemic with fasting, cold or illness.

Signs may be subtle under anaesthesia. Check glucose and give dextrose as protocols direct.

Why it matters in theatre

Children differ from adults in airway, size, heat loss and drug dosing. Treating them as small adults is a common cause of error.

Do not fast a baby for longer than needed.

pyloric-stenosis.caption: Babies with pyloric stenosis have projectile vomiting.
pyloric-stenosis.body:
In short: Babies with pyloric stenosis have projectile vomiting.

A Medical Before A Surgical Emergency

Babies with pyloric stenosis have projectile vomiting. They lose stomach acid and potassium, causing a low chloride metabolic alkalosis.

Correct fluids and electrolytes before surgery.

Why it matters in theatre

Children differ from adults in airway, size, heat loss and drug dosing. Treating them as small adults is a common cause of error.

Remember

It is an urgent operation, not an emergency one.

drug-dose-safety-in-children.title: Drug dose safety in children
drug-dose-safety-in-children.caption: Children's doses are calculated by weight, so a decimal point error can give ten times the dose.
drug-dose-safety-in-children.body:
In short: Children's doses are calculated by weight, so a decimal point error can give ten times the dose.

Ten-Fold Errors

Children's doses are calculated by weight, so a decimal point error can give ten times the dose.

Double-check the calculation, the concentration on the vial and the volume to draw up. Label every syringe.

Why it matters in theatre

Children differ from adults in airway, size, heat loss and drug dosing. Treating them as small adults is a common cause of error.

Remember

Two people should check every paediatric dose.

open-fractures.title: Open fractures
open-fractures.caption: An open fracture has a wound connecting to the broken bone.
open-fractures.body:
In short: An open fracture has a wound connecting to the broken bone.

An Emergency

An open fracture has a wound connecting to the broken bone. It carries a high risk of infection.

Treatment includes early antibiotics (often within an hour), tetanus cover, wound cleaning and fixation. The Gustilo grade guides the plan.

Why it matters in theatre

Bone and joint surgery uses force, power tools, implants and imaging. Knowing the special risks helps theatre staff prepare equipment and protect the patient.

Remember

Antibiotics early. Debridement soon.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about open fractures?

Antibiotics early. Debridement soon.

After Long-Bone Fractures

Fat droplets can enter the circulation after fractures of long bones, usually 24 to 72 hours later.

Signs include low oxygen, confusion and a petechial rash on the chest, neck and armpits.

Bone and joint surgery uses force, power tools, implants and imaging. Knowing the special risks helps theatre staff prepare equipment and protect the patient.

timing-of-hip-fracture-surgery.body:
In short: Operating on a hip fracture within about 36 to 48 hours of admission is linked to better outcomes in older patients.

Early Is Better

Operating on a hip fracture within about 36 to 48 hours of admission is linked to better outcomes in older patients. Some guidelines say the same day or the next day.

Optimise heart, fluids and anaemia, but do not delay for minor issues.

Why it matters in theatre

Bone and joint surgery uses force, power tools, implants and imaging. Knowing the special risks helps theatre staff prepare equipment and protect the patient.

plaster-of-paris-care.body:
In short: Plaster is exothermic: it warms as it sets.

Casting

Plaster is exothermic: it warms as it sets. It sets in a few minutes but takes about a day or more to dry fully.

Keep the limb raised, check the fingers or toes for colour, feeling and movement, and keep the plaster dry.

Why it matters in theatre

Bone and joint surgery uses force, power tools, implants and imaging. Knowing the special risks helps theatre staff prepare equipment and protect the patient.

Remember

Never wrap the plaster tightly.

saw-and-drill-safety.body:

Heat And Debris

Power tools generate heat that can damage bone cells. Irrigate with saline while cutting or drilling.

Check blades are fitted properly, use guards and keep the cord and hose clear of the sterile field.

cemented-vs-uncemented-implants.body:
In short: Cemented implants fix immediately and are often used in older patients with weaker bone.

Choices

Cemented implants fix immediately and are often used in older patients with weaker bone. Uncemented implants rely on bone growing into the surface and are often used in younger patients.

The surgeon chooses based on bone quality and age.

The limb is a specimen. Label it, and handle it according to policy and the patient's wishes.

Confirm The Level

Counting from the sacrum or from the cervical spine and a marker on the X-ray helps.

appendicectomy-in-short.body:

The Steps

A small incision (often Lanz or gridiron) is made over the right lower abdomen. The appendix is found, the blood supply (mesoappendix) is tied, and the base is ligated and cut.

A laparoscopic approach is common where equipment is available.

hernia-repair-and-mesh.body:
In short: Mesh repairs have lower recurrence than suture-only repairs for most adult hernias.

Reducing Recurrence

Mesh repairs have lower recurrence than suture-only repairs for most adult hernias. The Lichtenstein repair places mesh over the back wall of the canal.

Mesh infection is rare but serious.

Scalpel blade numbers

  • No. 11: pointed blade for stabs and incisions
  • No. 15: small curved blade for fine work
  • No. 22: larger blade for deep or thick tissue

Instruments are the working tools of surgery. Recognising each one by name and purpose lets you prepare and pass the right one quickly and care for it properly.

Mosquito forceps are small and fine. Spencer Wells are medium-sized. Kocher forceps are heavier and have teeth at the tip.

They clamp vessels and tissue and are placed with the curve pointing to the surgeon's plan.

Toothed Or Not

Toothed forceps (such as Adson) grip skin and fascia firmly. Non-toothed or atraumatic forceps (such as DeBakey) handle bowel and vessels with less damage.

Choose the type for the tissue.

Why it matters in theatre

Instruments are the working tools of surgery. Recognising each one by name and purpose lets you prepare and pass the right one quickly and care for it properly.

Remember

Wrong forceps, wrong tissue, more damage.

Mayo And Metzenbaum

Mayo scissors are heavier and used for cutting sutures and tough tissue. Metzenbaum scissors are slender and used for delicate tissue dissection.

Using Metzenbaum scissors to cut suture or dressings blunts them.

Instruments are the working tools of surgery. Recognising each one by name and purpose lets you prepare and pass the right one quickly and care for it properly.

Handheld retractors (Langenbeck, Deaver, Morris) are held by an assistant. Self-retaining retractors (Balfour, Weitlaner, Gelpi) hold the wound open alone.

Mayo-Hegar And Others

Needle holders have short jaws that grip the needle and a ratchet that locks. Mayo-Hegar is the standard. Tungsten carbide inserts give a better grip and last longer.

Instruments are the working tools of surgery. Recognising each one by name and purpose lets you prepare and pass the right one quickly and care for it properly.

Using the wrong instrument can crush tissue.

Instruments are the working tools of surgery. Recognising each one by name and purpose lets you prepare and pass the right one quickly and care for it properly.

Ready To Leave Recovery

The Aldrete score rates activity, breathing, circulation, consciousness and oxygen saturation, each from 0 to 2.

A total of 9 or more out of 10 is commonly used as the discharge point from recovery.

Why it matters in theatre

The period just after surgery is when airway problems, bleeding and pain often appear. Good recovery care catches them early.

Remember

Score before the patient leaves recovery.

airway-obstruction-in-recovery.title: Airway obstruction in recovery
airway-obstruction-in-recovery.caption: Snoring means the airway is partially blocked by the tongue or soft tissue.
airway-obstruction-in-recovery.body:
In short: Snoring means the airway is partially blocked by the tongue or soft tissue.

Snoring Is A Warning

Snoring means the airway is partially blocked by the tongue or soft tissue. See-saw chest movement with no air movement means a complete block.

Lift the chin, thrust the jaw, give oxygen and use an airway adjunct. Call for help.

Why it matters in theatre

The period just after surgery is when airway problems, bleeding and pain often appear. Good recovery care catches them early.

Remember

Treat noisy breathing as an obstruction until proven otherwise.

pain-assessment-after-surgery.body:

Ask And Measure

A 0 to 10 scale works for many adults. For children or those who cannot talk, use a face or behaviour scale.

Multimodal pain relief uses several drug types so lower opioid doses are needed.

Why it matters in theatre

The period just after surgery is when airway problems, bleeding and pain often appear. Good recovery care catches them early.

urine-output-as-a-vital-sign.body:
In short: A usual target is at least 0.5 mL per kg per hour in adults.

Kidney Perfusion

A usual target is at least 0.5 mL per kg per hour in adults. Low urine output can mean low blood volume, low blood pressure or a blocked catheter.

Check the catheter before assuming kidney failure.

Why it matters in theatre

The period just after surgery is when airway problems, bleeding and pain often appear. Good recovery care catches them early.

Remember

Report low output early.

signs-of-bleeding-after-surgery.body:

  • Restlessness, anxiety and cold, clammy skin

  • Blood in drains or soaked dressings

wound-infection-signs.body:

Surgical Site Infection

Redness, heat, swelling, pain, discharge and fever. They often appear around days 5 to 10 but may appear any time within 30 days (longer with implants).

Tell the team early. Early treatment prevents spread.

The period just after surgery is when airway problems, bleeding and pain often appear. Good recovery care catches them early.

Calcium protects the heart muscle. Insulin with glucose, and other measures, bring potassium down.

cataract-surgery-set-up.body:
In short: Cataract surgery is often done under topical or local anaesthesia with a microscope and a phacoemulsification machine.

Small Operation, Big Detail

Cataract surgery is often done under topical or local anaesthesia with a microscope and a phacoemulsification machine.

The patient must lie still and communicate. The field is small and strict aseptic technique is essential.

neurosurgery-positioning-and-pressure.title: Neurosurgery positioning and pressure
neurosurgery-positioning-and-pressure.caption: Head pins in a clamp hold the skull still.
neurosurgery-positioning-and-pressure.body:
In short: Head pins in a clamp hold the skull still.

Protect The Brain

Head pins in a clamp hold the skull still. Patients with raised pressure inside the skull are usually positioned with the head up about 30 degrees. High carbon dioxide levels raise brain pressure.

Avoid kinks in neck veins.

Why it matters in theatre

Each surgical specialty has its own equipment, positions and risks. A short overview helps you prepare for lists outside general surgery.

Remember

Never loosen the head clamp unless the surgeon agrees.

cystoscopy-basics.caption: Cystoscopy looks inside the bladder with a rigid or flexible scope.
cystoscopy-basics.body:
In short: Cystoscopy looks inside the bladder with a rigid or flexible scope.

Bladder Scope

Cystoscopy looks inside the bladder with a rigid or flexible scope. The patient is usually in lithotomy position and the bladder is filled with sterile fluid.

Antibiotic cover and gentle handling lower the risk of infection and bleeding.

Why it matters in theatre

Each surgical specialty has its own equipment, positions and risks. A short overview helps you prepare for lists outside general surgery.

vascular-surgery-and-heparin.body:
In short: Before clamping a major artery, heparin is usually given to stop clots forming.

Anticoagulation

Before clamping a major artery, heparin is usually given to stop clots forming. The clotting effect can be monitored with an activated clotting time.

Protamine can reverse heparin when the clamp is off.

Why it matters in theatre

Each surgical specialty has its own equipment, positions and risks. A short overview helps you prepare for lists outside general surgery.

skin-grafts-and-flaps.caption: A split-thickness graft takes part of the skin layer.
skin-grafts-and-flaps.body:
In short: A split-thickness graft takes part of the skin layer.

Plastic Surgery

A split-thickness graft takes part of the skin layer. A full-thickness graft takes the whole thickness and contracts less.

Flaps carry their own blood supply. Check colour, warmth and capillary refill often.

Why it matters in theatre

Each surgical specialty has its own equipment, positions and risks. A short overview helps you prepare for lists outside general surgery.

oral-and-dental-surgery.caption: A nasal tube is often used to keep the mouth free.
oral-and-dental-surgery.body:
In short: A nasal tube is often used to keep the mouth free.

Shared And Small Airways

A nasal tube is often used to keep the mouth free. A throat pack protects the airway from blood and debris and must be counted.

Bleeding, swelling and a difficult airway are the main hazards.

Why it matters in theatre

Each surgical specialty has its own equipment, positions and risks. A short overview helps you prepare for lists outside general surgery.

In short: On cardiopulmonary bypass the blood is drawn out of the body, oxygenated and returned.

Heart-Lung Machine

On cardiopulmonary bypass the blood is drawn out of the body, oxygenated and returned. The patient receives high-dose heparin first, and protamine to reverse it afterwards.

Patients are often cooled to protect organs.

Why it matters in theatre

Each surgical specialty has its own equipment, positions and risks. A short overview helps you prepare for lists outside general surgery.

The perfusion team runs the pump. Keep clear communication.

ventilator-alarms.body:
In short: High pressure alarms can mean kinks, secretions, coughing or bronchospasm.

High And Low Pressure

High pressure alarms can mean kinks, secretions, coughing or bronchospasm. Low pressure alarms can mean a leak or disconnection.

Look at the patient first, then at the machine. Use manual ventilation if there is doubt.

Theatre equipment can fail at any time. Knowing the common faults and first checks helps the team recover quickly and safely.

infusion-pump-safety.body:
In short: Confirm the drug, the concentration, the rate and the patient.

Check Every Time

Confirm the drug, the concentration, the rate and the patient. Use the correct line and check for free-flow protection when loading the set.

Double-check high-risk drugs with a second person.

In short: Check the battery, the pads and cables, the printer paper and a self-test.

Daily Checks

Check the battery, the pads and cables, the printer paper and a self-test. Know where the machine is kept.

Many biphasic defibrillators deliver shocks in the range of about 120 to 200 joules. Follow the manufacturer and the resuscitation protocol.

forced-air-warmers.body:
In short: A forced-air warmer must be used with its blanket.

Burn Risk

A forced-air warmer must be used with its blanket. Blowing hot air directly from the hose onto skin can cause burns.

Keep the blanket over the patient and do not place it under heavy items that restrict air flow.

Theatre equipment can fail at any time. Knowing the common faults and first checks helps the team recover quickly and safely.

Methicillin-Resistant Staph Aureus

Patients known to carry MRSA may be isolated, screened and treated before surgery. Contact precautions apply and theatre cleaning must be thorough.

Prophylactic antibiotic choice may need to change. Follow local policy.

clostridioides-difficile.caption: C.
clostridioides-difficile.body:
In short: C.

Spores Survive Alcohol

C. difficile forms spores that alcohol hand rub does not kill. Wash with soap and water, use gloves and gowns and clean with a sporicidal agent such as a chlorine-based product.

Unnecessary antibiotics raise the risk.

Why it matters in theatre

Infection control protects patients, staff and the community. Consistent routine practice matters more than any single product.

Remember

Soap and water, not just alcohol.

tuberculosis-and-theatre.body:

Airborne Risk

Active pulmonary TB spreads by tiny airborne droplets. Elective surgery is usually delayed until the patient is treated and no longer infectious.

If surgery is urgent, use FFP2 or N95 respirators and good ventilation.

Why it matters in theatre

Infection control protects patients, staff and the community. Consistent routine practice matters more than any single product.

A surgical mask is not enough for TB.

Treatment courses should have a review date.

preventing-wrong-site-surgery.title: Preventing wrong-site surgery
preventing-wrong-site-surgery.caption: Check the consent form, mark the site with the surgeon's initials while the patient is awake where possible, and verify at the Time Out against the notes and images.
preventing-wrong-site-surgery.body:
In short: Check the consent form, mark the site with the surgeon's initials while the patient is awake where possible, and verify at the Time Out against the notes and images.

Three Locks

Check the consent form, mark the site with the surgeon's initials while the patient is awake where possible, and verify at the Time Out against the notes and images.

Left and right errors are the most common.

Why it matters in theatre

Good clinical practice includes record keeping, honesty, confidentiality and speaking up. These habits protect patients and professionals alike.

Remember

Never rely on memory for left and right.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about preventing wrong-site surgery?

Never rely on memory for left and right.

incident-and-near-miss-reporting.title: Incident and near-miss reporting
incident-and-near-miss-reporting.caption: Reporting near misses, errors and equipment faults helps the team find the cause and fix it.
incident-and-near-miss-reporting.body:
In short: Reporting near misses, errors and equipment faults helps the team find the cause and fix it.

Learn, Not Blame

Reporting near misses, errors and equipment faults helps the team find the cause and fix it.

A fair, no-blame culture works best when the facts are recorded accurately and promptly.

Why it matters in theatre

Good clinical practice includes record keeping, honesty, confidentiality and speaking up. These habits protect patients and professionals alike.

Remember

Report even when no harm occurred.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about incident and near-miss reporting?

Report even when no harm occurred.

when-a-patient-dies-in-theatre.title: When a patient dies in theatre
when-a-patient-dies-in-theatre.caption: Handle the body with respect, follow the legal and hospital procedures and support the family and the team.
when-a-patient-dies-in-theatre.body:
In short: Handle the body with respect, follow the legal and hospital procedures and support the family and the team.

Dignity

Handle the body with respect, follow the legal and hospital procedures and support the family and the team.

Specimens, devices and lines may need to stay in place for investigation. Ask before removing anything.

Why it matters in theatre

Good clinical practice includes record keeping, honesty, confidentiality and speaking up. These habits protect patients and professionals alike.

Remember

Allow time for the team to debrief.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about when a patient dies in theatre?

Allow time for the team to debrief.

putting-the-patient-at-ease.title: Putting the patient at ease
putting-the-patient-at-ease.caption: A quick list on putting the patient at ease: Greet the patient by name and introduce yourself; Explain what you are doing before you do it.
putting-the-patient-at-ease.body:
In short: A quick list on putting the patient at ease: Greet the patient by name and introduce yourself; Explain what you are doing before you do it.

Putting the patient at ease

  • Greet the patient by name and introduce yourself
  • Explain what you are doing before you do it
  • Keep the patient covered and warm
  • Stay calm and kind, even in a busy theatre

Why it matters in theatre

Good clinical practice includes record keeping, honesty, confidentiality and speaking up. These habits protect patients and professionals alike.

Remember

Fear affects pain, blood pressure and recovery.

Check yourself

List the points covered under "Putting the patient at ease".

Greet the patient by name and introduce yourself; Explain what you are doing before you do it; Keep the patient covered and warm; Stay calm and kind, even in a busy theatre.

photos-and-social-media.title: Photos and social media
photos-and-social-media.caption: Photos and videos of patients or theatre cases need clear written consent and hospital permission.
photos-and-social-media.body:
In short: Photos and videos of patients or theatre cases need clear written consent and hospital permission.

Consent First

Photos and videos of patients or theatre cases need clear written consent and hospital permission. Faces, tattoos, scars and background details can identify a person.

Many hospitals prohibit phones in theatre.

Why it matters in theatre

Good clinical practice includes record keeping, honesty, confidentiality and speaking up. These habits protect patients and professionals alike.

Remember

If in doubt, do not post.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about photos and social media?

If in doubt, do not post.

the-abcde-approach.title: The ABCDE approach
the-abcde-approach.caption: A quick list on the abcde approach: Airway: open and clear?; Breathing: rate, effort, oxygen level.
the-abcde-approach.body:
In short: A quick list on the abcde approach: Airway: open and clear?; Breathing: rate, effort, oxygen level.

The ABCDE approach

  • Airway: open and clear?
  • Breathing: rate, effort, oxygen level
  • Circulation: pulse, blood pressure, bleeding
  • Disability and Exposure: consciousness, glucose, whole-body check

Why it matters in theatre

First-line emergency care follows simple, repeatable steps. Learning them well makes it easier to act calmly under pressure.

Remember

Treat each problem as you find it, in order.

Check yourself

List the points covered under "The ABCDE approach".

Airway: open and clear?; Breathing: rate, effort, oxygen level; Circulation: pulse, blood pressure, bleeding; Disability and Exposure: consciousness, glucose, whole-body check.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

cpr-for-adults.title: CPR for adults
cpr-for-adults.caption: Adult compressions go about 100 to 120 per minute and about 5 to 6 cm deep, allowing the chest to recoil fully.
cpr-for-adults.body:
In short: Adult compressions go about 100 to 120 per minute and about 5 to 6 cm deep, allowing the chest to recoil fully.

High-Quality Compressions

Adult compressions go about 100 to 120 per minute and about 5 to 6 cm deep, allowing the chest to recoil fully. Without an advanced airway the ratio is 30 compressions to 2 breaths.

Change compressors about every two minutes.

Why it matters in theatre

First-line emergency care follows simple, repeatable steps. Learning them well makes it easier to act calmly under pressure.

Remember

Minimise pauses in compressions.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about cpr for adults?

Minimise pauses in compressions.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

choking-in-an-adult.title: Choking in an adult
choking-in-an-adult.caption: If the patient can cough, encourage coughing.
choking-in-an-adult.body:
In short: If the patient can cough, encourage coughing.

Back Blows And Thrusts

If the patient can cough, encourage coughing. If the airway is blocked and the patient cannot speak, give up to 5 back blows, then 5 abdominal thrusts, and repeat.

If the patient becomes unresponsive, start CPR.

Why it matters in theatre

First-line emergency care follows simple, repeatable steps. Learning them well makes it easier to act calmly under pressure.

Remember

Follow your local first-aid guideline.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about choking in an adult?

Follow your local first-aid guideline.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

first-aid-for-burns.title: First aid for burns
first-aid-for-burns.caption: A quick list on first aid for burns: Stop the burning and remove clothing and jewellery that is not stuck; Cool with running water for about 20 minutes.
first-aid-for-burns.body:
In short: A quick list on first aid for burns: Stop the burning and remove clothing and jewellery that is not stuck; Cool with running water for about 20 minutes.

First aid for burns

  • Stop the burning and remove clothing and jewellery that is not stuck
  • Cool with running water for about 20 minutes
  • Cover with a clean, non-fluffy dressing
  • No ice, butter or creams. Seek medical help for large or deep burns

Why it matters in theatre

First-line emergency care follows simple, repeatable steps. Learning them well makes it easier to act calmly under pressure.

Remember

Cool early. The first 20 minutes matter.

Check yourself

List the points covered under "First aid for burns".

Stop the burning and remove clothing and jewellery that is not stuck; Cool with running water for about 20 minutes; Cover with a clean, non-fluffy dressing; No ice, butter or creams. Seek medical help for large or deep burns.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

controlling-severe-bleeding.title: Controlling severe bleeding
controlling-severe-bleeding.caption: A quick list on controlling severe bleeding: Apply firm direct pressure with a clean pad; Raise the limb if possible.
controlling-severe-bleeding.body:
In short: A quick list on controlling severe bleeding: Apply firm direct pressure with a clean pad; Raise the limb if possible.

Controlling severe bleeding

  • Apply firm direct pressure with a clean pad
  • Raise the limb if possible
  • Add more pads without removing soaked ones
  • Use a tourniquet for life-threatening limb bleeding

Why it matters in theatre

First-line emergency care follows simple, repeatable steps. Learning them well makes it easier to act calmly under pressure.

Remember

Note the time any tourniquet is applied.

Check yourself

List the points covered under "Controlling severe bleeding".

Apply firm direct pressure with a clean pad; Raise the limb if possible; Add more pads without removing soaked ones; Use a tourniquet for life-threatening limb bleeding.

types-of-shock.title: Types of shock
types-of-shock.caption: A quick list on types of shock: Hypovolaemic: blood or fluid loss; Cardiogenic: pump failure.
types-of-shock.body:
In short: A quick list on types of shock: Hypovolaemic: blood or fluid loss; Cardiogenic: pump failure.

Types of shock

  • Hypovolaemic: blood or fluid loss
  • Cardiogenic: pump failure
  • Distributive: septic, anaphylactic, neurogenic
  • Obstructive: tension pneumothorax, tamponade, clot

Why it matters in theatre

First-line emergency care follows simple, repeatable steps. Learning them well makes it easier to act calmly under pressure.

Remember

Find the type, because the treatment differs.

Check yourself

List the points covered under "Types of shock".

Hypovolaemic: blood or fluid loss; Cardiogenic: pump failure; Distributive: septic, anaphylactic, neurogenic; Obstructive: tension pneumothorax, tamponade, clot.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

seizure-first-aid.title: Seizure first aid
seizure-first-aid.caption: A quick list on seizure first aid: Protect the person from injury and time the seizure; Nothing in the mouth.
seizure-first-aid.body:
In short: A quick list on seizure first aid: Protect the person from injury and time the seizure; Nothing in the mouth.

Seizure first aid

  • Protect the person from injury and time the seizure
  • Nothing in the mouth
  • Place in the recovery position when the movements stop
  • Call for help if it lasts more than 5 minutes

Why it matters in theatre

First-line emergency care follows simple, repeatable steps. Learning them well makes it easier to act calmly under pressure.

Remember

Check glucose after any seizure.

Check yourself

List the points covered under "Seizure first aid".

Protect the person from injury and time the seizure; Nothing in the mouth; Place in the recovery position when the movements stop; Call for help if it lasts more than 5 minutes.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

low-blood-sugar.title: Low blood sugar
low-blood-sugar.caption: Signs include sweating, shakiness, confusion and reduced consciousness.
low-blood-sugar.body:
In short: Signs include sweating, shakiness, confusion and reduced consciousness.

Hypoglycaemia

Signs include sweating, shakiness, confusion and reduced consciousness. Check blood sugar.

A conscious patient can take sugary fluids. An unconscious patient needs intravenous glucose or glucagon from a trained person.

Why it matters in theatre

First-line emergency care follows simple, repeatable steps. Learning them well makes it easier to act calmly under pressure.

Remember

Never give food or drink to an unconscious patient.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about low blood sugar?

Never give food or drink to an unconscious patient.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

suspected-spinal-injury.title: Suspected spinal injury
suspected-spinal-injury.caption: If a spinal injury is possible, keep the head, neck and trunk in line.
suspected-spinal-injury.body:
In short: If a spinal injury is possible, keep the head, neck and trunk in line.

Move The Whole Body

If a spinal injury is possible, keep the head, neck and trunk in line. Use a log roll with a team and a trained person holding the head.

Minimise movement and protect the airway.

Why it matters in theatre

First-line emergency care follows simple, repeatable steps. Learning them well makes it easier to act calmly under pressure.

Remember

Never twist the spine.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about suspected spinal injury?

Never twist the spine.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

the-recovery-position.title: The recovery position
the-recovery-position.caption: Lay the person on their side with the upper leg bent so the body cannot roll, and the head tilted back slightly with the mouth facing down.
the-recovery-position.body:
In short: Lay the person on their side with the upper leg bent so the body cannot roll, and the head tilted back slightly with the mouth facing down.

Unconscious But Breathing

Lay the person on their side with the upper leg bent so the body cannot roll, and the head tilted back slightly with the mouth facing down.

Fluids can drain and the tongue does not block the airway.

Why it matters in theatre

First-line emergency care follows simple, repeatable steps. Learning them well makes it easier to act calmly under pressure.

Remember

Check breathing continuously.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about the recovery position?

Check breathing continuously.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

cardiac-output.title: Cardiac output
cardiac-output.caption: Cardiac output is heart rate multiplied by stroke volume.
cardiac-output.body:
In short: Cardiac output is heart rate multiplied by stroke volume.

Heart Rate × Stroke Volume

Cardiac output is heart rate multiplied by stroke volume. A resting adult has an output of roughly 5 L per minute.

Blood loss lowers stroke volume, and the heart rate rises to compensate.

Why it matters in theatre

Physiology explains how the body normally works. It makes sense of why anaesthesia, bleeding and fluids affect patients as they do.

Remember

A fast heart rate may mean low volume.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about cardiac output?

A fast heart rate may mean low volume.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

oxygen-delivery.title: Oxygen delivery
oxygen-delivery.caption: Oxygen delivery depends on cardiac output and the oxygen content of arterial blood.
oxygen-delivery.body:
In short: Oxygen delivery depends on cardiac output and the oxygen content of arterial blood.

What Delivers Oxygen

Oxygen delivery depends on cardiac output and the oxygen content of arterial blood. Content depends mainly on haemoglobin and its saturation.

Anaemia, low saturation or low output can all reduce oxygen delivery.

Why it matters in theatre

Physiology explains how the body normally works. It makes sense of why anaesthesia, bleeding and fluids affect patients as they do.

Remember

Oxygen delivery needs blood, lungs and heart.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about oxygen delivery?

Oxygen delivery needs blood, lungs and heart.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

mean-arterial-pressure.title: Mean arterial pressure
mean-arterial-pressure.caption: Mean arterial pressure (MAP) is roughly diastolic pressure plus one-third of the pulse pressure, or (systolic + 2 × diastolic) ÷ 3.
mean-arterial-pressure.body:
In short: Mean arterial pressure (MAP) is roughly diastolic pressure plus one-third of the pulse pressure, or (systolic + 2 × diastolic) ÷ 3.

The Perfusion Pressure

Mean arterial pressure (MAP) is roughly diastolic pressure plus one-third of the pulse pressure, or (systolic + 2 × diastolic) ÷ 3.

A MAP of about 65 mmHg or above is commonly used as a minimum for organ perfusion.

Why it matters in theatre

Physiology explains how the body normally works. It makes sense of why anaesthesia, bleeding and fluids affect patients as they do.

Remember

Treat a low MAP early.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about mean arterial pressure?

Treat a low MAP early.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

body-fluid-compartments.title: Body fluid compartments
body-fluid-compartments.caption: Total body water is about 60 percent of body weight in an adult male.
body-fluid-compartments.body:
In short: Total body water is about 60 percent of body weight in an adult male.

Where The Water Is

Total body water is about 60 percent of body weight in an adult male. About two-thirds is inside cells and one-third outside. About a quarter of the outside fluid is plasma.

The proportion is lower in women and in the elderly.

Why it matters in theatre

Physiology explains how the body normally works. It makes sense of why anaesthesia, bleeding and fluids affect patients as they do.

Remember

Fluids stay in different compartments depending on the type.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about body fluid compartments?

Fluids stay in different compartments depending on the type.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

crystalloid-choices.title: Crystalloid choices
crystalloid-choices.caption: Normal saline contains more chloride than plasma.
crystalloid-choices.body:
In short: Normal saline contains more chloride than plasma.

Saline And Balanced Solutions

Normal saline contains more chloride than plasma. Large volumes can cause a high-chloride acidosis. Balanced solutions such as Ringer's lactate are closer to plasma.

Choose by the patient's condition and local policy.

Why it matters in theatre

Physiology explains how the body normally works. It makes sense of why anaesthesia, bleeding and fluids affect patients as they do.

Remember

Monitor electrolytes during large infusions.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about crystalloid choices?

Monitor electrolytes during large infusions.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

acid-base-basics.title: Acid-base basics
acid-base-basics.caption: Breathing controls carbon dioxide (respiratory).
acid-base-basics.body:
In short: Breathing controls carbon dioxide (respiratory).

Respiratory And Metabolic

Breathing controls carbon dioxide (respiratory). The kidneys and metabolism control bicarbonate (metabolic).

When one is disturbed, the other compensates. A rising CO2 with a falling pH means respiratory acidosis.

Why it matters in theatre

Physiology explains how the body normally works. It makes sense of why anaesthesia, bleeding and fluids affect patients as they do.

Remember

Look at pH first, then find the cause.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about acid-base basics?

Look at pH first, then find the cause.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

the-oxygen-dissociation-curve.title: The oxygen dissociation curve
the-oxygen-dissociation-curve.caption: The curve shifts right (more oxygen released to tissues) with acidosis, a high CO2, fever and raised 2,3-DPG.
the-oxygen-dissociation-curve.body:
In short: The curve shifts right (more oxygen released to tissues) with acidosis, a high CO2, fever and raised 2,3-DPG.

When Haemoglobin Lets Go

The curve shifts right (more oxygen released to tissues) with acidosis, a high CO2, fever and raised 2,3-DPG. It shifts left with the opposite conditions.

This helps working tissues get more oxygen.

Why it matters in theatre

Physiology explains how the body normally works. It makes sense of why anaesthesia, bleeding and fluids affect patients as they do.

Remember

Think right shift, tissues get more.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about the oxygen dissociation curve?

Think right shift, tissues get more.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

kidney-basics-for-theatre.title: Kidney basics for theatre
kidney-basics-for-theatre.caption: The healthy glomerular filtration rate is roughly 90 to 120 mL per minute.
kidney-basics-for-theatre.body:
In short: The healthy glomerular filtration rate is roughly 90 to 120 mL per minute.

Gfr

The healthy glomerular filtration rate is roughly 90 to 120 mL per minute. Low blood pressure, dehydration and nephrotoxic drugs can reduce it.

Kidney function affects drug choice and dosing in anaesthesia.

Why it matters in theatre

Physiology explains how the body normally works. It makes sense of why anaesthesia, bleeding and fluids affect patients as they do.

Remember

Keep the blood pressure up in kidney patients.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about kidney basics for theatre?

Keep the blood pressure up in kidney patients.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

the-surgical-stress-response.title: The surgical stress response
the-surgical-stress-response.caption: Surgery triggers the release of cortisol and adrenaline.
the-surgical-stress-response.body:
In short: Surgery triggers the release of cortisol and adrenaline.

Body'S Response

Surgery triggers the release of cortisol and adrenaline. Blood sugar rises, the heart rate rises and the body retains fluid.

Good pain relief, warmth and early feeding reduce this response.

Why it matters in theatre

Physiology explains how the body normally works. It makes sense of why anaesthesia, bleeding and fluids affect patients as they do.

Remember

Stress hormones can delay recovery.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about the surgical stress response?

Stress hormones can delay recovery.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

how-pain-travels.title: How pain travels
how-pain-travels.caption: Pain signals travel from nociceptors by A-delta fibres (fast, sharp pain) and C fibres (slow, dull pain) to the spinal cord and then to the brain.
how-pain-travels.body:
In short: Pain signals travel from nociceptors by A-delta fibres (fast, sharp pain) and C fibres (slow, dull pain) to the spinal cord and then to the brain.

The Pathway

Pain signals travel from nociceptors by A-delta fibres (fast, sharp pain) and C fibres (slow, dull pain) to the spinal cord and then to the brain.

Local anaesthetics block these signals at the nerve. Opioids act in the spinal cord and brain.

Why it matters in theatre

Physiology explains how the body normally works. It makes sense of why anaesthesia, bleeding and fluids affect patients as they do.

Remember

Treat pain at more than one level.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about how pain travels?

Treat pain at more than one level.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

hypertension-and-surgery.title: Hypertension and surgery
hypertension-and-surgery.caption: Most patients should continue their usual blood pressure medicines.
hypertension-and-surgery.body:
In short: Most patients should continue their usual blood pressure medicines.

Blood Pressure Planning

Most patients should continue their usual blood pressure medicines. Poorly controlled hypertension raises the risk of wide swings in blood pressure under anaesthesia.

Some drugs, such as ACE inhibitors, may be held on the morning of surgery depending on local advice.

Why it matters in theatre

Many surgical patients also have long-term illnesses. Knowing how these change anaesthesia and recovery helps the team plan safely.

Remember

Follow the anaesthetist's instructions on medicines.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about hypertension and surgery?

Follow the anaesthetist's instructions on medicines.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

diabetes-and-surgery.title: Diabetes and surgery
diabetes-and-surgery.caption: Fasting and surgery change sugar levels.
diabetes-and-surgery.body:
In short: Fasting and surgery change sugar levels.

Sugar And Fasting

Fasting and surgery change sugar levels. Insulin and tablets may need to be adjusted. Surgery is best early in the day for diabetic patients.

Severe high sugar with ketones is an emergency (DKA).

Why it matters in theatre

Many surgical patients also have long-term illnesses. Knowing how these change anaesthesia and recovery helps the team plan safely.

Remember

Check glucose before, during and after surgery.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about diabetes and surgery?

Check glucose before, during and after surgery.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

asthma-in-the-theatre.title: Asthma in the theatre
asthma-in-the-theatre.caption: Asthma patients should continue their inhalers, including on the day of surgery.
asthma-in-the-theatre.body:
In short: Asthma patients should continue their inhalers, including on the day of surgery.

Airway Alert

Asthma patients should continue their inhalers, including on the day of surgery. Avoid known triggers and drugs that release histamine.

Bronchospasm can happen at induction or when the airway is stimulated.

Why it matters in theatre

Many surgical patients also have long-term illnesses. Knowing how these change anaesthesia and recovery helps the team plan safely.

Remember

Have bronchodilators ready.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about asthma in the theatre?

Have bronchodilators ready.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

sickle-cell-disease.title: Sickle cell disease
sickle-cell-disease.caption: Low oxygen, dehydration, cold, acidosis and infection can trigger sickling and painful crises.
sickle-cell-disease.body:
In short: Low oxygen, dehydration, cold, acidosis and infection can trigger sickling and painful crises.

Prevent Sickling

Low oxygen, dehydration, cold, acidosis and infection can trigger sickling and painful crises.

Hydrate well, keep the patient warm and oxygenated and avoid tourniquet time that is longer than needed. A haematologist usually guides transfusion.

Why it matters in theatre

Many surgical patients also have long-term illnesses. Knowing how these change anaesthesia and recovery helps the team plan safely.

Remember

Keep sickle patients warm, hydrated and oxygenated.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about sickle cell disease?

Keep sickle patients warm, hydrated and oxygenated.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

types-of-anaemia.title: Types of anaemia
types-of-anaemia.caption: A quick list on types of anaemia: Iron deficiency: most common, small pale red cells; Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency: large red cells.
types-of-anaemia.body:
In short: A quick list on types of anaemia: Iron deficiency: most common, small pale red cells; Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency: large red cells.

Types of anaemia

  • Iron deficiency: most common, small pale red cells
  • Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency: large red cells
  • Blood loss or chronic disease
  • Find the cause before elective surgery

Why it matters in theatre

Many surgical patients also have long-term illnesses. Knowing how these change anaesthesia and recovery helps the team plan safely.

Remember

Correct anaemia before major elective surgery.

Check yourself

List the points covered under "Types of anaemia".

Iron deficiency: most common, small pale red cells; Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency: large red cells; Blood loss or chronic disease; Find the cause before elective surgery.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

malaria-and-surgery.title: Malaria and surgery
malaria-and-surgery.caption: Active malaria can cause fever, anaemia, low platelets and organ problems.
malaria-and-surgery.body:
In short: Active malaria can cause fever, anaemia, low platelets and organ problems.

Fever, Anaemia, Low Platelets

Active malaria can cause fever, anaemia, low platelets and organ problems. Elective surgery is usually postponed until treatment is complete.

In an emergency, test, treat and tell the anaesthetist.

Why it matters in theatre

Many surgical patients also have long-term illnesses. Knowing how these change anaesthesia and recovery helps the team plan safely.

Remember

Test any febrile patient from a malaria area.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about malaria and surgery?

Test any febrile patient from a malaria area.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

hiv-and-surgery.title: HIV and surgery
hiv-and-surgery.caption: Patients living with HIV receive the same standard precautions as everyone else.
hiv-and-surgery.body:
In short: Patients living with HIV receive the same standard precautions as everyone else.

Universal Care

Patients living with HIV receive the same standard precautions as everyone else. Antiretroviral therapy should usually continue through the peri-operative period.

Their CD4 count and viral load help guide risk.

Why it matters in theatre

Many surgical patients also have long-term illnesses. Knowing how these change anaesthesia and recovery helps the team plan safely.

Remember

Do not delay care or label records unnecessarily.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about hiv and surgery?

Do not delay care or label records unnecessarily.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

tuberculosis-forms.title: Tuberculosis forms
tuberculosis-forms.caption: TB most often affects the lungs but can involve the spine (Pott's disease), lymph nodes, bones and other organs.
tuberculosis-forms.body:
In short: TB most often affects the lungs but can involve the spine (Pott's disease), lymph nodes, bones and other organs.

More Than The Lungs

TB most often affects the lungs but can involve the spine (Pott's disease), lymph nodes, bones and other organs.

Spinal TB can cause deformity or pressure on the cord and may need surgery.

Why it matters in theatre

Many surgical patients also have long-term illnesses. Knowing how these change anaesthesia and recovery helps the team plan safely.

Remember

Pulmonary TB needs airborne precautions.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about tuberculosis forms?

Pulmonary TB needs airborne precautions.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

heart-risk-and-exercise-capacity.title: Heart risk and exercise capacity
heart-risk-and-exercise-capacity.caption: Exercise capacity is a guide to heart risk.
heart-risk-and-exercise-capacity.body:
In short: Exercise capacity is a guide to heart risk.

Mets

Exercise capacity is a guide to heart risk. Being able to climb two flights of stairs or walk fast on a hill (around 4 METs or more) suggests lower risk.

Poor capacity, chest pain or breathlessness needs a fuller assessment.

Why it matters in theatre

Many surgical patients also have long-term illnesses. Knowing how these change anaesthesia and recovery helps the team plan safely.

Remember

Ask what the patient can do, not just the diagnosis.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about heart risk and exercise capacity?

Ask what the patient can do, not just the diagnosis.

obesity-and-the-airway.caption: Obese patients may be harder to ventilate by mask and desaturate faster.
obesity-and-the-airway.body:
In short: Obese patients may be harder to ventilate by mask and desaturate faster.

Plan Ahead

Obese patients may be harder to ventilate by mask and desaturate faster. Ramping the head and upper body can improve the view and the lung volume.

Equipment must be rated for the weight and positioning needs care.

Why it matters in theatre

Many surgical patients also have long-term illnesses. Knowing how these change anaesthesia and recovery helps the team plan safely.

Check table and equipment weight limits.

percentage-to-mg-per-ml.title: Percentage to mg per mL
percentage-to-mg-per-ml.caption: A 1 percent solution contains 1 g in 100 mL, which is 10 mg per mL.
percentage-to-mg-per-ml.body:
In short: A 1 percent solution contains 1 g in 100 mL, which is 10 mg per mL.

Step One

A 1 percent solution contains 1 g in 100 mL, which is 10 mg per mL. A 0.5 percent solution has 5 mg per mL and a 2 percent solution has 20 mg per mL.

Multiply the percentage by 10 to get mg per mL.

Why it matters in theatre

Dose and concentration errors can be fatal. Practising the basic calculations and double-checking them are core safety skills.

Remember

Check the vial concentration every time.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about percentage to mg per ml?

Check the vial concentration every time.

adrenaline-strengths.title: Adrenaline strengths
adrenaline-strengths.caption: Adrenaline 1:1000 contains 1 mg per mL.
adrenaline-strengths.body:
In short: Adrenaline 1:1000 contains 1 mg per mL.

1:1000 Vs 1:10,000

Adrenaline 1:1000 contains 1 mg per mL. Adrenaline 1:10,000 contains 0.1 mg per mL (1 mg in 10 mL).

Mixing them up is a serious error. Read the label and the dose route.

Why it matters in theatre

Dose and concentration errors can be fatal. Practising the basic calculations and double-checking them are core safety skills.

Remember

Never give 1:1000 intravenously without dilution.

the-basic-dose-formula.title: The basic dose formula
the-basic-dose-formula.caption: Volume to give = (dose wanted ÷ dose available) × volume it is in.
the-basic-dose-formula.body:
In short: Volume to give = (dose wanted ÷ dose available) × volume it is in.

What You Want Over What You Have

Volume to give = (dose wanted ÷ dose available) × volume it is in.

For example, if you need 5 mg and the vial has 10 mg in 2 mL, the volume is (5 ÷ 10) × 2 = 1 mL.

Why it matters in theatre

Dose and concentration errors can be fatal. Practising the basic calculations and double-checking them are core safety skills.

Remember

Double-check by estimating whether the answer makes sense.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about the basic dose formula?

Double-check by estimating whether the answer makes sense.

drip-rate.title: Drip rate
drip-rate.caption: Drops per minute = (volume in mL × drop factor) ÷ time in minutes.
drip-rate.body:
In short: Drops per minute = (volume in mL × drop factor) ÷ time in minutes.

Drops Per Minute

Drops per minute = (volume in mL × drop factor) ÷ time in minutes. A common adult giving set has 20 drops per mL, and a paediatric set has 60 micro-drops per mL. Check the set label.

Example: 1000 mL over 8 hours with 20 drops per mL is about 42 drops per minute.

Why it matters in theatre

Dose and concentration errors can be fatal. Practising the basic calculations and double-checking them are core safety skills.

Remember

Check the drop factor on the pack.

Check yourself

Check the drop factor on the pack.

rate-in-ml-per-hour.title: Rate in mL per hour
rate-in-ml-per-hour.caption: Rate in mL per hour = volume ÷ time in hours.
rate-in-ml-per-hour.body:
In short: Rate in mL per hour = volume ÷ time in hours.

Pump Settings

Rate in mL per hour = volume ÷ time in hours.

Example: 500 mL over 4 hours is 125 mL per hour.

For a drug infusion, work out the dose per hour first, then convert to volume.

Why it matters in theatre

Dose and concentration errors can be fatal. Practising the basic calculations and double-checking them are core safety skills.

Remember

Always program the pump from a written calculation.

Always program the pump from a written calculation.

weight-based-doses.body:

Mg Per Kg

Multiply the dose per kg by the patient's weight. A 70 kg adult at 3 mg per kg is 210 mg.

Use an actual or ideal body weight as the drug protocol says. Check that the answer is below the maximum dose.

body-mass-index.body:
In short: BMI = weight in kg ÷ (height in metres squared).

Bmi

BMI = weight in kg ÷ (height in metres squared). WHO adult categories: below 18.5 underweight, 18.5 to 24.9 normal, 25 to 29.9 overweight, 30 or above obese.

BMI is a guide and does not show body composition.

Why it matters in theatre

infusion-concentrations.body:
In short: Concentration = amount of drug ÷ volume.

Mg Per Ml

Concentration = amount of drug ÷ volume. For example, 50 mg of drug in 50 mL of fluid is 1 mg per mL.

Write the concentration clearly on the syringe label.

Why it matters in theatre

Dose and concentration errors can be fatal. Practising the basic calculations and double-checking them are core safety skills.

Label every syringe, every time.

temperature-and-pressure-conversions.body:
In short: Fahrenheit = Celsius × 9 ÷ 5 + 32.

Quick Conversions

Fahrenheit = Celsius × 9 ÷ 5 + 32. For pressure, 1 kPa is about 7.5 mmHg, and 1 cmH2O is about 0.74 mmHg.

Machines may show different units, so check before acting.

Why it matters in theatre

NPO means nothing by mouth. PRN means as needed. BP is blood pressure and HR is heart rate. IV is intravenous and IM is intramuscular.

Unclear abbreviations cause errors. Follow your hospital's approved list.

circle-of-willis.title: Circle of Willis
circle-of-willis.caption: The Circle of Willis is a ring of arteries at the base of the brain.
circle-of-willis.body:
In short: The Circle of Willis is a ring of arteries at the base of the brain.

Brain Blood Supply

The Circle of Willis is a ring of arteries at the base of the brain. It links the anterior circulation (from the internal carotid arteries) with the posterior circulation (from the vertebral and basilar arteries).

It can provide backup blood flow if one vessel narrows.

Why it matters in theatre

Anatomy is the map surgeons and theatre staff work from. Knowing landmarks and structures at risk explains why operations are done the way they are.

Remember

Cerebral perfusion pressure matters in head surgery.

the-coronary-arteries.title: The coronary arteries
the-coronary-arteries.caption: The left anterior descending artery supplies much of the front of the left ventricle and the septum.
the-coronary-arteries.body:
In short: The left anterior descending artery supplies much of the front of the left ventricle and the septum.

Heart Blood Supply

The left anterior descending artery supplies much of the front of the left ventricle and the septum. The circumflex supplies the side. The right coronary artery supplies the right heart and usually the lower wall and the nodes.

Blockage of the LAD is often called the widow-maker.

Why it matters in theatre

Anatomy is the map surgeons and theatre staff work from. Knowing landmarks and structures at risk explains why operations are done the way they are.

Remember

Know where the chest pain may be coming from.

lungs-and-bronchi.title: Lungs and bronchi
lungs-and-bronchi.caption: The right lung has three lobes and the left lung has two, with the lingula part of the upper lobe.
lungs-and-bronchi.body:
In short: The right lung has three lobes and the left lung has two, with the lingula part of the upper lobe.

Right Vs Left

The right lung has three lobes and the left lung has two, with the lingula part of the upper lobe. The right main bronchus is shorter, wider and more vertical.

Inhaled objects and a tube pushed too far usually go into the right bronchus.

Why it matters in theatre

Anatomy is the map surgeons and theatre staff work from. Knowing landmarks and structures at risk explains why operations are done the way they are.

Remember

Check breath sounds on both sides after intubation.

liver-anatomy-and-blood-flow.title: Liver anatomy and blood flow
liver-anatomy-and-blood-flow.caption: The liver is divided into eight segments, each with its own blood supply and drainage, which lets surgeons remove parts of it.
liver-anatomy-and-blood-flow.body:
In short: The liver is divided into eight segments, each with its own blood supply and drainage, which lets surgeons remove parts of it.

Eight Segments

The liver is divided into eight segments, each with its own blood supply and drainage, which lets surgeons remove parts of it.

The portal vein brings most of the blood volume. The hepatic artery supplies a quarter of the flow but about half the oxygen.

Why it matters in theatre

Anatomy is the map surgeons and theatre staff work from. Knowing landmarks and structures at risk explains why operations are done the way they are.

Remember

Liver surgery needs good plans for bleeding.

portal-hypertension-and-varices.title: Portal hypertension and varices
portal-hypertension-and-varices.caption: When the liver is diseased, pressure in the portal vein rises.
portal-hypertension-and-varices.body:
In short: When the liver is diseased, pressure in the portal vein rises.

Where Blood Finds A Way Around

When the liver is diseased, pressure in the portal vein rises. Blood diverts through connecting veins around the lower oesophagus, the rectum and the umbilicus. These swell as varices.

Oesophageal varices can bleed massively.

Why it matters in theatre

Anatomy is the map surgeons and theatre staff work from. Knowing landmarks and structures at risk explains why operations are done the way they are.

Remember

Be ready for sudden bleeding.

the-kidneys.title: The kidneys
the-kidneys.caption: The kidneys lie behind the peritoneum at about T12 to L3.
the-kidneys.body:
In short: The kidneys lie behind the peritoneum at about T12 to L3.

Retroperitoneal Organs

The kidneys lie behind the peritoneum at about T12 to L3. The right kidney sits a little lower because of the liver.

Each kidney is supplied by a renal artery from the aorta and drains through the renal vein to the vena cava.

Why it matters in theatre

Anatomy is the map surgeons and theatre staff work from. Knowing landmarks and structures at risk explains why operations are done the way they are.

Remember

The flank position can stretch the kidney vessels.

the-spleen.title: The spleen
the-spleen.caption: The spleen lies under the left ribs, roughly ribs 9 to 11.
the-spleen.body:
In short: The spleen lies under the left ribs, roughly ribs 9 to 11.

Protected By The Ribs

The spleen lies under the left ribs, roughly ribs 9 to 11. It is the most commonly injured organ in blunt abdominal trauma.

People who lose their spleen are at higher risk of infection by encapsulated bacteria and need vaccines and sometimes antibiotics.

Why it matters in theatre

Anatomy is the map surgeons and theatre staff work from. Knowing landmarks and structures at risk explains why operations are done the way they are.

Remember
