femoral-artery-pulse-and-access.title: Femoral artery pulse and access
femoral-artery-pulse-and-access.caption: The femoral pulse is felt at the mid-inguinal point, halfway between the front hip bone and the pubic bone.
femoral-artery-pulse-and-access.body:
In short: The femoral pulse is felt at the mid-inguinal point, halfway between the front hip bone and the pubic bone.

Groin Landmark

The femoral pulse is felt at the mid-inguinal point, halfway between the front hip bone and the pubic bone.

It is a common entry point for catheters, but bleeding or haematoma can follow, so apply firm pressure after removing devices.

Why it matters

Leg anatomy matters for orthopaedic and vascular surgery, regional blocks, injections and tourniquet use. Several nerves are easily damaged by pressure.

Remember

Press well after removing a sheath.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about femoral artery pulse and access?

Press well after removing a sheath.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

sciatic-nerve.title: Sciatic nerve
sciatic-nerve.caption: The sciatic nerve, made of roots L4 to S3, leaves the pelvis below the piriformis muscle and runs down the back of the thigh.
sciatic-nerve.body:
In short: The sciatic nerve, made of roots L4 to S3, leaves the pelvis below the piriformis muscle and runs down the back of the thigh.

The Big Nerve

The sciatic nerve, made of roots L4 to S3, leaves the pelvis below the piriformis muscle and runs down the back of the thigh.

Above the knee it divides into the tibial and common peroneal nerves.

Why it matters

Leg anatomy matters for orthopaedic and vascular surgery, regional blocks, injections and tourniquet use. Several nerves are easily damaged by pressure.

Remember

Largest nerve in the body.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about sciatic nerve?

Largest nerve in the body.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

safe-site-for-buttock-injections.title: Safe site for buttock injections
safe-site-for-buttock-injections.caption: Intramuscular buttock injections go into the upper outer quadrant of the buttock, away from the sciatic nerve, which lies in the lower inner part.
safe-site-for-buttock-injections.body:
In short: Intramuscular buttock injections go into the upper outer quadrant of the buttock, away from the sciatic nerve, which lies in the lower inner part.

Avoid The Nerve

Intramuscular buttock injections go into the upper outer quadrant of the buttock, away from the sciatic nerve, which lies in the lower inner part.

The lateral thigh is also commonly used. Choose a site by local protocol.

Why it matters

Leg anatomy matters for orthopaedic and vascular surgery, regional blocks, injections and tourniquet use. Several nerves are easily damaged by pressure.

Remember

Upper outer quadrant is safest.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about safe site for buttock injections?

Upper outer quadrant is safest.

common-peroneal-nerve.title: Common peroneal nerve
common-peroneal-nerve.caption: The common peroneal nerve winds around the neck of the fibula just under the skin and is easily pressed.
common-peroneal-nerve.body:
In short: The common peroneal nerve winds around the neck of the fibula just under the skin and is easily pressed.

Foot Drop Risk

The common peroneal nerve winds around the neck of the fibula just under the skin and is easily pressed.

Pressure from leg holders, tight casts or lithotomy positions can injure it, causing foot drop. Pad the outer knee and check position.

Why it matters

Leg anatomy matters for orthopaedic and vascular surgery, regional blocks, injections and tourniquet use. Several nerves are easily damaged by pressure.

Remember

Pad the fibular head.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about common peroneal nerve?

Pad the fibular head.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

femoral-nerve.title: Femoral nerve
femoral-nerve.caption: The femoral nerve arises from L2 to L4 and supplies the quadriceps muscle and skin of the front of the thigh.
femoral-nerve.body:
In short: The femoral nerve arises from L2 to L4 and supplies the quadriceps muscle and skin of the front of the thigh.

Quadriceps Nerve

The femoral nerve arises from L2 to L4 and supplies the quadriceps muscle and skin of the front of the thigh.

A femoral nerve block can give good pain relief after thigh or hip fracture and knee surgery, but weakens the quadriceps.

Why it matters

Leg anatomy matters for orthopaedic and vascular surgery, regional blocks, injections and tourniquet use. Several nerves are easily damaged by pressure.

Remember

Block eases pain but weakens the knee.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about femoral nerve?

Block eases pain but weakens the knee.

great-saphenous-vein.title: Great saphenous vein
great-saphenous-vein.caption: The great saphenous vein runs up the inner leg from in front of the ankle's inner bone to the groin, where it joins the femoral vein.
great-saphenous-vein.body:
In short: The great saphenous vein runs up the inner leg from in front of the ankle's inner bone to the groin, where it joins the femoral vein.

Long Vein

The great saphenous vein runs up the inner leg from in front of the ankle's inner bone to the groin, where it joins the femoral vein.

It is used for emergency cut-down access and as a bypass graft, and is often involved in varicose veins.

Why it matters

Leg anatomy matters for orthopaedic and vascular surgery, regional blocks, injections and tourniquet use. Several nerves are easily damaged by pressure.

Remember

Found in front of the medial malleolus.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about great saphenous vein?

Found in front of the medial malleolus.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

popliteal-fossa.title: Popliteal fossa
popliteal-fossa.caption: A quick list on popliteal fossa: Diamond space behind the knee; Tibial nerve - most superficial.
popliteal-fossa.body:
In short: A quick list on popliteal fossa: Diamond space behind the knee; Tibial nerve - most superficial.

Popliteal fossa

  • Diamond space behind the knee
  • Tibial nerve - most superficial
  • Popliteal vein - in the middle
  • Popliteal artery - deepest, next to bone

Why it matters

Leg anatomy matters for orthopaedic and vascular surgery, regional blocks, injections and tourniquet use. Several nerves are easily damaged by pressure.

Remember

Nerve, vein, artery: top to deep.

compartments-of-the-leg.title: Compartments of the leg
compartments-of-the-leg.caption: A quick list on compartments of the leg: Anterior - lifts the foot; Lateral - turns the foot outward.

In short: A quick list on compartments of the leg: Anterior - lifts the foot; Lateral - turns the foot outward.

Compartments of the leg

  • Anterior - lifts the foot
  • Lateral - turns the foot outward
  • Superficial posterior - calf muscles
  • Deep posterior - toe flexors
  • Tight fascia can trap swelling in each

Why it matters

Leg anatomy matters for orthopaedic and vascular surgery, regional blocks, injections and tourniquet use. Several nerves are easily damaged by pressure.

Four compartments, each can swell.

thigh-tourniquet-basics.title: Thigh tourniquet basics
thigh-tourniquet-basics.caption: A thigh tourniquet uses a wide cuff over padding at the upper thigh.
thigh-tourniquet-basics.body:
In short: A thigh tourniquet uses a wide cuff over padding at the upper thigh.

Bloodless Field

A thigh tourniquet uses a wide cuff over padding at the upper thigh. Nerves under the cuff can be squeezed if pressure or time is excessive.

Record inflation time, follow local protocol and release it slowly when told, watching the patient's condition.

Why it matters

Leg anatomy matters for orthopaedic and vascular surgery, regional blocks, injections and tourniquet use. Several nerves are easily damaged by pressure.

Remember

Note the time, protect the nerves.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about thigh tourniquet basics?

Note the time, protect the nerves.

regions-of-the-vertebral-column.title: Regions of the vertebral column
regions-of-the-vertebral-column.caption: A quick list on regions of the vertebral column: Cervical - 7 vertebrae in the neck; Thoracic - 12 with ribs attached.
regions-of-the-vertebral-column.body:
In short: A quick list on regions of the vertebral column: Cervical - 7 vertebrae in the neck; Thoracic - 12 with ribs attached.

Regions of the vertebral column

  • Cervical - 7 vertebrae in the neck
  • Thoracic - 12 with ribs attached
  • Lumbar - 5 large vertebrae
  • Sacrum - 5 fused
  • Coccyx - 4 small fused

Why it matters

The spine protects the cord and is the route for spinal and epidural anaesthesia. Understanding it also supports safe handling of trauma and positioning for surgery.

Remember

7, 12, 5, 5, 4.

Check yourself

List the points covered under "Regions of the vertebral column".

parts-of-a-typical-vertebra.title: Parts of a typical vertebra
parts-of-a-typical-vertebra.caption: A typical vertebra has a body in front for weight bearing, and an arch behind made of pedicles and laminae.
parts-of-a-typical-vertebra.body:
In short: A typical vertebra has a body in front for weight bearing, and an arch behind made of pedicles and laminae.

Building Block

A typical vertebra has a body in front for weight bearing, and an arch behind made of pedicles and laminae.

The spinous and transverse processes carry muscles. The hole formed by the arch, the vertebral foramen, protects the spinal cord.

Why it matters

The spine protects the cord and is the route for spinal and epidural anaesthesia. Understanding it also supports safe handling of trauma and positioning for surgery.

Remember

Body bears, arch protects.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about parts of a typical vertebra?

Body bears, arch protects.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

atlas-and-axis.title: Atlas and axis
atlas-and-axis.caption: The atlas (C1) has no body and holds the skull; nodding mainly happens at this joint.
atlas-and-axis.body:
In short: The atlas (C1) has no body and holds the skull; nodding mainly happens at this joint.

Top Two Bones

The atlas (C1) has no body and holds the skull; nodding mainly happens at this joint. The axis (C2) has the dens, a peg around which the head turns.

Damage here is dangerous, so protect the neck in trauma and rheumatoid arthritis.

Why it matters

The spine protects the cord and is the route for spinal and epidural anaesthesia. Understanding it also supports safe handling of trauma and positioning for surgery.

Remember

Yes: atlas nods, axis turns.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about atlas and axis?

Yes: atlas nods, axis turns.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

intervertebral-disc.title: Intervertebral disc
intervertebral-disc.caption: A disc has a soft core, the nucleus pulposus, inside a tough ring, the annulus fibrosus.
intervertebral-disc.body:
In short: A disc has a soft core, the nucleus pulposus, inside a tough ring, the annulus fibrosus.

Shock Absorber

A disc has a soft core, the nucleus pulposus, inside a tough ring, the annulus fibrosus.

Herniation often occurs to the back and side in the lower lumbar spine, pressing on a nerve root and causing sciatica or leg weakness.

Why it matters

The spine protects the cord and is the route for spinal and epidural anaesthesia. Understanding it also supports safe handling of trauma and positioning for surgery.

Remember

Disc bulge presses a nerve.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about intervertebral disc?

Disc bulge presses a nerve.

where-the-spinal-cord-ends.title: Where the spinal cord ends
where-the-spinal-cord-ends.caption: In adults the spinal cord usually ends around L1 to L2, and in young children a little lower.
where-the-spinal-cord-ends.body:
In short: In adults the spinal cord usually ends around L1 to L2, and in young children a little lower.

Conus And Cauda Equina

In adults the spinal cord usually ends around L1 to L2, and in young children a little lower. Below it lies a bundle of nerve roots, the cauda equina.

Lumbar punctures and spinals are done below this level.

Why it matters

The spine protects the cord and is the route for spinal and epidural anaesthesia. Understanding it also supports safe handling of trauma and positioning for surgery.

Remember

Cord ends, roots continue.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about where the spinal cord ends?

Cord ends, roots continue.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

layers-crossed-by-a-spinal-needle.title: Layers crossed by a spinal needle
layers-crossed-by-a-spinal-needle.caption: A quick list on layers crossed by a spinal needle: Skin and subcutaneous tissue; Supraspinous then interspinous ligament.
layers-crossed-by-a-spinal-needle.body:
In short: A quick list on layers crossed by a spinal needle: Skin and subcutaneous tissue; Supraspinous then interspinous ligament.

Layers crossed by a spinal needle

  • Skin and subcutaneous tissue
  • Supraspinous then interspinous ligament
  • Ligamentum flavum (a distinct resistance)
  • Epidural space, then the dura
  • Arachnoid and subarachnoid space (CSF)

Why it matters

The spine protects the cord and is the route for spinal and epidural anaesthesia. Understanding it also supports safe handling of trauma and positioning for surgery.

Remember

Ligament, epidural, dura, CSF.

Check yourself

List the points covered under "Layers crossed by a spinal needle".

tuffier-s-line.title: Tuffier's line
tuffier-s-line.caption: A line between the highest points of the iliac crests usually crosses around L4 or the L4-5 space.
tuffier-s-line.body:
In short: A line between the highest points of the iliac crests usually crosses around L4 or the L4-5 space.

A Guide Only

A line between the highest points of the iliac crests usually crosses around L4 or the L4-5 space.

It can be inaccurate, as clinical estimates often point too high. Many practitioners check with ultrasound and choose a lower space to keep needles below the cord.

Why it matters

The spine protects the cord and is the route for spinal and epidural anaesthesia. Understanding it also supports safe handling of trauma and positioning for surgery.

Remember

Landmarks can lie.

Landmarks can lie.

epidural-space.title: Epidural space
epidural-space.caption: The epidural space lies between the dura and the bony canal, containing fat, veins and nerve roots.
epidural-space.body:
In short: The epidural space lies between the dura and the bony canal, containing fat, veins and nerve roots.

Space Outside The Dura

The epidural space lies between the dura and the bony canal, containing fat, veins and nerve roots.

In pregnancy the veins are engorged, so catheters can enter a vessel more easily. Always aspirate and test as per protocol.

Why it matters

The spine protects the cord and is the route for spinal and epidural anaesthesia. Understanding it also supports safe handling of trauma and positioning for surgery.

Remember

Check for blood before injecting.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about epidural space?

Check for blood before injecting.

curves-of-the-spine.title: Curves of the spine
curves-of-the-spine.caption: The spine has four curves.
curves-of-the-spine.body:
In short: The spine has four curves.

Natural Curves

The spine has four curves. The neck and lower back curve inward (lordosis); the chest and sacrum curve outward (kyphosis).

The curves absorb shock and balance the body. Positioning for surgery should respect them, using pads under the lumbar spine and neck.

Why it matters

The spine protects the cord and is the route for spinal and epidural anaesthesia. Understanding it also supports safe handling of trauma and positioning for surgery.

Remember

Support the curves when positioning.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about curves of the spine?

Support the curves when positioning.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

three-column-spine-stability.title: Three-column spine stability
three-column-spine-stability.caption: The spine can be thought of as anterior, middle and posterior columns.
three-column-spine-stability.body:
In short: The spine can be thought of as anterior, middle and posterior columns.

Unstable Injuries

The spine can be thought of as anterior, middle and posterior columns. Injury to two or more columns often makes it unstable.

Until cleared, suspect injury in trauma patients, keep the spine in line, and use log-rolling with trained helpers.

Why it matters

The spine protects the cord and is the route for spinal and epidural anaesthesia. Understanding it also supports safe handling of trauma and positioning for surgery.

Remember

Treat the spine as broken until proven safe.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about three-column spine stability?

Treat the spine as broken until proven safe.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

central-and-peripheral-systems.title: Central and peripheral systems
central-and-peripheral-systems.caption: The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord.
central-and-peripheral-systems.body:
In short: The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord.

Two Main Parts

The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord. The peripheral nervous system is every nerve outside them, carrying signals in and out.

The peripheral part includes somatic nerves for muscles and autonomic nerves for organs and glands.

Why it matters

Anaesthesia works on the nervous system, and many surgical risks involve nerves or the brain. A clear grasp of structure and function improves monitoring and safety.

Remember

Brain and cord command, nerves carry.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about central and peripheral systems?

Brain and cord command, nerves carry.

the-three-meninges.title: The three meninges
the-three-meninges.caption: A quick list on the three meninges: Dura mater - tough outer layer; Arachnoid mater - thin middle web.
the-three-meninges.body:
In short: A quick list on the three meninges: Dura mater - tough outer layer; Arachnoid mater - thin middle web.

The three meninges

  • Dura mater - tough outer layer
  • Arachnoid mater - thin middle web
  • Pia mater - fine layer on the brain
  • Subarachnoid space lies between arachnoid and pia
  • CSF circulates in the subarachnoid space

Why it matters

Anaesthesia works on the nervous system, and many surgical risks involve nerves or the brain. A clear grasp of structure and function improves monitoring and safety.

Remember

Dura, arachnoid, pia: outside in.

cerebrospinal-fluid-pathway.title: Cerebrospinal fluid pathway
cerebrospinal-fluid-pathway.caption: CSF is made mostly in the choroid plexus of the brain ventricles.
cerebrospinal-fluid-pathway.body:
In short: CSF is made mostly in the choroid plexus of the brain ventricles.

Csf Circulation

CSF is made mostly in the choroid plexus of the brain ventricles. It flows through the ventricles into the space around the brain and cord, and is absorbed into the blood.

Blockage can cause hydrocephalus, sometimes treated with a shunt.

Why it matters

Anaesthesia works on the nervous system, and many surgical risks involve nerves or the brain. A clear grasp of structure and function improves monitoring and safety.

Remember

Made inside, absorbed outside.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about cerebrospinal fluid pathway?

Made inside, absorbed outside.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

brain-arterial-ring.title: Brain arterial ring
brain-arterial-ring.caption: The circle of Willis is a ring of arteries at the base of the brain fed by the internal carotids and the basilar artery.
brain-arterial-ring.body:
In short: The circle of Willis is a ring of arteries at the base of the brain fed by the internal carotids and the basilar artery.

Brain Backup

The circle of Willis is a ring of arteries at the base of the brain fed by the internal carotids and the basilar artery.

It can help keep flow going if one vessel narrows, though many people have normal variations that make it incomplete.

Why it matters

Anaesthesia works on the nervous system, and many surgical risks involve nerves or the brain. A clear grasp of structure and function improves monitoring and safety.

Remember

Ring road for the brain.

Check yourself

Ring road for the brain.

sympathetic-and-parasympathetic.title: Sympathetic and parasympathetic
sympathetic-and-parasympathetic.caption: A quick list on sympathetic and parasympathetic: Sympathetic: fight or flight; Faster heart rate, wider pupils, raised pressure.
sympathetic-and-parasympathetic.body:
In short: A quick list on sympathetic and parasympathetic: Sympathetic: fight or flight; Faster heart rate, wider pupils, raised pressure.

Sympathetic and parasympathetic

  • Sympathetic: fight or flight
  • Faster heart rate, wider pupils, raised pressure
  • Parasympathetic: rest and digest
  • Slower heart rate, more gut activity
  • Surgery stress tips the balance

Why it matters

Anaesthesia works on the nervous system, and many surgical risks involve nerves or the brain. A clear grasp of structure and function improves monitoring and safety.

Remember

Opposite effects, balanced action.

reflex-arc.title: Reflex arc
reflex-arc.caption: A reflex arc has a sensor, a sensory nerve, a relay in the spinal cord or brainstem, a motor nerve and a muscle or gland.
reflex-arc.body:
In short: A reflex arc has a sensor, a sensory nerve, a relay in the spinal cord or brainstem, a motor nerve and a muscle or gland.

Fast Response

A reflex arc has a sensor, a sensory nerve, a relay in the spinal cord or brainstem, a motor nerve and a muscle or gland.

Because the signal skips the higher brain, response is fast. Anaesthesia can dull or abolish reflexes such as the gag and cough.

Why it matters

Anaesthesia works on the nervous system, and many surgical risks involve nerves or the brain. A clear grasp of structure and function improves monitoring and safety.

Remember

No thinking required.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about reflex arc?

No thinking required.

nerve-fibres-and-local-anaesthetic.title: Nerve fibres and local anaesthetic
nerve-fibres-and-local-anaesthetic.caption: Nerve signals travel along axons, and myelin speeds them up.
nerve-fibres-and-local-anaesthetic.body:
In short: Nerve signals travel along axons, and myelin speeds them up.

Why Blocks Behave

Nerve signals travel along axons, and myelin speeds them up. Local anaesthetic blocks sodium channels so the signal cannot pass.

Small, thinly myelinated fibres, such as those for pain and temperature, are usually blocked before touch and movement.

Why it matters

Anaesthesia works on the nervous system, and many surgical risks involve nerves or the brain. A clear grasp of structure and function improves monitoring and safety.

Remember

Pain goes first, power goes last.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about nerve fibres and local anaesthetic?

Pain goes first, power goes last.

glasgow-coma-scale-parts.caption: A quick list on glasgow coma scale parts: Eye opening (E); Verbal response (V).
glasgow-coma-scale-parts.body:
In short: A quick list on glasgow coma scale parts: Eye opening (E); Verbal response (V).

Glasgow Coma Scale parts

  • Eye opening (E)
  • Verbal response (V)
  • Motor response (M)
  • Total ranges from 3 to 15
  • Record the parts as well as the total

Anaesthesia works on the nervous system, and many surgical risks involve nerves or the brain. A clear grasp of structure and function improves monitoring and safety.

Remember

Three parts, three to fifteen.

vagus-nerve.title: Vagus nerve
vagus-nerve.caption: The vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) supplies the throat, heart, lungs and gut.
vagus-nerve.body:
In short: The vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) supplies the throat, heart, lungs and gut.

Wandering Nerve

The vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) supplies the throat, heart, lungs and gut.

Stimulation, for example by traction, pressure on the eye, or airway handling, can slow the heart, and sometimes cause a sudden fall in pulse. Stop the stimulus and call the anaesthetist.

Why it matters

Anaesthesia works on the nervous system, and many surgical risks involve nerves or the brain. A clear grasp of structure and function improves monitoring and safety.

Remember

Slow pulse: stop pulling.

classes-of-bone.title: Classes of bone
classes-of-bone.caption: Bones are grouped by shape: long (femur), short (wrist and ankle bones), flat (skull, ribs, sternum), irregular (vertebrae) and sesamoid (the patella, set in a tendon).
classes-of-bone.body:
In short: Bones are grouped by shape: long (femur), short (wrist and ankle bones), flat (skull, ribs, sternum), irregular (vertebrae) and sesamoid (the patella, set in a tendon).

Five Shapes

Bones are grouped by shape: long (femur), short (wrist and ankle bones), flat (skull, ribs, sternum), irregular (vertebrae) and sesamoid (the patella, set in a tendon).

Shape suits function: long bones act as levers, flat bones protect organs.

Why it matters

Orthopaedic and trauma lists are common in theatre. Understanding bone structure, healing and joint types helps you prepare equipment and handle patients safely.

Remember

Shape follows function.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about classes of bone?

Shape follows function.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

structure-of-bone.title: Structure of bone
structure-of-bone.caption: Hard compact bone forms the outer shell.
structure-of-bone.body:
In short: Hard compact bone forms the outer shell.

Inside A Bone

Hard compact bone forms the outer shell. Spongy bone inside is a honeycomb that contains marrow, where blood cells are made.

The periosteum, the outer skin of the bone, is rich in nerves and blood vessels, so a bone injury or drilling can be painful.

Why it matters

Orthopaedic and trauma lists are common in theatre. Understanding bone structure, healing and joint types helps you prepare equipment and handle patients safely.

Remember

Periosteum feels pain.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about structure of bone?

Periosteum feels pain.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

stages-of-fracture-healing.title: Stages of fracture healing
stages-of-fracture-healing.caption: A broken bone first forms a haematoma.
stages-of-fracture-healing.body:
In short: A broken bone first forms a haematoma.

Bone Repair

A broken bone first forms a haematoma. Soft callus of cartilage then bridges the gap, which hardens into bony callus.

Remodelling over months reshapes the bone along lines of stress. Stable fixation and good nutrition support each stage.

Why it matters

Orthopaedic and trauma lists are common in theatre. Understanding bone structure, healing and joint types helps you prepare equipment and handle patients safely.

Remember

Blood, soft, hard, remodel.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about stages of fracture healing?

Blood, soft, hard, remodel.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

why-fractures-heal-slowly.title: Why fractures heal slowly
why-fractures-heal-slowly.caption: Healing needs blood supply, stability and good nutrition.
why-fractures-heal-slowly.body:
In short: Healing needs blood supply, stability and good nutrition.

Delayed Union

Healing needs blood supply, stability and good nutrition. Poor blood flow, infection, smoking, diabetes and too much movement can delay or prevent union.

Some bones, like the scaphoid and neck of femur, have fragile blood supply and are prone to problems.

Why it matters

Orthopaedic and trauma lists are common in theatre. Understanding bone structure, healing and joint types helps you prepare equipment and handle patients safely.

Remember

Good blood and stillness help.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about why fractures heal slowly?

Good blood and stillness help.

features-of-a-synovial-joint.title: Features of a synovial joint
features-of-a-synovial-joint.caption: A quick list on features of a synovial joint: Articular cartilage covers bone ends; Joint capsule surrounds the joint.
features-of-a-synovial-joint.body:
In short: A quick list on features of a synovial joint: Articular cartilage covers bone ends; Joint capsule surrounds the joint.

Features of a synovial joint

  • Articular cartilage covers bone ends
  • Joint capsule surrounds the joint
  • Synovial membrane makes the fluid
  • Synovial fluid lubricates and feeds cartilage
  • Ligaments add stability

Why it matters

Orthopaedic and trauma lists are common in theatre. Understanding bone structure, healing and joint types helps you prepare equipment and handle patients safely.

Remember

Capsule, membrane, fluid.

Check yourself

List the points covered under "Features of a synovial joint".

Articular cartilage covers bone ends; Joint capsule surrounds the joint; Synovial membrane makes the fluid; Synovial fluid lubricates and feeds cartilage; Ligaments add stability.

types-of-synovial-joint.title: Types of synovial joint
types-of-synovial-joint.caption: Hinge joints, like the elbow, bend one way.
types-of-synovial-joint.body:
In short: Hinge joints, like the elbow, bend one way.

Shape Decides Motion

Hinge joints, like the elbow, bend one way. Ball and socket joints, like the hip, move in many directions. Pivot joints, like the neck's first and second bones, rotate.

Plane joints glide, and the saddle joint at the thumb base gives great movement.

Why it matters

Orthopaedic and trauma lists are common in theatre. Understanding bone structure, healing and joint types helps you prepare equipment and handle patients safely.

Remember

Shape decides the movement.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about types of synovial joint?

Shape decides the movement.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

hip-joint-and-femoral-neck.title: Hip joint and femoral neck
hip-joint-and-femoral-neck.caption: The hip is a deep ball and socket joint.
hip-joint-and-femoral-neck.body:
In short: The hip is a deep ball and socket joint.

Deep And Strong

The hip is a deep ball and socket joint. The head of the femur gets blood through small vessels running up the neck.

A neck fracture can disrupt these, risking bone death (avascular necrosis). Older adults with hip fractures usually need prompt surgery.

Why it matters

Orthopaedic and trauma lists are common in theatre. Understanding bone structure, healing and joint types helps you prepare equipment and handle patients safely.

Remember

Neck fracture can starve the head.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about hip joint and femoral neck?

Neck fracture can starve the head.

knee-ligaments-and-menisci.title: Knee ligaments and menisci
knee-ligaments-and-menisci.caption: The anterior cruciate ligament stops the shin sliding forward and the posterior cruciate stops it sliding back.
knee-ligaments-and-menisci.body:
In short: The anterior cruciate ligament stops the shin sliding forward and the posterior cruciate stops it sliding back.

Stabilising The Knee

The anterior cruciate ligament stops the shin sliding forward and the posterior cruciate stops it sliding back. Menisci are C-shaped cartilages that cushion the joint.

Twisting injuries often tear them, and may need arthroscopy.

Why it matters

Orthopaedic and trauma lists are common in theatre. Understanding bone structure, healing and joint types helps you prepare equipment and handle patients safely.

Remember

Twist injury, think cruciate.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about knee ligaments and menisci?

Twist injury, think cruciate.

growth-plates-in-children.title: Growth plates in children
growth-plates-in-children.caption: In children the growth plate, or physis, is weaker than nearby ligaments, so injuries often break the plate rather than tear a ligament.
growth-plates-in-children.body:
In short: In children the growth plate, or physis, is weaker than nearby ligaments, so injuries often break the plate rather than tear a ligament.

Weak Point

In children the growth plate, or physis, is weaker than nearby ligaments, so injuries often break the plate rather than tear a ligament.

Damage can affect growth, so injuries near joints in children need accurate assessment and follow-up.

Why it matters

Orthopaedic and trauma lists are common in theatre. Understanding bone structure, healing and joint types helps you prepare equipment and handle patients safely.

Remember

Child's joint injury: think growth plate.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about growth plates in children?

Child's joint injury: think growth plate.

osteoporosis-and-fragility-fractures.title: Osteoporosis and fragility fractures
osteoporosis-and-fragility-fractures.caption: Osteoporosis makes bones lose density and become brittle, mostly in older people, especially after menopause.
osteoporosis-and-fragility-fractures.body:
In short: Osteoporosis makes bones lose density and become brittle, mostly in older people, especially after menopause.

Thin Bones

Osteoporosis makes bones lose density and become brittle, mostly in older people, especially after menopause. Low-impact falls can break the hip, wrist or spine.

Handle patients gently during positioning and transfers, and support the limbs.

Why it matters

Orthopaedic and trauma lists are common in theatre. Understanding bone structure, healing and joint types helps you prepare equipment and handle patients safely.

Remember

Lift gently, support joints.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about osteoporosis and fragility fractures?

Lift gently, support joints.

layers-of-the-eye.title: Layers of the eye
layers-of-the-eye.caption: A quick list on layers of the eye: Outer - sclera (white) and cornea (clear front); Middle - choroid, ciliary body and iris.
layers-of-the-eye.body:
In short: A quick list on layers of the eye: Outer - sclera (white) and cornea (clear front); Middle - choroid, ciliary body and iris.

Layers of the eye

  • Outer - sclera (white) and cornea (clear front)
  • Middle - choroid, ciliary body and iris
  • Inner - retina, the light-sensing layer
  • Lens sits behind the iris
  • Vitreous fills the back, aqueous the front

Why it matters

Eye and ear surgery have special anaesthetic and positioning needs, and reflexes from these organs affect the heart. Basic anatomy explains why.

Remember

Three layers form the wall.

Check yourself

List the points covered under "Layers of the eye".

Outer - sclera (white) and cornea (clear front); Middle - choroid, ciliary body and iris; Inner - retina, the light-sensing layer; Lens sits behind the iris; Vitreous fills the back, aqueous the front.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

pupil-size-and-drugs.title: Pupil size and drugs
pupil-size-and-drugs.caption: The iris muscles change pupil size.
pupil-size-and-drugs.body:
In short: The iris muscles change pupil size.

Window Of The Eye

The iris muscles change pupil size. Sympathetic action widens the pupil, while parasympathetic action through the oculomotor nerve narrows it.

Opioids usually make pupils small, whereas atropine-like drugs widen them. Unequal or fixed pupils in a head injury are an emergency.

Why it matters

Eye and ear surgery have special anaesthetic and positioning needs, and reflexes from these organs affect the heart. Basic anatomy explains why.

Remember

Check pupils, report differences.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about pupil size and drugs?

Check pupils, report differences.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

aqueous-humour-and-glaucoma.title: Aqueous humour and glaucoma
aqueous-humour-and-glaucoma.caption: The ciliary body makes aqueous humour, which drains at the angle between iris and cornea.
aqueous-humour-and-glaucoma.body:
In short: The ciliary body makes aqueous humour, which drains at the angle between iris and cornea.

Eye Pressure

The ciliary body makes aqueous humour, which drains at the angle between iris and cornea.

If drainage is blocked, eye pressure rises, which can damage the optic nerve. Patients with glaucoma should continue their eye drops and tell the team.

Why it matters

Eye and ear surgery have special anaesthetic and positioning needs, and reflexes from these organs affect the heart. Basic anatomy explains why.

Remember

Keep glaucoma drops going.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about aqueous humour and glaucoma?

Keep glaucoma drops going.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

cornea-and-eye-protection.title: Cornea and eye protection
cornea-and-eye-protection.caption: The cornea has no blood vessels and is very sensitive.
cornea-and-eye-protection.body:
In short: The cornea has no blood vessels and is very sensitive.

Clear But Fragile

The cornea has no blood vessels and is very sensitive. During anaesthesia the blink reflex is lost, so the eyes dry and scratch easily.

Tape or cover the eyes, use lubricant if ordered, and avoid pressure from masks, drapes or the patient lying face down.

Why it matters

Eye and ear surgery have special anaesthetic and positioning needs, and reflexes from these organs affect the heart. Basic anatomy explains why.

Remember

Protect eyes under anaesthesia.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about cornea and eye protection?

Protect eyes under anaesthesia.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

retina-and-the-optic-nerve.title: Retina and the optic nerve
retina-and-the-optic-nerve.caption: The retina has rods, which see in dim light, and cones, which see colour and detail.
retina-and-the-optic-nerve.body:
In short: The retina has rods, which see in dim light, and cones, which see colour and detail.

Seeing Cells

The retina has rods, which see in dim light, and cones, which see colour and detail. Signals leave through the optic nerve.

In long prone cases, pressure on the eye or low blood pressure can threaten vision, so keep the head and eyes free from pressure.

Why it matters

Eye and ear surgery have special anaesthetic and positioning needs, and reflexes from these organs affect the heart. Basic anatomy explains why.

Remember

No pressure on eyes when prone.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about retina and the optic nerve?

No pressure on eyes when prone.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

parts-of-the-ear.title: Parts of the ear
parts-of-the-ear.caption: The outer ear collects sound to the eardrum.
parts-of-the-ear.body:
In short: The outer ear collects sound to the eardrum.

Outer, Middle, Inner

The outer ear collects sound to the eardrum. The middle ear has three tiny bones, the ossicles, that pass vibration on.

The inner ear holds the cochlea for hearing and the vestibule and canals for balance. The Eustachian tube links the middle ear to the throat.

Why it matters

Eye and ear surgery have special anaesthetic and positioning needs, and reflexes from these organs affect the heart. Basic anatomy explains why.

Remember

Sound travels in, then becomes a signal.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about parts of the ear?

Sound travels in, then becomes a signal.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

middle-ear-pressure.title: Middle ear pressure
middle-ear-pressure.caption: The Eustachian tube links the middle ear to the nasopharynx and equalises pressure either side of the eardrum.
middle-ear-pressure.body:
In short: The Eustachian tube links the middle ear to the nasopharynx and equalises pressure either side of the eardrum.

Eustachian Tube

The Eustachian tube links the middle ear to the nasopharynx and equalises pressure either side of the eardrum.

Nitrous oxide moves into closed air spaces faster than nitrogen leaves, so it can raise middle ear pressure. It is often avoided in some ear surgery.

Why it matters

Eye and ear surgery have special anaesthetic and positioning needs, and reflexes from these organs affect the heart. Basic anatomy explains why.

Remember

Gas can build in closed spaces.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about middle ear pressure?

Gas can build in closed spaces.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

inner-ear-and-nausea.title: Inner ear and nausea
inner-ear-and-nausea.caption: The semicircular canals and vestibule detect head movement.
inner-ear-and-nausea.body:
In short: The semicircular canals and vestibule detect head movement.

Balance Organ

The semicircular canals and vestibule detect head movement. Disturbing them, as in ear surgery or when moving after anaesthesia, can cause dizziness and vomiting.

Move patients slowly, give anti-sickness medicines as ordered, and have a bowl ready.

Why it matters

Eye and ear surgery have special anaesthetic and positioning needs, and reflexes from these organs affect the heart. Basic anatomy explains why.

Remember

Slow moves, ready bowl.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about inner ear and nausea?

Slow moves, ready bowl.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

skin-sensation-receptors.title: Skin sensation receptors
skin-sensation-receptors.caption: Skin has receptors for light touch, pressure, vibration, warmth, cold and pain.
skin-sensation-receptors.body:
In short: Skin has receptors for light touch, pressure, vibration, warmth, cold and pain.

Skin Senses

Skin has receptors for light touch, pressure, vibration, warmth, cold and pain. Pain is sensed by free nerve endings called nociceptors.

Proprioception, the sense of position, comes from receptors in muscles and joints. Regional blocks can remove some of these senses and not others.

Why it matters

Eye and ear surgery have special anaesthetic and positioning needs, and reflexes from these organs affect the heart. Basic anatomy explains why.

Remember

Different fibres, different senses.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about skin sensation receptors?

Different fibres, different senses.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

cardiac-output-explained.title: Cardiac output explained
cardiac-output-explained.caption: Cardiac output is the volume of blood the heart pumps each minute.
cardiac-output-explained.body:
In short: Cardiac output is the volume of blood the heart pumps each minute.

Heart Rate X Stroke Volume

Cardiac output is the volume of blood the heart pumps each minute. It equals heart rate multiplied by stroke volume.

Anaesthetic drugs can lower either part, so output often falls unless the body compensates.

Why it matters

Understanding how the heart and circulation work explains why blood pressure and rhythm change under anaesthesia, and how to respond to bleeding or shock.

Remember

Output = rate times stroke volume.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about cardiac output explained?

Output = rate times stroke volume.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

determinants-of-stroke-volume.title: Determinants of stroke volume
determinants-of-stroke-volume.caption: A quick list on determinants of stroke volume: Preload: how full the ventricle is before beating; Contractility: the strength of the squeeze.
determinants-of-stroke-volume.body:
In short: A quick list on determinants of stroke volume: Preload: how full the ventricle is before beating; Contractility: the strength of the squeeze.

Determinants of stroke volume

  • Preload: how full the ventricle is before beating
  • Contractility: the strength of the squeeze
  • Afterload: the resistance the heart pumps against
  • Low volume, weak heart or high resistance all
  • reduce the output

Why it matters

Understanding how the heart and circulation work explains why blood pressure and rhythm change under anaesthesia, and how to respond to bleeding or shock.

Remember

Preload, contractility, afterload.

Check yourself

List the points covered under "Determinants of stroke volume".

Preload: how full the ventricle is before beating; Contractility: the strength of the squeeze; Afterload: the resistance the heart pumps against; Low volume, weak heart or high resistance all; reduce the output.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

frank-starling-law.title: Frank-Starling law
frank-starling-law.caption: Within limits, the more the heart muscle is stretched by filling, the harder it contracts.
frank-starling-law.body:
In short: Within limits, the more the heart muscle is stretched by filling, the harder it contracts.

Stretch And Squeeze

Within limits, the more the heart muscle is stretched by filling, the harder it contracts. This matches output to the blood returning.

In a failing or overfilled heart the relationship flattens, and extra fluid no longer helps.

Why it matters

Understanding how the heart and circulation work explains why blood pressure and rhythm change under anaesthesia, and how to respond to bleeding or shock.

Remember

More filling, stronger beat, up to a point.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about frank-starling law?

More filling, stronger beat, up to a point.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

map-and-organ-perfusion.title: MAP and organ perfusion
map-and-organ-perfusion.caption: Mean arterial pressure (MAP) is the average pressure driving blood through organs.
map-and-organ-perfusion.body:
In short: Mean arterial pressure (MAP) is the average pressure driving blood through organs.

Perfusion Pressure

Mean arterial pressure (MAP) is the average pressure driving blood through organs. It is roughly cardiac output multiplied by systemic vascular resistance.

Many teams aim to keep MAP above a set target during surgery so the brain and kidneys stay perfused.

Why it matters

Understanding how the heart and circulation work explains why blood pressure and rhythm change under anaesthesia, and how to respond to bleeding or shock.

Remember

MAP drives organ blood flow.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about map and organ perfusion?

MAP drives organ blood flow.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

the-baroreceptor-reflex.title: The baroreceptor reflex
the-baroreceptor-reflex.caption: Stretch sensors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch detect blood pressure.
the-baroreceptor-reflex.body:
In short: Stretch sensors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch detect blood pressure.

Fast Bp Control

Stretch sensors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch detect blood pressure. If pressure falls, they signal the brainstem to raise heart rate and tighten vessels.

Anaesthetic agents can blunt this reflex, so positioning changes may cause sudden drops.

Why it matters

Understanding how the heart and circulation work explains why blood pressure and rhythm change under anaesthesia, and how to respond to bleeding or shock.

Remember

Sensors in the neck and aorta guard pressure.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about the baroreceptor reflex?

Sensors in the neck and aorta guard pressure.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

cardiac-conduction-pathway.title: Cardiac conduction pathway
cardiac-conduction-pathway.caption: A quick list on cardiac conduction pathway: Sinoatrial node starts the impulse; Atrioventricular node delays it briefly.
cardiac-conduction-pathway.body:
In short: A quick list on cardiac conduction pathway: Sinoatrial node starts the impulse; Atrioventricular node delays it briefly.

Cardiac conduction pathway

  • Sinoatrial node starts the impulse
  • Atrioventricular node delays it briefly
  • Bundle of His splits into left and right branches
  • Purkinje fibres spread it through the ventricles
  • The order gives a coordinated beat

Why it matters

Understanding how the heart and circulation work explains why blood pressure and rhythm change under anaesthesia, and how to respond to bleeding or shock.

Remember

SA node, AV node, His, Purkinje.

Check yourself

List the points covered under "Cardiac conduction pathway".

Sinoatrial node starts the impulse; Atrioventricular node delays it briefly; Bundle of His splits into left and right branches; Purkinje fibres spread it through the ventricles; The order gives a coordinated beat.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

reading-the-ecg-waves.title: Reading the ECG waves
reading-the-ecg-waves.caption: The P wave shows atrial depolarisation.
reading-the-ecg-waves.body:
In short: The P wave shows atrial depolarisation.

P, Qrs And T

The P wave shows atrial depolarisation. The QRS complex shows ventricular depolarisation. The T wave shows ventricular repolarisation.

The monitor trace helps spot rhythm changes, but always check the patient and pulse too.

Why it matters

Understanding how the heart and circulation work explains why blood pressure and rhythm change under anaesthesia, and how to respond to bleeding or shock.

Remember

Treat the patient, not just the trace.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about reading the ecg waves?

Treat the patient, not just the trace.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

venous-return-and-the-muscle-pump.title: Venous return and the muscle pump
venous-return-and-the-muscle-pump.caption: Veins have valves, and contracting leg muscles squeeze blood towards the heart.
venous-return-and-the-muscle-pump.body:
In short: Veins have valves, and contracting leg muscles squeeze blood towards the heart.

Blood Back To The Heart

Veins have valves, and contracting leg muscles squeeze blood towards the heart. Breathing movements also assist.

An anaesthetised, paralysed patient loses this pump, so blood may pool in the legs and venous return falls.

Why it matters

Understanding how the heart and circulation work explains why blood pressure and rhythm change under anaesthesia, and how to respond to bleeding or shock.

Remember

Muscles help return blood.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about venous return and the muscle pump?

Muscles help return blood.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

coronary-blood-flow-timing.title: Coronary blood flow timing
coronary-blood-flow-timing.caption: Most blood flow to the left ventricle occurs during diastole, when the muscle relaxes and vessels are not squeezed.
coronary-blood-flow-timing.body:
In short: Most blood flow to the left ventricle occurs during diastole, when the muscle relaxes and vessels are not squeezed.

Heart Feeds In Diastole

Most blood flow to the left ventricle occurs during diastole, when the muscle relaxes and vessels are not squeezed.

A very fast heart rate shortens diastole, and low diastolic pressure cuts supply, raising the risk of ischaemia.

Why it matters

Understanding how the heart and circulation work explains why blood pressure and rhythm change under anaesthesia, and how to respond to bleeding or shock.

Remember

Fast rates steal filling and feeding time.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about coronary blood flow timing?

Fast rates steal filling and feeding time.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

compensation-in-blood-loss.title: Compensation in blood loss
compensation-in-blood-loss.caption: A quick list on compensation in blood loss: Heart rate rises first; Vessels constrict to protect core organs.
compensation-in-blood-loss.body:
In short: A quick list on compensation in blood loss: Heart rate rises first; Vessels constrict to protect core organs.

Compensation in blood loss

  • Heart rate rises first
  • Vessels constrict to protect core organs
  • Skin turns cool, pale and clammy
  • Pulse pressure narrows
  • Blood pressure falls late, a worrying sign

Why it matters

Understanding how the heart and circulation work explains why blood pressure and rhythm change under anaesthesia, and how to respond to bleeding or shock.

Remember

Low pressure is a late sign of shock.

Check yourself

List the points covered under "Compensation in blood loss".

Heart rate rises first; Vessels constrict to protect core organs; Skin turns cool, pale and clammy; Pulse pressure narrows; Blood pressure falls late, a worrying sign.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

tidal-volume-and-minute-ventilation.title: Tidal volume and minute ventilation
tidal-volume-and-minute-ventilation.caption: Tidal volume is the air moved in one normal breath.
tidal-volume-and-minute-ventilation.body:
In short: Tidal volume is the air moved in one normal breath.

Volume Per Minute

Tidal volume is the air moved in one normal breath. Minute ventilation is tidal volume multiplied by respiratory rate.

Part of each breath fills the airways only (dead space) and takes no part in gas exchange.

Why it matters

Airway and breathing problems are the commonest threats to anaesthetised patients, so knowing how oxygen and ventilation work helps you spot trouble early.

Remember

Minute volume = breath size x rate.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about tidal volume and minute ventilation?

Minute volume = breath size x rate.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

functional-residual-capacity.title: Functional residual capacity
functional-residual-capacity.caption: FRC is the air left in the lungs after a normal breath out.
functional-residual-capacity.body:
In short: FRC is the air left in the lungs after a normal breath out.

The Oxygen Store

FRC is the air left in the lungs after a normal breath out. It acts as an oxygen reserve during apnoea.

Lying flat, obesity, pregnancy and anaesthesia reduce FRC, so oxygen levels fall faster when breathing stops.

Why it matters

Airway and breathing problems are the commonest threats to anaesthetised patients, so knowing how oxygen and ventilation work helps you spot trouble early.

Remember

Lower FRC means faster desaturation.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about functional residual capacity?

Lower FRC means faster desaturation.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

ventilation-and-perfusion-matching.title: Ventilation and perfusion matching
ventilation-and-perfusion-matching.caption: Efficient gas exchange needs air and blood in the same place.
ventilation-and-perfusion-matching.body:
In short: Efficient gas exchange needs air and blood in the same place.

V/Q Balance

Efficient gas exchange needs air and blood in the same place. Alveoli with air but no blood are dead space. Alveoli with blood but no air act as shunt.

Poor matching is a common cause of low oxygen levels.

Why it matters

Airway and breathing problems are the commonest threats to anaesthetised patients, so knowing how oxygen and ventilation work helps you spot trouble early.

Remember

Air and blood must meet.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about ventilation and perfusion matching?

Air and blood must meet.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

oxyhaemoglobin-dissociation-curve.title: Oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve
oxyhaemoglobin-dissociation-curve.caption: The curve shows how haemoglobin binds oxygen at different pressures.
oxyhaemoglobin-dissociation-curve.body:
In short: The curve shows how haemoglobin binds oxygen at different pressures.

S-Shaped Curve

The curve shows how haemoglobin binds oxygen at different pressures. A shift right means oxygen is released more easily to tissues.

Heat, acidity and raised carbon dioxide shift it right. Cold and alkalosis shift it left.

Why it matters

Airway and breathing problems are the commonest threats to anaesthetised patients, so knowing how oxygen and ventilation work helps you spot trouble early.

Remember

Right shift releases oxygen to tissues.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve?

Right shift releases oxygen to tissues.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

control-of-breathing.title: Control of breathing
control-of-breathing.caption: Breathing is set by respiratory centres in the brainstem.
control-of-breathing.body:
In short: Breathing is set by respiratory centres in the brainstem.

Brainstem Drive

Breathing is set by respiratory centres in the brainstem. Chemoreceptors respond mainly to carbon dioxide and hydrogen ion levels, and to low oxygen.

Opioids and many anaesthetics blunt this drive, so monitor breathing closely.

Why it matters

Airway and breathing problems are the commonest threats to anaesthetised patients, so knowing how oxygen and ventilation work helps you spot trouble early.

Remember

CO2 is the main driver of breathing.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about control of breathing?

CO2 is the main driver of breathing.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

work-of-breathing-signs.title: Work of breathing signs
work-of-breathing-signs.caption: A quick list on work of breathing signs: Nasal flaring and tracheal tug; Intercostal and subcostal recession.
work-of-breathing-signs.body:
In short: A quick list on work of breathing signs: Nasal flaring and tracheal tug; Intercostal and subcostal recession.

Work of breathing signs

  • Nasal flaring and tracheal tug
  • Intercostal and subcostal recession
  • Use of neck and shoulder muscles
  • Rapid, shallow or laboured breaths
  • Sweating and inability to speak in full sentences

Why it matters

Airway and breathing problems are the commonest threats to anaesthetised patients, so knowing how oxygen and ventilation work helps you spot trouble early.

Remember

Recession means the patient is working hard.

Check yourself

List the points covered under "Work of breathing signs".

Nasal flaring and tracheal tug; Intercostal and subcostal recession; Use of neck and shoulder muscles; Rapid, shallow or laboured breaths; Sweating and inability to speak in full sentences.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

surfactant-and-lung-compliance.title: Surfactant and lung compliance
surfactant-and-lung-compliance.caption: Surfactant lowers surface tension inside alveoli and stops them collapsing at the end of a breath.
surfactant-and-lung-compliance.body:
In short: Surfactant lowers surface tension inside alveoli and stops them collapsing at the end of a breath.

Keeping Alveoli Open

Surfactant lowers surface tension inside alveoli and stops them collapsing at the end of a breath.

Premature babies may lack it and develop respiratory distress. Damaged lungs in adults also become stiff and hard to inflate.

Why it matters

Airway and breathing problems are the commonest threats to anaesthetised patients, so knowing how oxygen and ventilation work helps you spot trouble early.

Remember

Surfactant stops alveolar collapse.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about surfactant and lung compliance?

Surfactant stops alveolar collapse.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

atelectasis-under-anaesthesia.title: Atelectasis under anaesthesia
atelectasis-under-anaesthesia.caption: Small areas of lung can collapse soon after induction, especially in the dependent parts, after high oxygen concentrations, or from reduced FRC.
atelectasis-under-anaesthesia.body:
In short: Small areas of lung can collapse soon after induction, especially in the dependent parts, after high oxygen concentrations, or from reduced FRC.

Collapsed Lung Units

Small areas of lung can collapse soon after induction, especially in the dependent parts, after high oxygen concentrations, or from reduced FRC.

Deep breaths, positive end-expiratory pressure and early sitting up may help reopen them.

Why it matters

Airway and breathing problems are the commonest threats to anaesthetised patients, so knowing how oxygen and ventilation work helps you spot trouble early.

Remember

Encourage deep breaths after surgery.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about atelectasis under anaesthesia?

Encourage deep breaths after surgery.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

hypoxaemia-versus-hypoxia.title: Hypoxaemia versus hypoxia
hypoxaemia-versus-hypoxia.caption: Hypoxaemia means low oxygen in the blood.
hypoxaemia-versus-hypoxia.body:
In short: Hypoxaemia means low oxygen in the blood.

Blood Versus Tissue

Hypoxaemia means low oxygen in the blood. Hypoxia means low oxygen reaching the tissues.

Tissues can be hypoxic even with normal blood oxygen if there is severe anaemia, poor circulation or poisoning that blocks use of oxygen.

Why it matters

Airway and breathing problems are the commonest threats to anaesthetised patients, so knowing how oxygen and ventilation work helps you spot trouble early.

Remember

Oxygen delivery needs blood, flow and haemoglobin.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about hypoxaemia versus hypoxia?

Oxygen delivery needs blood, flow and haemoglobin.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

causes-of-hypoxaemia.title: Causes of hypoxaemia
causes-of-hypoxaemia.caption: A quick list on causes of hypoxaemia: Low inspired oxygen; Hypoventilation.
causes-of-hypoxaemia.body:
In short: A quick list on causes of hypoxaemia: Low inspired oxygen; Hypoventilation.

Causes of hypoxaemia

  • Low inspired oxygen
  • Hypoventilation
  • V/Q mismatch
  • Shunt
  • Diffusion problems, such as lung fibrosis

Why it matters

Airway and breathing problems are the commonest threats to anaesthetised patients, so knowing how oxygen and ventilation work helps you spot trouble early.

Remember

Five routes to low oxygen.

Check yourself

List the points covered under "Causes of hypoxaemia".

Low inspired oxygen; Hypoventilation; V/Q mismatch; Shunt; Diffusion problems, such as lung fibrosis.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

the-nephron-at-a-glance.title: The nephron at a glance
the-nephron-at-a-glance.caption: Each nephron has a glomerulus that filters blood, and tubules that reabsorb useful substances and secrete waste.
the-nephron-at-a-glance.body:
In short: Each nephron has a glomerulus that filters blood, and tubules that reabsorb useful substances and secrete waste.

Filter And Adjust

Each nephron has a glomerulus that filters blood, and tubules that reabsorb useful substances and secrete waste.

The result is urine, with water, salt and acid levels adjusted to the body's needs.

Why it matters

The kidneys control fluid, salts and drug clearance. Theatre events like bleeding and low pressure can injure them, so these basics guide safe care.

Remember

Filter first, then fine-tune.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about the nephron at a glance?

Filter first, then fine-tune.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

glomerular-filtration-rate.title: Glomerular filtration rate
glomerular-filtration-rate.caption: GFR is the volume of blood filtered by the kidneys each minute.
glomerular-filtration-rate.body:
In short: GFR is the volume of blood filtered by the kidneys each minute.

How Well Kidneys Filter

GFR is the volume of blood filtered by the kidneys each minute. It is the best overall measure of kidney function.

It falls with age, dehydration, low blood pressure and kidney disease, which can slow elimination of some drugs.

Why it matters

The kidneys control fluid, salts and drug clearance. Theatre events like bleeding and low pressure can injure them, so these basics guide safe care.

Remember

Low GFR means slower drug clearance.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about glomerular filtration rate?

Low GFR means slower drug clearance.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

autoregulation-of-kidney-flow.title: Autoregulation of kidney flow
autoregulation-of-kidney-flow.caption: Healthy kidneys keep blood flow and filtration fairly constant across a wide range of blood pressures.
autoregulation-of-kidney-flow.body:
In short: Healthy kidneys keep blood flow and filtration fairly constant across a wide range of blood pressures.

Steady Filtration

Healthy kidneys keep blood flow and filtration fairly constant across a wide range of blood pressures.

Below that range, filtration falls. Prolonged low blood pressure in theatre can therefore injure the kidneys.

Why it matters

The kidneys control fluid, salts and drug clearance. Theatre events like bleeding and low pressure can injure them, so these basics guide safe care.

Remember

Avoid long spells of low pressure.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about autoregulation of kidney flow?

Avoid long spells of low pressure.

renin-angiotensin-aldosterone-system.title: Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system
renin-angiotensin-aldosterone-system.caption: A quick list on renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system: Low pressure or low sodium triggers renin release; Renin leads to angiotensin II formation.
renin-angiotensin-aldosterone-system.body:
In short: A quick list on renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system: Low pressure or low sodium triggers renin release; Renin leads to angiotensin II formation.

Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system

  • Low pressure or low sodium triggers renin release
  • Renin leads to angiotensin II formation
  • Angiotensin II narrows vessels
  • Aldosterone makes the kidney retain salt and water
  • The net effect raises blood pressure and volume

Why it matters

The kidneys control fluid, salts and drug clearance. Theatre events like bleeding and low pressure can injure them, so these basics guide safe care.

Remember

RAAS defends blood pressure.

antidiuretic-hormone.title: Antidiuretic hormone
antidiuretic-hormone.caption: ADH is released by the pituitary when blood is concentrated or volume is low.
antidiuretic-hormone.body:
In short: ADH is released by the pituitary when blood is concentrated or volume is low.

Water Conservation

ADH is released by the pituitary when blood is concentrated or volume is low. It makes the kidney collecting ducts reabsorb more water.

Pain, nausea, stress and surgery can raise ADH, so urine output may fall even when the patient is not dehydrated.

Why it matters

The kidneys control fluid, salts and drug clearance. Theatre events like bleeding and low pressure can injure them, so these basics guide safe care.

Remember

Stress raises ADH.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about antidiuretic hormone?

Stress raises ADH.

kidneys-and-acid-base-balance.title: Kidneys and acid-base balance
kidneys-and-acid-base-balance.caption: The kidneys excrete hydrogen ions and regulate bicarbonate.
kidneys-and-acid-base-balance.body:
In short: The kidneys excrete hydrogen ions and regulate bicarbonate.

Slow But Powerful

The kidneys excrete hydrogen ions and regulate bicarbonate. They respond over hours to days, while the lungs respond within minutes.

This is why the lungs compensate quickly for metabolic acidosis, and kidneys correct respiratory problems slowly.

Why it matters

The kidneys control fluid, salts and drug clearance. Theatre events like bleeding and low pressure can injure them, so these basics guide safe care.

Remember

Lungs are fast, kidneys are slow.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about kidneys and acid-base balance?

Lungs are fast, kidneys are slow.

potassium-handling.title: Potassium handling
potassium-handling.caption: Most potassium is inside cells, and the kidneys control how much is lost.
potassium-handling.body:
In short: Most potassium is inside cells, and the kidneys control how much is lost.

A Narrow Range

Most potassium is inside cells, and the kidneys control how much is lost. Both high and low blood levels affect heart rhythm.

Kidney failure, tissue damage, acidosis and some drugs can raise potassium, so watch for tall T waves on the ECG.

Why it matters

The kidneys control fluid, salts and drug clearance. Theatre events like bleeding and low pressure can injure them, so these basics guide safe care.

Remember

Potassium problems change the ECG.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about potassium handling?

Potassium problems change the ECG.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

nephrotoxic-risks-to-remember.title: Nephrotoxic risks to remember
nephrotoxic-risks-to-remember.caption: A quick list on nephrotoxic risks to remember: Some antibiotics, such as aminoglycosides; Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.
nephrotoxic-risks-to-remember.body:
In short: A quick list on nephrotoxic risks to remember: Some antibiotics, such as aminoglycosides; Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

Nephrotoxic risks to remember

  • Some antibiotics, such as aminoglycosides
  • Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
  • IV contrast agents
  • Prolonged low blood pressure
  • Muscle breakdown releasing myoglobin

Why it matters

The kidneys control fluid, salts and drug clearance. Theatre events like bleeding and low pressure can injure them, so these basics guide safe care.

Remember

Protect the kidneys in at-risk patients.

Check yourself

List the points covered under "Nephrotoxic risks to remember".

Some antibiotics, such as aminoglycosides; Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs; IV contrast agents; Prolonged low blood pressure; Muscle breakdown releasing myoglobin.

erythropoietin-from-the-kidney.title: Erythropoietin from the kidney
erythropoietin-from-the-kidney.caption: The kidneys make erythropoietin, which signals bone marrow to produce red cells when oxygen delivery is low.
erythropoietin-from-the-kidney.body:
In short: The kidneys make erythropoietin, which signals bone marrow to produce red cells when oxygen delivery is low.

Blood And Kidney

The kidneys make erythropoietin, which signals bone marrow to produce red cells when oxygen delivery is low.

Chronic kidney disease reduces this hormone, which is why many patients have long-term anaemia.

Why it matters

The kidneys control fluid, salts and drug clearance. Theatre events like bleeding and low pressure can injure them, so these basics guide safe care.

Remember

Failing kidneys can mean anaemia.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about erythropoietin from the kidney?

Failing kidneys can mean anaemia.

liver-functions-overview.title: Liver functions overview
liver-functions-overview.caption: A quick list on liver functions overview: Makes clotting factors and albumin; Metabolises many drugs.
liver-functions-overview.body:
In short: A quick list on liver functions overview: Makes clotting factors and albumin; Metabolises many drugs.

Liver functions overview

  • Makes clotting factors and albumin
  • Metabolises many drugs
  • Stores glycogen and releases glucose
  • Makes bile and clears bilirubin
  • Converts ammonia to urea

Why it matters

The gut and liver affect drug effects, fasting, bleeding and recovery. This knowledge helps you understand why some patients need special precautions.

Remember

The liver does many jobs at once.

Check yourself

List the points covered under "Liver functions overview".

Makes clotting factors and albumin; Metabolises many drugs; Stores glycogen and releases glucose; Makes bile and clears bilirubin; Converts ammonia to urea.

hepatic-dual-blood-supply.title: Hepatic dual blood supply
hepatic-dual-blood-supply.caption: The liver receives blood from the hepatic artery, which carries oxygen, and from the portal vein, which carries nutrients from the gut.
hepatic-dual-blood-supply.body:
In short: The liver receives blood from the hepatic artery, which carries oxygen, and from the portal vein, which carries nutrients from the gut.

Two Inflows

The liver receives blood from the hepatic artery, which carries oxygen, and from the portal vein, which carries nutrients from the gut.

Anaesthesia and surgery can lower liver blood flow, which is one reason liver patients need careful management.

Why it matters

The gut and liver affect drug effects, fasting, bleeding and recovery. This knowledge helps you understand why some patients need special precautions.

Remember

Keep pressure up to protect liver flow.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about hepatic dual blood supply?

Keep pressure up to protect liver flow.

first-pass-metabolism.title: First-pass metabolism
first-pass-metabolism.caption: Drugs absorbed from the gut pass through the liver before reaching general circulation.
first-pass-metabolism.body:
In short: Drugs absorbed from the gut pass through the liver before reaching general circulation.

Gut To Liver

Drugs absorbed from the gut pass through the liver before reaching general circulation. Some are largely broken down there.

This is why some medicines are given by injection, under the tongue or through other routes, and not swallowed.

Why it matters

The gut and liver affect drug effects, fasting, bleeding and recovery. This knowledge helps you understand why some patients need special precautions.

Remember

Oral route means liver first.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about first-pass metabolism?

Oral route means liver first.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

bile-and-fat-digestion.title: Bile and fat digestion
bile-and-fat-digestion.caption: Bile salts help break fats into small droplets so they can be digested and absorbed.
bile-and-fat-digestion.body:
In short: Bile salts help break fats into small droplets so they can be digested and absorbed.

Why Bile Matters

Bile salts help break fats into small droplets so they can be digested and absorbed. The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile.

Blocked bile flow can cause pale stools, dark urine and jaundice, and may impair absorption of vitamin K.

Why it matters

The gut and liver affect drug effects, fasting, bleeding and recovery. This knowledge helps you understand why some patients need special precautions.

Remember

Bile helps absorb fat and vitamin K.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about bile and fat digestion?

Bile helps absorb fat and vitamin K.

bilirubin-and-jaundice.title: Bilirubin and jaundice
bilirubin-and-jaundice.caption: A quick list on bilirubin and jaundice: Pre-hepatic: too much red cell breakdown; Hepatic: liver cells cannot process bilirubin.
bilirubin-and-jaundice.body:
In short: A quick list on bilirubin and jaundice: Pre-hepatic: too much red cell breakdown; Hepatic: liver cells cannot process bilirubin.

Bilirubin and jaundice

  • Pre-hepatic: too much red cell breakdown
  • Hepatic: liver cells cannot process bilirubin
  • Post-hepatic: bile flow is blocked
  • Yellow skin and eyes are the common sign
  • Tests and imaging help find the cause

Why it matters

The gut and liver affect drug effects, fasting, bleeding and recovery. This knowledge helps you understand why some patients need special precautions.

Remember

Jaundice has three broad causes.

Check yourself

List the points covered under "Bilirubin and jaundice".

Pre-hepatic: too much red cell breakdown; Hepatic: liver cells cannot process bilirubin; Post-hepatic: bile flow is blocked; Yellow skin and eyes are the common sign; Tests and imaging help find the cause.

gut-motility-and-ileus.title: Gut motility and ileus
gut-motility-and-ileus.caption: Surgery, opioids, electrolyte disturbance and handling of the bowel can slow or stop gut movement.
gut-motility-and-ileus.body:
In short: Surgery, opioids, electrolyte disturbance and handling of the bowel can slow or stop gut movement.

A Slowed Bowel

Surgery, opioids, electrolyte disturbance and handling of the bowel can slow or stop gut movement. This is called ileus.

Signs include bloating, vomiting and no passage of wind. Early mobilising and minimising opioids may help.

Why it matters

The gut and liver affect drug effects, fasting, bleeding and recovery. This knowledge helps you understand why some patients need special precautions.

Remember

Ileus is common after abdominal surgery.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about gut motility and ileus?

Ileus is common after abdominal surgery.

gastric-emptying-and-fasting.title: Gastric emptying and fasting
gastric-emptying-and-fasting.caption: Anaesthesia removes protective airway reflexes, so stomach contents may travel into the lungs.
gastric-emptying-and-fasting.body:
In short: Anaesthesia removes protective airway reflexes, so stomach contents may travel into the lungs.

Why We Fast

Anaesthesia removes protective airway reflexes, so stomach contents may travel into the lungs. Fasting lets the stomach empty.

Pain, trauma, pregnancy, diabetes and bowel obstruction can slow emptying, so these patients may need precautions.

Why it matters

The gut and liver affect drug effects, fasting, bleeding and recovery. This knowledge helps you understand why some patients need special precautions.

Remember

Fasting does not guarantee an empty stomach.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about gastric emptying and fasting?

Fasting does not guarantee an empty stomach.
