Protect Participants

Studies with people need ethical approval, voluntary informed consent and protection of privacy. Participants may withdraw at any time without penalty.

Honest reporting is essential. Never invent, alter or copy data or results.

Why it matters

Understanding research helps you judge claims, improve practice and complete required projects. Even simple studies need clear questions, ethics and honest methods.

Remember

Respect, consent, honesty.

Check yourself

Respect, consent, honesty.

sampling-and-bias.body:

Who Is Included

A sample should represent the group studied. If only easy or willing participants are chosen, results may mislead.

Bias can also come from how data are collected or how questions are worded. Plan to reduce it and be open about limits.

Why it matters

Understanding research helps you judge claims, improve practice and complete required projects. Even simple studies need clear questions, ethics and honest methods.

Remember

A biased sample gives biased answers.

A biased sample gives biased answers.

Data Quality

Why it matters

Understanding research helps you judge claims, improve practice and complete required projects. Even simple studies need clear questions, ethics and honest methods.

Keep a list of references as you read. Copying can lead to serious academic penalties.

Why it matters

Understanding research helps you judge claims, improve practice and complete required projects. Even simple studies need clear questions, ethics and honest methods.

acute-abdomen-first-steps.caption: An acute abdomen is sudden severe abdominal pain that may need surgery.
acute-abdomen-first-steps.body:
In short: An acute abdomen is sudden severe abdominal pain that may need surgery.

Act Early

An acute abdomen is sudden severe abdominal pain that may need surgery. Start with airway, breathing and circulation, then give oxygen, set up IV access and send bloods.

Not Small Adults

Normal core temperature is about 36.5 to 37.5 degrees Celsius. A fever is usually taken as 38 degrees or more. Below about 36 degrees is hypothermia risk in theatre.

Patients fast before general anaesthesia to reduce the risk of stomach contents reaching the lungs. Eating as usual can force a delay or cancellation.

Antibiotics work against bacteria, not viruses. Using them for colds or flu does not help and can cause harm and resistance.

Take antibiotics only when prescribed, and finish the course as directed.

In short: Wounds usually heal better when protected from dirt and kept moist and covered with a suitable dressing.

Moist Healing

Wounds usually heal better when protected from dirt and kept moist and covered with a suitable dressing.

Follow the surgeon's instructions, as some wounds need special care.

Common myths can lead to unsafe habits. Knowing the facts helps staff and patients make safer choices.

Remember

Cover and protect the wound.

myth-pain-shows-how-bad-it-is.title: Myth: pain shows how bad it is
myth-pain-shows-how-bad-it-is.caption: Pain does not always reflect how serious an injury is.
myth-pain-shows-how-bad-it-is.body:
In short: Pain does not always reflect how serious an injury is.

Pain And Severity

Pain does not always reflect how serious an injury is. Some serious problems, such as early internal bleeding, cause little pain at first.

Assess signs, history and examination, not pain alone.

Why it matters

Common myths can lead to unsafe habits. Knowing the facts helps staff and patients make safer choices.

Remember

Do not judge by pain alone.

fact-clean-hands-stop-infection.title: Fact: clean hands stop infection
fact-clean-hands-stop-infection.caption: Cleaning hands at the right moments is one of the most effective ways to stop infection from spreading.
fact-clean-hands-stop-infection.body:
In short: Cleaning hands at the right moments is one of the most effective ways to stop infection from spreading.

Simple And Powerful

Cleaning hands at the right moments is one of the most effective ways to stop infection from spreading. Alcohol rub works if hands are not visibly dirty.

Use soap and water when hands are soiled.

Why it matters

Common myths can lead to unsafe habits. Knowing the facts helps staff and patients make safer choices.

Remember

Clean hands save lives.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about fact: clean hands stop infection?

Clean hands save lives.

myth-gloves-replace-hand-washing.title: Myth: gloves replace hand washing
myth-gloves-replace-hand-washing.caption: Gloves can have tiny holes, and hands become contaminated when they are removed.
myth-gloves-replace-hand-washing.body:
In short: Gloves can have tiny holes, and hands become contaminated when they are removed.

Gloves Are Not Enough

Gloves can have tiny holes, and hands become contaminated when they are removed. Always clean hands before putting on and after taking off gloves.

Change gloves between patients and tasks.

Why it matters

Common myths can lead to unsafe habits. Knowing the facts helps staff and patients make safer choices.

Remember

Gloves are an extra layer.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about myth: gloves replace hand washing?

Gloves are an extra layer.

myth-anaesthesia-is-just-sleep.title: Myth: anaesthesia is just sleep
myth-anaesthesia-is-just-sleep.caption: General anaesthesia is a carefully controlled state of unconsciousness, with drugs to block pain and often muscle movement.
myth-anaesthesia-is-just-sleep.body:
In short: General anaesthesia is a carefully controlled state of unconsciousness, with drugs to block pain and often muscle movement.

A Controlled State

General anaesthesia is a carefully controlled state of unconsciousness, with drugs to block pain and often muscle movement. The patient needs airway support and monitoring.

It is quite different from natural sleep.

Why it matters

Common myths can lead to unsafe habits. Knowing the facts helps staff and patients make safer choices.

Remember

It is controlled and monitored.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about myth: anaesthesia is just sleep?

It is controlled and monitored.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

myth-sterile-means-clean.title: Myth: sterile means clean
myth-sterile-means-clean.caption: Clean means visible dirt is removed, while sterile means free of all living microorganisms.
myth-sterile-means-clean.body:
In short: Clean means visible dirt is removed, while sterile means free of all living microorganisms.

Sterile Vs Clean

Clean means visible dirt is removed, while sterile means free of all living microorganisms. An item can look clean and not be sterile.

Sterile items need correct packaging and storage.

Why it matters

Common myths can lead to unsafe habits. Knowing the facts helps staff and patients make safer choices.

Remember

Clean first, then sterilise.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about myth: sterile means clean?

Clean first, then sterilise.

fact-counts-protect-patients.title: Fact: counts protect patients
fact-counts-protect-patients.caption: Counting swabs, needles and instruments before, during and after surgery helps prevent anything being left inside the patient.
fact-counts-protect-patients.body:
In short: Counting swabs, needles and instruments before, during and after surgery helps prevent anything being left inside the patient.

The Count

Counting swabs, needles and instruments before, during and after surgery helps prevent anything being left inside the patient.

If the count is wrong, the team stops to search and follows local policy.

Why it matters

Common myths can lead to unsafe habits. Knowing the facts helps staff and patients make safer choices.

Remember

A wrong count means stop and search.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about fact: counts protect patients?

A wrong count means stop and search.

t-or-f-spinal-suits-everyone.title: T or F: spinal suits everyone
t-or-f-spinal-suits-everyone.caption: False.
t-or-f-spinal-suits-everyone.body:
In short: False.

Statement Check

False. Spinal anaesthesia is common, but it is not suitable for patients with some clotting problems, infection at the site, raised intracranial pressure or who refuse it.

The anaesthetist assesses each patient.

Why it matters

Testing yourself with simple statements reveals gaps in understanding. Think about the reasons, not only the answer.

Remember

Every technique has exceptions.

Check yourself

Every technique has exceptions.

t-or-f-a-patient-may-refuse-care.title: T or F: a patient may refuse care
t-or-f-a-patient-may-refuse-care.caption: True.
t-or-f-a-patient-may-refuse-care.body:
In short: True.

Statement Check

True. A patient with capacity has the right to refuse treatment even when clinicians disagree. The team should explain risks and document the decision.

There are special rules in emergencies and when capacity is missing.

Why it matters

Testing yourself with simple statements reveals gaps in understanding. Think about the reasons, not only the answer.

Remember

Respect capacity and document.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about t or f: a patient may refuse care?

Respect capacity and document.

t-or-f-nitrous-relaxes-muscles.title: T or F: nitrous relaxes muscles
t-or-f-nitrous-relaxes-muscles.caption: False.
t-or-f-nitrous-relaxes-muscles.body:
In short: False.

Statement Check

False. Nitrous oxide is an anaesthetic gas that gives pain relief and mild sedation. It does not relax muscles.

Muscle relaxants are separate drugs.

Why it matters

Testing yourself with simple statements reveals gaps in understanding. Think about the reasons, not only the answer.

Remember

N2O is not a muscle relaxant.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about t or f: nitrous relaxes muscles?

N2O is not a muscle relaxant.

t-or-f-tourniquet-pain-is-good.title: T or F: tourniquet pain is good
t-or-f-tourniquet-pain-is-good.caption: False.
t-or-f-tourniquet-pain-is-good.body:
In short: False.

Statement Check

False. Tourniquet pain is a common problem during longer limb operations and means the limb is under pressure. It is not a sign of success.

Time and pressure should be recorded.

Why it matters

Testing yourself with simple statements reveals gaps in understanding. Think about the reasons, not only the answer.

Remember

Record the tourniquet time.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about t or f: tourniquet pain is good?

Record the tourniquet time.

t-or-f-group-o-is-universal-donor.title: T or F: group O is universal donor
t-or-f-group-o-is-universal-donor.caption: Mostly true for red cells.
t-or-f-group-o-is-universal-donor.body:
In short: Mostly true for red cells.

Statement Check

Mostly true for red cells. O negative red cells can be given in emergencies when the recipient's group is unknown. Plasma works the other way around.

Crossmatching is used whenever there is time.

Why it matters

Testing yourself with simple statements reveals gaps in understanding. Think about the reasons, not only the answer.

Remember

Group first when you can.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about t or f: group o is universal donor?

Group first when you can.

t-or-f-reuse-single-use-items.title: T or F: reuse single-use items
t-or-f-reuse-single-use-items.caption: False.
t-or-f-reuse-single-use-items.body:
In short: False.

Statement Check

False. Single-use items are designed and tested for one use only. Cleaning and reuse can fail to remove contaminants and may damage the device.

Only items labelled reusable should be reprocessed.

Why it matters

Testing yourself with simple statements reveals gaps in understanding. Think about the reasons, not only the answer.

Remember

Single-use means once.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about t or f: reuse single-use items?

Single-use means once.

t-or-f-fever-always-means-infection.title: T or F: fever always means infection
t-or-f-fever-always-means-infection.caption: False.
t-or-f-fever-always-means-infection.body:
In short: False.

Statement Check

False. Infection is a common cause, but fever can also follow surgery, transfusion, drug reactions, blood clots and inflammation.

Assess the cause, rather than assuming.

Why it matters

Testing yourself with simple statements reveals gaps in understanding. Think about the reasons, not only the answer.

Remember

Look for the cause.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about t or f: fever always means infection?

Look for the cause.

t-or-f-oxygen-is-not-flammable.title: T or F: oxygen is not flammable
t-or-f-oxygen-is-not-flammable.caption: False.
t-or-f-oxygen-is-not-flammable.body:
In short: False.

Statement Check

False. Oxygen does not burn by itself, but it makes other materials burn much more fiercely. Extra care is needed with diathermy, lasers and alcohol-based preparations.

Oxygen-enriched air raises fire risk.

Why it matters

Testing yourself with simple statements reveals gaps in understanding. Think about the reasons, not only the answer.

Remember

Oxygen feeds fires.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about t or f: oxygen is not flammable?

Oxygen feeds fires.

t-or-f-safety-is-the-surgeon-s-job.title: T or F: safety is the surgeon's job
t-or-f-safety-is-the-surgeon-s-job.caption: False.
t-or-f-safety-is-the-surgeon-s-job.body:
In short: False.

Statement Check

False. Patient safety is a team responsibility. Everyone in theatre can speak up, check, count and stop the procedure if they see a problem.

Checklists support this.

Why it matters

Testing yourself with simple statements reveals gaps in understanding. Think about the reasons, not only the answer.

Remember

Safety belongs to everybody.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about t or f: safety is the surgeon's job?

Safety belongs to everybody.

t-or-f-any-glove-stops-chemicals.title: T or F: any glove stops chemicals
t-or-f-any-glove-stops-chemicals.caption: False.
t-or-f-any-glove-stops-chemicals.body:
In short: False.

Statement Check

False. Different glove materials protect against different hazards. Check the manufacturer's information when handling chemicals or cytotoxic drugs.

Latex allergy also needs an alternative.

Why it matters

Testing yourself with simple statements reveals gaps in understanding. Think about the reasons, not only the answer.

Remember

Match the glove to the hazard.

Match the glove to the hazard.

snapshot-low-saturation-new-tube.title: Snapshot: low saturation, new tube
snapshot-low-saturation-new-tube.caption: Oxygen saturation drops soon after intubation.
snapshot-low-saturation-new-tube.body:
In short: Oxygen saturation drops soon after intubation.

What Would You Check?

Oxygen saturation drops soon after intubation. Think of the DOPE reminder: displaced tube, obstruction, pneumothorax and equipment failure.

Ask for help, give 100 percent oxygen, check the tube and circuit, and reassess breath sounds.

Why it matters

Short cases help you practise thinking through a problem. In real situations, follow your hospital's protocol and call for senior help.

Remember

Check the tube, then the circuit.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about snapshot: low saturation, new tube?

Check the tube, then the circuit.

snapshot-wrong-blood-bag.title: Snapshot: wrong blood bag
snapshot-wrong-blood-bag.caption: A patient shivers and has a fever soon after a transfusion begins.
snapshot-wrong-blood-bag.body:
In short: A patient shivers and has a fever soon after a transfusion begins.

Stop The Transfusion

A patient shivers and has a fever soon after a transfusion begins. Stop the transfusion, keep the line open with saline, check the patient and the bag details, and tell the senior staff.

The unit and paperwork are returned for checking.

Why it matters

Short cases help you practise thinking through a problem. In real situations, follow your hospital's protocol and call for senior help.

Remember

Stop, check, report.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about snapshot: wrong blood bag?

Stop, check, report.

snapshot-swab-count-is-wrong.title: Snapshot: swab count is wrong
snapshot-swab-count-is-wrong.caption: At closure the count is one swab short.
snapshot-swab-count-is-wrong.body:
In short: At closure the count is one swab short.

What Next?

At closure the count is one swab short. The team tells the surgeon, searches the field, floor and bins, and then follows hospital policy, which may include imaging.

The event is documented.

Why it matters

Short cases help you practise thinking through a problem. In real situations, follow your hospital's protocol and call for senior help.

Remember

Do not close until it is resolved.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about snapshot: swab count is wrong?

Do not close until it is resolved.

snapshot-the-pale-post-op-patient.title: Snapshot: the pale post-op patient
snapshot-the-pale-post-op-patient.caption: A patient is pale, restless and has a fast pulse hours after surgery.
snapshot-the-pale-post-op-patient.body:
In short: A patient is pale, restless and has a fast pulse hours after surgery.

Hidden Bleeding

A patient is pale, restless and has a fast pulse hours after surgery. Think of bleeding.

Call for senior help, give oxygen, check the wound and drains, and prepare for fluid and blood replacement.

Why it matters

Short cases help you practise thinking through a problem. In real situations, follow your hospital's protocol and call for senior help.

Remember

Fast pulse can mean bleeding.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about snapshot: the pale post-op patient?

Fast pulse can mean bleeding.

snapshot-chest-pain-in-recovery.title: Snapshot: chest pain in recovery
snapshot-chest-pain-in-recovery.caption: Chest pain with shortness of breath after surgery could be a heart event or a blood clot in the lung.
snapshot-chest-pain-in-recovery.body:
In short: Chest pain with shortness of breath after surgery could be a heart event or a blood clot in the lung.

Urgent Assessment

Chest pain with shortness of breath after surgery could be a heart event or a blood clot in the lung.

Call for help, give oxygen, monitor and prepare for ECG and further tests as the team directs.

Short cases help you practise thinking through a problem. In real situations, follow your hospital's protocol and call for senior help.

Remember

Call for help early.

Call for help early.

snapshot-skin-burn-after-surgery.caption: A patient has a burn under the diathermy pad.
snapshot-skin-burn-after-surgery.body:
In short: A patient has a burn under the diathermy pad.

What Happened?

A patient has a burn under the diathermy pad. Review the pad placement, contact and skin state.

Report the incident, treat the burn and record the details so the cause can be reviewed.

Why it matters

Short cases help you practise thinking through a problem. In real situations, follow your hospital's protocol and call for senior help.

Remember

Report every burn.

Report every burn.

snapshot-child-with-rising-heat.caption: A child's temperature and heart rate rise quickly during anaesthesia.
snapshot-child-with-rising-heat.body:
In short: A child's temperature and heart rate rise quickly during anaesthesia.

Think Early

A child's temperature and heart rate rise quickly during anaesthesia. Consider overheating, infection and rare causes such as malignant hyperthermia.

Call for senior help, stop triggering agents if suspected and cool the child.

Why it matters

Short cases help you practise thinking through a problem. In real situations, follow your hospital's protocol and call for senior help.

Remember

Tell the anaesthetist at once.

Check yourself

Tell the anaesthetist at once.

snapshot-needlestick-injury.caption: A scrub nurse is pricked by a used needle.
snapshot-needlestick-injury.body:
In short: A scrub nurse is pricked by a used needle.

First Steps

A scrub nurse is pricked by a used needle. Let the wound bleed gently, wash with soap and water, report immediately and attend for assessment and preventive treatment if indicated.

Document the incident.

Why it matters

Short cases help you practise thinking through a problem. In real situations, follow your hospital's protocol and call for senior help.

Remember

Wash, report, assess.

Check yourself

Wash, report, assess.

snapshot-missing-consent-form.title: Snapshot: missing consent form
snapshot-missing-consent-form.caption: A patient arrives without a signed consent form for a planned operation.
snapshot-missing-consent-form.body:
In short: A patient arrives without a signed consent form for a planned operation.

Stop The List

A patient arrives without a signed consent form for a planned operation. Do not proceed.

Inform the surgical team, confirm the patient's wishes and obtain valid consent unless it is an emergency under local rules.

Why it matters

Short cases help you practise thinking through a problem. In real situations, follow your hospital's protocol and call for senior help.

Remember

No valid consent, no operation.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about snapshot: missing consent form?

No valid consent, no operation.

snapshot-a-patient-who-looks-unwell.title: Snapshot: a patient who looks unwell
snapshot-a-patient-who-looks-unwell.caption: A recovery patient looks unwell although observations look near normal.
snapshot-a-patient-who-looks-unwell.body:
In short: A recovery patient looks unwell although observations look near normal.

Trust Your Concern

A recovery patient looks unwell although observations look near normal. Many serious problems show early as a feeling that something is wrong.

Recheck, escalate and give clear details of your concern.

Why it matters

Short cases help you practise thinking through a problem. In real situations, follow your hospital's protocol and call for senior help.

Remember

Escalate worry as well as numbers.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about snapshot: a patient who looks unwell?

Escalate worry as well as numbers.

why-we-crossmatch.title: Why we crossmatch
why-we-crossmatch.caption: Crossmatching mixes the patient's blood with donor blood to check for a reaction before transfusion.
why-we-crossmatch.body:
In short: Crossmatching mixes the patient's blood with donor blood to check for a reaction before transfusion.

Blood Compatibility

Crossmatching mixes the patient's blood with donor blood to check for a reaction before transfusion. It helps prevent serious transfusion reactions.

Group and save is a lighter test for when blood may be needed.

Why it matters

Tests help diagnose problems and plan safe care. Knowing what each test shows explains why the team orders it.

Remember

Check before blood goes in.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about why we crossmatch?

Check before blood goes in.

inr-and-prothrombin-time.title: INR and prothrombin time
inr-and-prothrombin-time.caption: INR measures how long blood takes to clot and is often used for patients taking warfarin or with liver disease.
inr-and-prothrombin-time.body:
In short: INR measures how long blood takes to clot and is often used for patients taking warfarin or with liver disease.

Clotting Tests

INR measures how long blood takes to clot and is often used for patients taking warfarin or with liver disease.

A high INR means a higher bleeding risk, so results matter before surgery and some blocks.

Why it matters

Tests help diagnose problems and plan safe care. Knowing what each test shows explains why the team orders it.

Remember

High INR means more bleeding risk.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about inr and prothrombin time?

High INR means more bleeding risk.

platelet-count.title: Platelet count
platelet-count.caption: Platelets help form clots.
platelet-count.body:
In short: Platelets help form clots.

Clot-Forming Cells

Platelets help form clots. A low count increases the risk of bleeding, and the safe level for surgery depends on the type of operation.

Some drugs affect platelet function even when the count is normal.

Why it matters

Tests help diagnose problems and plan safe care. Knowing what each test shows explains why the team orders it.

Remember

Count and function both matter.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about platelet count?

Count and function both matter.

chest-x-ray-basics.title: Chest X-ray basics
chest-x-ray-basics.caption: A chest X-ray can show lung disease, fluid, a collapsed lung, heart size and the position of tubes and lines.
chest-x-ray-basics.body:
In short: A chest X-ray can show lung disease, fluid, a collapsed lung, heart size and the position of tubes and lines.

What It Shows

A chest X-ray can show lung disease, fluid, a collapsed lung, heart size and the position of tubes and lines.

It gives a flat image, so some problems are missed. Clinical assessment is still needed.

Why it matters

Tests help diagnose problems and plan safe care. Knowing what each test shows explains why the team orders it.

Remember

Match the picture to the patient.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about chest x-ray basics?

Match the picture to the patient.

ecg-what-it-records.title: ECG: what it records
ecg-what-it-records.caption: An ECG records the electrical activity of the heart.
ecg-what-it-records.body:
In short: An ECG records the electrical activity of the heart.

Heart Electricity

An ECG records the electrical activity of the heart. It can show abnormal rhythm, signs of heart muscle damage and changes caused by electrolyte problems.

It does not show how well the heart pumps.

Why it matters

Tests help diagnose problems and plan safe care. Knowing what each test shows explains why the team orders it.

Remember

An ECG shows rhythm, not pump.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about ecg: what it records?

An ECG shows rhythm, not pump.

echo-heart-ultrasound.title: Echo: heart ultrasound
echo-heart-ultrasound.caption: An echo uses ultrasound to show heart size, valves and pumping function.
echo-heart-ultrasound.body:
In short: An echo uses ultrasound to show heart size, valves and pumping function.

Ultrasound Of The Heart

An echo uses ultrasound to show heart size, valves and pumping function. It does not use radiation.

It helps plan anaesthesia in patients with known or suspected heart disease.

Why it matters

Tests help diagnose problems and plan safe care. Knowing what each test shows explains why the team orders it.

Remember

Safe, painless and useful.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about echo: heart ultrasound?

Safe, painless and useful.

urine-dipstick.title: Urine dipstick
urine-dipstick.caption: A urine dipstick can detect blood, protein, glucose, ketones and signs of infection.
urine-dipstick.body:
In short: A urine dipstick can detect blood, protein, glucose, ketones and signs of infection.

Quick Bedside Test

A urine dipstick can detect blood, protein, glucose, ketones and signs of infection. It is quick but not perfect, so results are interpreted with symptoms.

Collect a clean sample when infection is suspected.

Why it matters

Tests help diagnose problems and plan safe care. Knowing what each test shows explains why the team orders it.

Remember

A screening tool, not a final answer.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about urine dipstick?

A screening tool, not a final answer.

sputum-and-wound-swabs.title: Sputum and wound swabs
sputum-and-wound-swabs.caption: Take samples before antibiotics when possible, use the correct container and label it with the patient's details and site.
sputum-and-wound-swabs.body:
In short: Take samples before antibiotics when possible, use the correct container and label it with the patient's details and site.

Collect Properly

Take samples before antibiotics when possible, use the correct container and label it with the patient's details and site.

Send promptly, because delay can change the result.

Tests help diagnose problems and plan safe care. Knowing what each test shows explains why the team orders it.

Remember

A good sample gives a good result.

A good sample gives a good result.

histology-vs-cytology.caption: Histology studies a piece of tissue.
histology-vs-cytology.body:
In short: Histology studies a piece of tissue.

Tissue Or Cells

Histology studies a piece of tissue. Cytology studies individual cells, such as from fluid or a swab.

Both help diagnose cancer and other diseases.

Why it matters

Tests help diagnose problems and plan safe care. Knowing what each test shows explains why the team orders it.

Remember

Label and send specimens carefully.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about histology vs cytology?

Label and send specimens carefully.

rapid-malaria-test.title: Rapid malaria test
rapid-malaria-test.caption: Rapid diagnostic tests detect malaria antigens from a finger-prick sample and give a result in minutes.
rapid-malaria-test.body:

Chart observations so that trends are clear.

Put things back where they belong.

preventive-maintenance-schedules.body:

Check Before It Fails

Preventive maintenance means servicing equipment on a planned schedule instead of waiting for a fault. Records show when each item was last checked and when it is next due.

Tagging equipment with the service date helps theatre staff spot items that are overdue.

Why it matters

Understanding the basic science behind theatre machines helps staff use them safely, spot problems early and communicate well with biomedical engineers.

Remember

Overdue service means do not rely on it.

central-and-peripheral-nerves.caption: The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord.
central-and-peripheral-nerves.body:
In short: The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord.

Two Main Parts

The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord. The peripheral nervous system is the nerves that carry messages between the body and the centre.

Anaesthesia and nerve blocks work by changing how these messages travel.

Why it matters

Anaesthesia works on the nervous system, and many surgical risks involve nerves or the brain. A clear grasp of structure and function improves monitoring and safety.

Remember

Brain and cord at the centre, nerves outside.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about central and peripheral nerves?

In short: A quick list on kidney functions in brief: Filter blood and remove waste; Control water and salt balance.

Kidney functions in brief

  • Filter blood and remove waste
  • Control water and salt balance
  • Help control blood pressure
  • Make erythropoietin for red cells
  • Activate vitamin D

Why it matters

The kidneys control fluid, salts and drug clearance. Theatre events like bleeding and low pressure can injure them, so these basics guide safe care.

Remember

The kidneys do far more than make urine.

Check yourself

List the points covered under "Kidney functions in brief".

resting-and-action-potentials.title: Resting and action potentials
resting-and-action-potentials.caption: Nerve cells keep a charge difference across their membrane at rest.
resting-and-action-potentials.body:
In short: Nerve cells keep a charge difference across their membrane at rest.

Nerves Use Electricity

Nerve cells keep a charge difference across their membrane at rest. When a stimulus is strong enough, sodium channels open and an electrical signal runs along the nerve.

Local anaesthetics block these sodium channels so the signal cannot pass.

Why it matters

Nerves, pain pathways and the brain are the targets of anaesthesia and analgesia, so understanding them explains how and why our drugs work.

Remember

Block the sodium channel, block the signal.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about resting and action potentials?

Block the sodium channel, block the signal.

typhoid-fever-basics.caption: Typhoid spreads through contaminated food and water.
typhoid-fever-basics.body:
In short: Typhoid spreads through contaminated food and water.

Salmonella Typhi

Typhoid spreads through contaminated food and water. It causes prolonged fever, headache, abdominal pain and sometimes constipation or diarrhoea.

Complications can include gut bleeding or perforation, which may need emergency surgery.

Why it matters

Malaria, typhoid, schistosomiasis and other tropical illnesses are commonly seen in East Africa, and they affect fitness for anaesthesia and surgery and complicate emergencies.

Remember

Clean water and handwashing prevent it.

Check yourself

Clean water and handwashing prevent it.

dengue-and-chikungunya.caption: Both are spread by Aedes mosquitoes and cause fever and joint or muscle pain.
dengue-and-chikungunya.body:
In short: Both are spread by Aedes mosquitoes and cause fever and joint or muscle pain.

Mosquito-Borne Fevers

Both are spread by Aedes mosquitoes and cause fever and joint or muscle pain. Dengue may cause bleeding or a drop in blood pressure in severe cases.

Testing and local guidance decide care. Avoid aspirin and anti-inflammatory drugs unless advised.

Why it matters

Malaria, typhoid, schistosomiasis and other tropical illnesses are commonly seen in East Africa, and they affect fitness for anaesthesia and surgery and complicate emergencies.

Remember

Fever plus bleeding signs needs urgent review.

signs-of-undernutrition-in-children.title: Signs of undernutrition in children
signs-of-undernutrition-in-children.caption: Poor growth, thin arms, swollen feet, thin or pale hair and a lack of energy can signal undernutrition.
signs-of-undernutrition-in-children.body:

Spot It Early

Poor growth, thin arms, swollen feet, thin or pale hair and a lack of energy can signal undernutrition. A mid-upper arm band and weight-for-height checks help classify it.

Early feeding support and referral reduce complications.

Why it matters

Nutritional state strongly affects surgical risk, wound healing and recovery, and community nutrition work addresses the causes upstream.

Remember

Measure, do not guess.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about signs of undernutrition in children?

Measure, do not guess.

choosing-a-fluid-for-a-patient.title: Choosing a fluid for a patient
choosing-a-fluid-for-a-patient.caption: Balanced crystalloids and normal saline are common choices for replacing fluid loss.
choosing-a-fluid-for-a-patient.body:
In short: Balanced crystalloids and normal saline are common choices for replacing fluid loss.

Match Fluid To Need

Balanced crystalloids and normal saline are common choices for replacing fluid loss. Dextrose solutions give mostly water and some energy.

The choice depends on the cause of loss, blood tests and the patient's heart and kidney function.

Why it matters

Almost every theatre patient has IV access and fluids. Safe cannulation, fluid choice and line care prevent infection and harm.

Prescribe fluid like a drug.

common-drug-side-effects-vs-allergy.body:

Not Always Allergy

Side effects are known effects such as nausea or drowsiness. Allergy is an immune reaction with rash, swelling, wheeze or low blood pressure.

Record exactly what happened, as wrong allergy labels limit treatment.

Why it matters

Reactions to drugs and materials can be sudden and life-threatening. Early recognition, treatment and reporting save lives.

Remember

Record what the reaction was.

Record what the reaction was.

Photos And Privacy

Photographs or recordings of patients should follow hospital policy and need consent, even when the face is not visible. Personal phones are not secure places for patient images.

Remove identifiers from teaching material.

Why it matters

Theatre staff care for people at their most vulnerable. Knowing consent, confidentiality, records and professional limits protects patients and keeps your own practice safe.

No consent, no picture.

Arrive early, dress neatly and listen carefully to each question before answering.

A good interview shows safety awareness, teamwork and reliability as well as knowledge. Preparation helps you present your real strengths clearly.

A welcoming theatre is safer because people ask questions instead of guessing.

Surgery is a team activity, and most errors involve communication rather than technical skill. Good teamwork keeps patients safe and workplaces pleasant.

A good welcome prevents mistakes.

Blood From The Gut

Vomiting blood or passing black or bloody stool signals gut bleeding. Priorities are airway, breathing, circulation, two large IV lines and blood tests with crossmatch.

Endoscopy or surgery may be needed to find and stop the source.

Why it matters

Surgical emergencies need quick recognition, resuscitation and teamwork. Theatre staff who understand the typical presentations prepare rooms, blood and equipment faster.

Resuscitate while searching for the cause.

A Limb Without Blood

A sudden blocked artery can cause a painful, pale, cold limb with weak or absent pulses and possible numbness or weakness.

It is a surgical emergency, as muscle and nerves begin to suffer within hours.

Why it matters

Surgical emergencies need quick recognition, resuscitation and teamwork. Theatre staff who understand the typical presentations prepare rooms, blood and equipment faster.

Remember

post-operative-urinary-retention.title: Post-operative urinary retention
post-operative-urinary-retention.caption: Pain, drugs, spinal anaesthesia and surgery near the pelvis can stop the bladder emptying.
post-operative-urinary-retention.body:
In short: Pain, drugs, spinal anaesthesia and surgery near the pelvis can stop the bladder emptying.

Cannot Pass Urine

Pain, drugs, spinal anaesthesia and surgery near the pelvis can stop the bladder emptying. Signs are discomfort, a swollen lower abdomen and no urine passed.

A bladder scan or catheter relieves the problem.

Why it matters

Many serious problems appear after the patient leaves theatre. Early recognition and reporting by the whole team can prevent harm and save lives.

Remember

Check the bladder before blaming pain.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about post-operative urinary retention?

Check the bladder before blaming pain.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

secondary-haemorrhage.title: Secondary haemorrhage
secondary-haemorrhage.caption: Bleeding that begins days after surgery is often linked with infection or a slipping tie.
secondary-haemorrhage.body:
In short: Bleeding that begins days after surgery is often linked with infection or a slipping tie.

Late Bleeding

Bleeding that begins days after surgery is often linked with infection or a slipping tie. It may soak dressings or cause a sudden fall in blood pressure.

Apply pressure, call for help and prepare for resuscitation.

Why it matters

Many serious problems appear after the patient leaves theatre. Early recognition and reporting by the whole team can prevent harm and save lives.

Remember

Bleeding can return days later.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about secondary haemorrhage?

Bleeding can return days later.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

fever-after-surgery.title: Fever after surgery
fever-after-surgery.caption: A quick list on fever after surgery: Early: atelectasis or inflammation after surgery; Days 3 to 5: urinary or chest infection.
fever-after-surgery.body:
In short: A quick list on fever after surgery: Early: atelectasis or inflammation after surgery; Days 3 to 5: urinary or chest infection.

Fever after surgery

  • Early: atelectasis or inflammation after surgery
  • Days 3 to 5: urinary or chest infection
  • Days 5 to 7: wound infection or line sepsis
  • Later: abscess or deep infection

Why it matters

Many serious problems appear after the patient leaves theatre. Early recognition and reporting by the whole team can prevent harm and save lives.

Remember

Look for the cause, not just the number.

Check yourself

List the points covered under "Fever after surgery".

Early: atelectasis or inflammation after surgery; Days 3 to 5: urinary or chest infection; Days 5 to 7: wound infection or line sepsis; Later: abscess or deep infection.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

splinting-a-fracture.title: Splinting a fracture
splinting-a-fracture.caption: A quick list on splinting a fracture: Check pulses, feeling and movement first; Support the joints above and below.
splinting-a-fracture.body:
In short: A quick list on splinting a fracture: Check pulses, feeling and movement first; Support the joints above and below.

Splinting a fracture

  • Check pulses, feeling and movement first
  • Support the joints above and below
  • Pad bony points
  • Re-check circulation after splinting

Why it matters

Road traffic crashes and falls make fractures a daily reality. Safe handling, splinting and recognising limb-threatening problems protect function.

Remember

Immobilise, then recheck.

Check yourself

List the points covered under "Splinting a fracture".

Check pulses, feeling and movement first; Support the joints above and below; Pad bony points; Re-check circulation after splinting.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

dehydration-in-children.title: Dehydration in children
dehydration-in-children.caption: Sunken eyes, dry mouth, fewer wet nappies, lethargy and fast breathing suggest dehydration.
dehydration-in-children.body:
In short: Sunken eyes, dry mouth, fewer wet nappies, lethargy and fast breathing suggest dehydration.

Watch The Fluids

Sunken eyes, dry mouth, fewer wet nappies, lethargy and fast breathing suggest dehydration. Oral rehydration solution is the first-line treatment for most children.

Severe cases need IV fluids and urgent care.

Why it matters

Children deteriorate quickly and need equipment and doses matched to size. Calm, prepared teams give them the best chance.

Remember

Small, frequent sips of ORS.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about dehydration in children?

Small, frequent sips of ORS.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

heat-illness.title: Heat illness
heat-illness.caption: Heat exhaustion causes heavy sweating, headache and weakness.
heat-illness.body:
In short: Heat exhaustion causes heavy sweating, headache and weakness.

Heat Exhaustion And Stroke

Heat exhaustion causes heavy sweating, headache and weakness. Heat stroke includes confusion and a very high temperature and is life-threatening.

Move to a cool place, remove extra clothing and cool the body. Call for help.

Why it matters

Heat, cold, water, bites and stings produce emergencies that arrive at casualty and sometimes theatre. Simple first aid greatly improves outcomes.

Remember

Confusion in the heat is an emergency.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about heat illness?

Confusion in the heat is an emergency.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

drowning-first-aid.title: Drowning first aid
drowning-first-aid.caption: Make sure the scene is safe before reaching the person.
drowning-first-aid.body:
In short: Make sure the scene is safe before reaching the person.

Rescue Safely

Make sure the scene is safe before reaching the person. Remove them from the water and check breathing.

Because the problem is lack of oxygen, start with rescue breaths if the person is not breathing, then compressions. Call for help.

Why it matters

Heat, cold, water, bites and stings produce emergencies that arrive at casualty and sometimes theatre. Simple first aid greatly improves outcomes.

Remember

Oxygen first for drowning.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about drowning first aid?

Oxygen first for drowning.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

secondary-triage.title: Secondary triage
secondary-triage.caption: After the first quick sort, patients are re-assessed in a calmer place.
secondary-triage.body:
In short: After the first quick sort, patients are re-assessed in a calmer place.

Second Look

After the first quick sort, patients are re-assessed in a calmer place. Their condition may have changed, and some need to move to a higher priority.

Re-triage regularly and record each change.

Why it matters

Disasters, crashes and conflicts can overwhelm a hospital. Theatre teams must understand triage, plans and damage control to work well under pressure.

Remember

Triage is repeated, not once.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about secondary triage?

Triage is repeated, not once.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

atelectasis-vs-pneumonia.title: Atelectasis vs pneumonia
atelectasis-vs-pneumonia.caption: Atelectasis is a partly collapsed area of lung and often appears in the first days after surgery.
atelectasis-vs-pneumonia.body:
In short: Atelectasis is a partly collapsed area of lung and often appears in the first days after surgery.

Chest Problems After Surgery

Atelectasis is a partly collapsed area of lung and often appears in the first days after surgery. Pneumonia is an infection and may follow when secretions are not cleared.

Deep breathing, coughing and early walking reduce the risk of both.

Why it matters

Many serious problems appear after the patient leaves theatre. Early recognition and reporting by the whole team can prevent harm and save lives.

Remember

Keep the lungs working after surgery.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about atelectasis vs pneumonia?

Keep the lungs working after surgery.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

taste-and-smell-pathways.title: Taste and smell pathways
taste-and-smell-pathways.caption: Smell uses nerve endings high in the nose that connect to the olfactory nerve.
taste-and-smell-pathways.body:
In short: Smell uses nerve endings high in the nose that connect to the olfactory nerve.

Chemical Senses

Smell uses nerve endings high in the nose that connect to the olfactory nerve. Taste buds on the tongue send signals through the facial and glossopharyngeal nerves.

Smell and taste work together, so a blocked nose can make food seem bland.

Why it matters

Eye and ear surgery have special anaesthetic and positioning needs, and reflexes from these organs affect the heart. Basic anatomy explains why.

Remember

Smell and taste work as a pair.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about taste and smell pathways?

Smell and taste work as a pair.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

uterine-inversion.title: Uterine inversion
uterine-inversion.caption: Uterine inversion is a rare complication after birth in which the womb turns inside out.
uterine-inversion.body:
In short: Uterine inversion is a rare complication after birth in which the womb turns inside out.

Uterus Turned Inside Out

Uterine inversion is a rare complication after birth in which the womb turns inside out. It can cause severe bleeding and shock.

Call for help, resuscitate and prepare for urgent replacement as directed by the senior team.

Why it matters

Obstetric emergencies can threaten two lives at once, and caesarean sections are a major part of theatre work. Teamwork and speed are essential.

Remember

Call for help and resuscitate at once.

Check yourself

What is the main thing to remember about uterine inversion?

Call for help and resuscitate at once.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

a-life-becoming.title: A Life Becoming
a-life-becoming.summary: A memoir in progress — faith, family, and figuring himself out. Not a success story, in his own words: 'just the truth worth becoming.'
a-life-becoming.excerpt: "You will be. Not because everything will work out perfectly. But because you'll learn that you're strong — stronger than you think, right now."

notes-from-the-sterile-field.title: Notes from the Sterile Field
notes-from-the-sterile-field.summary: A first-hand account of training as a Perioperative Theatre Technologist in Kenya — the attachment, the mistakes, the cases that stayed with him, and what nobody tells students before they scrub in for the first time.
notes-from-the-sterile-field.excerpt: "Nobody tells you the hardest part isn't the instruments. It's standing still, hands ready, while someone else's whole body depends on you not flinching."

the-theatre-companion.title: The Theatre Companion
the-theatre-companion.summary: A study companion for Perioperative Theatre Technology students — anatomy mnemonics, safety checklists, and OT quizzes, pulled together from his own content and study notes into one reference.
the-theatre-companion.excerpt: "Everything here started as a graphic that took me thirty minutes to make and would have taken three hours to find in a textbook."

the-smooth-sailing.title: The Smooth Sailing
the-smooth-sailing.summary: A practical handbook on surviving a demanding clinical diploma program — the adjustment, the pressure, the parts nobody prepares you for before the first attachment.
the-smooth-sailing.excerpt: "Stepping into a clinical diploma is like embarking on an exhilarating adventure filled with opportunities and challenges — most of them scheduled for 6 a.m."

correction.title: Correction
correction.summary: A slow, personal book about life's unresolved questions — for anyone who survived childhood, endured setbacks, questioned their path, and still got up the next day.
correction.excerpt: "The first forty years of life give us the text; the next thirty supply the commentary." — Schopenhauer, quoted, then immediately argued with.

faq023.answer: Perioperative Theatre Technology covers everything around a surgical procedure — pre-op prep, intra-op support, sterile technique, and post-op care. It's what my diploma is in.

faq024.answer: My field attachment was at Likuyani Sub-County Hospital, Feb–Apr 2024 — scrubbed for c-section cases, ran sterilisation, learned the WHO checklist inside out.

faq025.answer: "Oh Oh Oh To Touch And Feel Very Good Velvet AH" — the classic cranial nerves mnemonic. Full breakdown on the Content page.

faq026.answer: Three phases: Sign In (before anaesthesia), Time Out (before incision), Sign Out (before leaving theatre). There's a full graphic and a downloadable PDF on Materials.

faq027.answer: Steam autoclave is the most common method for surgical instruments — pressurized steam at 121–134°C. Full breakdown on the Content page and a study PDF on Materials.

faq028.answer: I don't always test my code, but when I do, I do it in production. (I make more medical content than jokes, to be fair.)

faq029.answer: Introvert, calm under pressure. Talks more once you land on a topic I care about — usually anatomy or theatre tech.

faq032.answer: Every blog post, content page, and book page has a QR code (bottom of the page) linking back to that exact page — generated live in your browser, not a static image.

faq038.answer: DRSABCD — Danger, Response, Send for help, Airway, Breathing, CPR, Defibrillation. Full breakdown on the Materials page.

faq039.answer: Positioning injuries are a real risk in theatre — lithotomy risks the common peroneal nerve, lateral decubitus risks the brachial plexus, prone risks eye/face pressure. Full graphic on the Content page.

faq040.answer: Eight carpal bones in two rows: Scaphoid, Lunate, Triquetrum, Pisiform (proximal); Trapezium, Trapezoid, Capitate, Hamate (distal). Full graphic on the Content page.

faq041.answer: Full PPE in theatre typically means cap, mask, gown, gloves, and eye protection where indicated. See the Content page for the full breakdown.

faq042.answer: Surgical hand scrub, then sterile gown, then sterile gloves — in that order. Several posts on the Content page walk through the technique step by step.

faq043.answer: Four main types: hypovolaemic, cardiogenic, distributive, and obstructive. Full graphic on the Content page.

faq044.answer: There's a full graphic on the Content page covering the main fracture types — worth a look if you're studying this.

faq045.answer: O- is the universal donor, AB+ is the universal recipient. Full compatibility chart on the Content page.

faq046.answer: Normal adult ranges roughly: heart rate 60-100 bpm, temperature 36.1-37.2°C, respiratory rate 12-20/min. Full graphic on the Content page.

faq047.answer: Diathermy uses electrical current to cut tissue or stop bleeding during surgery — one of the most-used tools in the OT. Content page has the full graphic.

faq048.answer: Specimen handling is all about double identification and clear lab communication — mislabeling is one of the most preventable theatre errors. Full graphic on Content.

faq049.answer: Biomedical waste segregation follows a 4-bin, color-coded WHO standard. Full breakdown on the Content page.

faq050.answer: The fire triangle in theatre: fuel (drapes, prep solution), oxidizer (oxygen-enriched air), and ignition (diathermy/laser). Full graphic on the Content page and a study PDF on Materials.

faq051.answer: At the cyber café: printing & photocopying, typing & document formatting, eCitizen/KRA returns filing, and basic computer training packages.

faq052.answer: A Life Becoming — my memoir in progress. Faith, family, and figuring myself out. Not a success story, just the truth worth becoming.

faq053.answer: The Theatre Companion and Notes from the Sterile Field are two of my books in progress, both built directly around Perioperative Theatre Technology. Sneak peeks on the Writing page.

faq055.answer: Nosocomial means hospital-acquired — infections picked up during a hospital stay rather than brought in by the patient. Study PDF on Materials covers this in depth.

glossary.definition: The absence of harmful microorganisms — the whole goal of sterile technique.
A surgical connection made between two tubular structures, like two ends of bowel.
Removal of dead or damaged tissue from a wound to help it heal.
Using electrical current to cut tissue or stop bleeding during surgery.
Stopping blood flow — one of the surgeon's constant jobs mid-procedure.
A thread used to tie off a blood vessel or duct.
The membrane lining the abdominal cavity and covering most abdominal organs.
A surgical incision into the abdominal wall to access the abdominal cavity.
Keyhole surgery using small incisions and a camera instead of one large cut.
A life-threatening response to infection spreading through the body.
Loss of sensation, induced deliberately to allow surgery without pain.
Pain relief, without necessarily causing loss of consciousness.
Insufficient oxygen reaching the body's tissues.
Low oxygen levels specifically in the blood.
An abnormally fast heart rate, typically over 100 beats per minute in adults.
An abnormally slow heart rate, typically under 60 beats per minute in adults.
Abnormally low blood pressure.
Abnormally high blood pressure, sustained over time.
The medical term for vomiting.
Difficult or laboured breathing.
A temporary pause in breathing.
A bluish tinge to skin or lips caused by low oxygen levels.
Swelling caused by excess fluid trapped in body tissues.
An abnormal collection of fluid in a body cavity.
A localized collection of blood outside blood vessels.
Death of body tissue, often due to lack of blood supply.
Restricted blood supply to tissue, causing a shortage of oxygen.
A blockage in a blood vessel caused by a clot or foreign material that has travelled there.
The formation of a blood clot inside a blood vessel.
The passage of blood through the vessels of an organ or tissue.
A process that destroys all forms of microbial life, including spores.
A process that reduces microorganisms to a safe level, without necessarily killing spores.
A window-like opening, such as in a surgical drape.
Inserting a thin tube into a vein or body cavity to give fluids or drugs.
Inserting a tube into the airway to help a patient breathe.
Removing a breathing tube once a patient can breathe unaided.
Treatment given to prevent a disease or complication before it occurs.
A specific reason NOT to use a treatment because it could cause harm.
An additional condition existing alongside a patient's primary condition.
Examining by touch, feeling for size, texture, or tenderness.
Listening to internal sounds of the body, usually with a stethoscope.
Tapping on the body to assess the underlying structures by sound.
The reopening or splitting of a surgical wound along the suture line.
Protrusion of internal organs through a wound opening — a surgical emergency.
Severe blood loss, to the point of being life-threatening.
The body's ability to maintain a stable internal environment.
A condition with no identifiable cause.
A condition caused inadvertently by medical treatment itself.
Originating in a hospital — used especially for hospital-acquired infections.
Care focused on comfort and symptom relief rather than cure.
Surgical removal of the appendix.
Surgical removal of the gallbladder.
Surgical removal of the uterus.
Delivery of a baby through an incision in the abdomen and uterus.
A surgical incision into the chest wall.
A surgical opening made in the skull.
A surgical opening in the windpipe to allow breathing.
A surgical opening connecting the colon to the abdominal wall.
Removal of a tissue sample for laboratory examination.
Surgical removal of tissue or an organ by cutting.
A cut made in the skin or tissue during surgery.
A stitch used to close a wound or incision.
An area kept free of microorganisms for use during a procedure.
The team member who manages instruments and assists the surgeon directly.
The non-sterile team member who fetches supplies and manages theatre flow.
A machine that sterilizes equipment using pressurized steam.
Practices that prevent contamination of a sterile field or patient.
A microorganism capable of causing disease.
Reducing microbes on living tissue, such as the skin, before surgery.
Sorting patients by urgency so the most critical are treated first.
A severe, potentially life-threatening allergic reaction.
A rare, dangerous reaction to certain anaesthetic agents causing high temperature and rigidity.
Inhaling fluid or stomach contents into the lungs.
Partial or complete collapse of a lung or part of it.
Air trapped in the space between the lung and chest wall.
Blood collecting in the space between the lung and chest wall.
Abnormal buildup of fluid in the abdomen.
Yellowing of the skin and eyes due to excess bilirubin.
Temporary paralysis of the bowel after surgery, stopping normal movement.
Inflammation of the peritoneum, often due to infection.
A collection of pus surrounded by inflamed tissue.
A spreading bacterial infection of the skin and underlying tissue.

about.description: About Ezra Ogombo, content creator and Perioperative Theatre Technology diploma graduate from Matunda, Kenya, making medical education content for Instagram, TikTok and Facebook as @ezraogombo.
about.heading: 24, Kenyan, quiet until provoked by a good idea.
about.intro: Born August 2nd. Grew up around Matunda, Moi's Bridge. Two things run my life right now: theatre technology, and making that world easier to understand for other people.
about.body:
education.log

Diploma in Perioperative Theatre Technology (2023–2025, graduated December 2025; institution listed on my CV). Practical score 78%.

Field attachment — Likuyani Sub-County Hospital, Feb–Apr 2024. Scrubbed for caesarean section cases, ran sterilisation (CSSD), theatre setup and turnover, WHO Surgical Safety Checklist adherence.

Certifications — Quality Improvement (Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust), Basic Life Support, Infection Prevention & Control.

day-job.log

Alongside creating content and looking for theatre practice, I work the front desk at a cyber café — JULO Enterprises. Printing, typing, eCitizen and KRA services, and teaching basic computer skills to walk-in clients. Temporary, but it's kept my tech instincts sharp.

The content side

I turn what I'm learning into short, memorable posts — anatomy mnemonics, OT quizzes, positioning and safety checklists — for Instagram, TikTok, and Facebook. If a concept took me three readings to actually get, there's a good chance it'll take you thirty seconds once I've turned it into a graphic. See the content page.

The theatre side

Perioperative work is precise and mostly invisible — nobody notices the person who made sure the theatre ran smoothly, and that's exactly the appeal. No room for guessing. Every step has a reason.

Also true about me

Introvert. Talks more once you land on the right topic — usually anatomy, sometimes Kenyan history and culture (I'm slowly writing books on both — see the writing page). Coding is a hobby on the side, mostly playing with AI tools for fun — ask me on WhatsApp if you're curious, but it's not the main thing I do.

privacy.title: Privacy — Ezra Ogombo
privacy.description: How this website handles comments, orders, contact messages and anonymous analytics.
privacy.heading: Privacy.
privacy.intro: Short version: only what's needed to run the site, nothing sold.
privacy.body:
What is stored

  • Comments, reactions and shares — the name you type and your comment are saved and shown publicly. Don't post personal details.
  • Contact form — name, email/phone and message are saved so I can reply.
  • Orders for paid materials — name, phone, email, delivery address (WhatsApp/SMS/email) and the M-Pesa message you paste are saved to verify payment and send your file. Only the site admin can read them.
  • Newsletter — your email, only to send updates. Ask and it will be removed.
  • Analytics — anonymous page-view counts (page, day, device type, referring site). No cookies, no tracking across sites; Do-Not-Track is respected.

On your device

Your browser remembers your theme, the name you used to comment and which posts you reacted to (so a like can be undone). Clearing site data removes this.

Third parties

Files are delivered through Google Drive, the database runs on Google Firebase, and PDFs are generated in your browser. Share buttons open the network you choose.

Your requests

To remove a comment, message, order or subscription, email me.
